facts.claim: About 29% of Earth's surface is land and 71% is ocean. Our Natural Earth computation gives 28.7% land, or 29.1% if Antarctic ice shelves are counted as land.
facts.spoken_form: Only about twenty-nine percent of Earth's surface is land. The other seventy-one percent is ocean.
facts.source_title: CIA World Factbook, 'World' entry, Area (archived JSON mirror, Factbook retired Feb 2026); NOAA Ocean Service 'How many oceans are there?'
facts.quote: note: 70.9% of the world's surface is water, 29.1% is land. Also NOAA: "the vast body of water that covers 71 percent of the Earth" (https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/howmanyoceans.html)
facts.caveat: The land share depends on whether ice shelves, the Caspian Sea and lakes count as land. Natural Earth land excludes the ice shelves and the Caspian and includes lakes. Its 28.7% becomes 29.05% once the 0.6M sq mi of Antarctic ice shelves are added. The CIA Factbook was retired in Feb 2026, so cite it as an archived source.

facts.claim: Earth's total land area is about 148.9 million km², or 57.5 million sq mi. The whole surface is 510.1 million km² (196.9 million sq mi).
facts.spoken_form: All the land on Earth adds up to about fifty-seven million square miles.
facts.source_title: CIA World Factbook, 'World' entry, Area (archived JSON mirror)
facts.quote: "total ": 510.072 million sq km ... "land": 148.94 million sq km
facts.caveat: Our Natural Earth polygons give 146.6M km² (56.6M sq mi), or 148.2M km² (57.2M sq mi) with ice shelves. On screen, use the published figure rounded: about 57 million sq mi.

facts.claim: About 68% of Earth's land lies north of the equator. We computed 68.1% from Natural Earth (50m and 10m, 0.025–0.5° grids). It is 67.4% if Antarctic ice shelves count as land. Wikipedia, citing ABC-CLIO 2002, gives 67.3%.
facts.spoken_form: About two-thirds of all land, sixty-eight percent, sits north of the equator.
facts.source_title: Our computation (Natural Earth 50m land, 0.1° equal-weight raster); cross-check: Wikipedia 'Northern Hemisphere' citing Life on Earth (ABC-CLIO, 2002) p.528
facts.quote: COMPUTED: "nh_share_of_land": 0.6807232761926936 (land only); "nh_share": 0.6735971258442854 (land + ice shelves). PUBLISHED: "Its surface is 60.7% water, compared with 80.9% water in the case of the Southern Hemisphere, and it contains 67.3% of Earth's land."
facts.caveat: The figure is 67–68% depending on whether Antarctic ice shelves count as land. Safest spoken forms: 'about two-thirds', or 'sixty-eight percent' with the on-screen note 'Natural Earth data'.

facts.claim: The Northern Hemisphere is about 39% land; the Southern Hemisphere is about 18–19% land. The north therefore holds just over twice as much land as the south (68:32).
facts.spoken_form: The northern half of the planet is about two-fifths land. The southern half is less than one-fifth land, so the north has more than twice as much land.
facts.source_title: Our computation (Natural Earth 50m); cross-check Wikipedia 'Northern Hemisphere'
facts.quote: COMPUTED: "nh_land_frac": 0.39138623190143484, "sh_land_frac": 0.1835702086811029. PUBLISHED: "Its surface is 60.7% water, compared with 80.9% water in the case of the Southern Hemisphere"
facts.caveat: The southern figure rises to about 19% if Antarctic ice shelves count as land, which matches the published 80.9% water.

facts.claim: About 87–88% of humanity lives in the Northern Hemisphere.
facts.spoken_form: And nearly nine in ten people live up there too.
facts.source_title: Wikipedia 'Northern Hemisphere' (computed from World Population Yearbook 2019, 2015 data)
facts.quote: As of 2015, approximately 6.4 billion people live somewhere in the northern hemisphere, which is around 87.0% of the Earth's total human population of 7.3 billion people.
facts.caveat: We did not compute this ourselves; there was no population grid offline. Kummu & Varis 2011 (Applied Geography 31:495) was not accessible to confirm their exact figure, and secondary reports range from 87% to 90%. Say 'nearly nine in ten', never 'ninety percent'.

facts.claim: The 'land hemisphere', the half of the globe holding the most land, is centred on western Europe. Our exact optimum is 40.8°N 1.7°E, in the sea about 32 mi (52 km) SE of Tarragona, Spain. This matches IGN geodesist J.-G. Affholder's modern determination (40.68°N 1.59°E, 'about 50 km SSE of Tarragona'). Older answers are Île Dumet, Brittany (Berget 1913) and Nantes (Boggs 1945). The maximum is extremely flat: any centre from about 39–50°N, 6°W–3°E captures within 0.1 percentage point of the maximum.
facts.spoken_form: Find the half of the planet with the most land, and its centre lands in western Europe, somewhere between Brittany and the coast of Spain.
facts.display: LAND HEMISPHERE: CENTRED ON W. EUROPE
facts.source_title: Affholder, J.-G. (IGN), 'Une nouvelle détermination du pôle des terres émergées', CFC No.176 (June 2003) pp.49–; Berget 1913; Boggs 1945; our computation
facts.quote: "Le centre des terres émergées (pôle Méditerranée) se trouve pour sa part au large de Tarragone, à une cinquantaine de kilomètres au SSE de cette ville." and "Le maximum absolu correspond au pôle Méditerranée, mais la différence relative entre les deux valeurs de S n'est que de 0,04%." COMPUTED: "center_lat": 40.81, "center_lon": 1.705
facts.caveat: The exact spot is not well defined. A centre at Nantes captures 81.19% of land against 81.24% at the optimum. Do not claim a single town 'is' the centre; say 'western Europe' or 'near France and Spain'. Wikipedia cites Affholder as 'Le Monde des Cartes 173–174 (2002)', but the PDF footer reads 'CFC (N°176 – Juin 2003)'.

facts.claim: The land hemisphere contains about 80–81% of all land: 81.2% computed (80.4% with ice shelves). Berget's 1913 measurement gives 80.1% (115.4M of 144.1M km²).
facts.spoken_form: That one half of the globe holds about four-fifths of all the land on Earth.
facts.source_title: Berget, A. (1913) 'Répartition géographique des Océans (détermination du pôle continental)', Annales de l'Institut océanographique t.V fasc.9 (archive.org scan); Wikipedia 'Land and water hemispheres'
facts.quote: "Superficie des terres de l'hémisphère continental,.. 115.403.561 kilomètres carrés." ... "Superficie des terres de l'hémisphère océanique... 28.715.289 kilomètres carrés." Wikipedia: "The land hemisphere contains 80% of the planet's land, but is itself only 47% land." COMPUTED: "share_of_all_land": 0.8124023205711048
facts.caveat: The Berget quote comes from OCR text of the archive.org scan and may contain small OCR errors; the numbers are legible. Say 'about four-fifths'.

facts.claim: Even the land hemisphere is mostly water: about 47% land and 53% water. We computed 46.7% land; Berget 1913 found 45.5% land and 54.5% water.
facts.spoken_form: And here's the kicker. Even that most land-packed half of the planet is still fifty-three percent water.
facts.source_title: Wikipedia 'Land and water hemispheres' (citing Boggs 1945); Berget 1913 p.10; our computation
facts.quote: "However, even in the land hemisphere, the water area still slightly exceeds the land area (with 53 percent water to 47 percent land)." Berget: "Dans l'hémisphère continental, nous avons donc 54,5 p. 100 d'eau et 45,5 p. 100 de terres". COMPUTED: "land_frac_in_land_hemisphere": 0.46709594655655623
facts.caveat: No hemisphere you can draw is majority land. That is a strong, safe line.

facts.claim: The opposite 'water hemisphere' is about 89% water: 89.2% computed (88.6% with ice shelves), Berget 1913 88.7%, Boggs 1945 89%. Its centre is in the Pacific near New Zealand. The classic 1945 centre (47°13′S 178°28′E) is about 45 mi (74 km) from NZ's Bounty Islands and about 170 mi (275 km) from the Antipodes Islands. Our modern optimum puts it about 270 mi east of NZ's North Island.
facts.spoken_form: Now flip the globe over. The opposite half is eighty-nine percent water, centred in the empty Pacific just off New Zealand.
facts.source_title: Wikipedia 'Land and water hemispheres' (citing Boggs, S.W. 1945, 'This Hemisphere', Journal of Geography 44(9):345–355); Berget 1913
facts.quote: "The water hemisphere is approximately 89 percent water (almost all pertaining to the World Ocean), 6 percent dry land and 5 percent polar ice cap." and "located at 47°13′S 178°28′E (near New Zealand's Bounty Islands in the Pacific Ocean)". Berget: "dans l'hémisphère océanique, nous avons 88,7 p. 100 d'eau et 11,3 p. 100 ... seulement de terres" COMPUTED: "water_frac_in_water_hemisphere": 0.8921395059740185
facts.caveat: BRIEF CORRECTION: the centre is NOT at the Antipodes Islands. The 1945 centre is nearest the Bounty Islands, and the modern optimum is further north-east. Say 'southeast of New Zealand' or 'near New Zealand'. Berget's own line: the water hemisphere holds 'nine times more water than land'.

facts.claim: Only about 13% of Earth's land has land directly opposite it on the far side of the planet. We computed 13.07% on Natural Earth 50m at 0.1°. Across 110m/50m/10m data and 0.025–0.5° grids it ranges from 13.0% to 13.3%, and reaches 13.5% if ice shelves count as land. WorldAtlas (2017) gives about 15%.
facts.spoken_form: Of all the land on Earth, only about one-eighth has land on the opposite side of the planet.
facts.display: ONLY 13% OF LAND HAS LAND OPPOSITE
facts.source_title: Our computation (scripts/full.py, basic.py; Natural Earth public domain); cross-check WorldAtlas, Sawe 2017 'What Is An Antipode In Geography?'
facts.quote: COMPUTED: "land_with_antipodal_land_frac_of_land": 0.13065859249431155 (50m, 0.1°); 0.1310141172055747 (10m, 0.025°). PUBLISHED: "About 15% of the territorial land is antipodal to another land"
facts.caveat: Every variant we ran gives 13.0–13.5%, so the published 15% looks a little high, and its method is not stated. Say 'about one in eight' or 'about thirteen percent', not fifteen.

facts.claim: Land sits opposite land on only about 3.8% of Earth's total surface (3.9% with ice shelves), about 7.4 million sq mi counting both sides. Published estimates: about 3% (Spilhaus 1991) and 4.4% (WorldAtlas 2017).
facts.spoken_form: Put another way, less than four percent of the planet's surface is land with land directly underneath it on the far side.
facts.source_title: Our computation; Spilhaus, A. (1991) Atlas of the World with Geophysical Boundaries, American Philosophical Society, p.2 (via Wikipedia 'Antipodes on Earth' citation); WorldAtlas 2017
facts.quote: COMPUTED: "land_land_frac_surface": 0.03756149963602683. PUBLISHED: Spilhaus 1991 p.2 (quoted in the Wikipedia citation): "Only about three percent of the surface of the earth is antipodal land." WorldAtlas: "with an approximate representation of about 4.4% of the Earth's surface."
facts.caveat: The brief's 'under 5%' is safe. 'About four percent' is more precise and sits between the two published figures. The Spilhaus quote is second-hand: the Google Books page would not render the text, so we have it via Wikipedia's citation.

facts.claim: If land were scattered at random, independent of what is opposite, about 29% of land (equal to the land fraction) would have land opposite, and land-on-land would cover about 8.3% of the surface. The real values, 13% and 3.8%, are less than half of what chance predicts (ratio 0.45).
facts.spoken_form: If the continents were sprinkled at random, about twenty-nine percent of land would have land on the other side. The real number is thirteen. Less than half what pure chance predicts.
facts.source_title: Probability identity plus our computation
facts.quote: COMPUTED: "land_frac_surface": 0.28747822029126885, "expected_random_landland_surface": 0.0826437271418353, "land_land_frac_surface": 0.03756149963602683, "ratio_actual_to_random": 0.45449910035595087
facts.caveat: The 29% expectation is exact under independence: P(antipode is land) = land fraction. Real land comes in big clumps, so see N13 for a fairer null that keeps the continents' real shapes.

facts.claim: A fairer test keeps the continents' real shapes. Lay a copy of all Earth's land over the original at 12,000 uniformly random orientations: the average overlap is 28.6% of land (SD 8.1 points). Only about 1.2% of orientations overlap as little as Earth's real antipodal arrangement (13.1%).
facts.spoken_form: Take a copy of every continent, spin it to a random angle and lay it over the real Earth. Do that twelve thousand times, and only about one spin in a hundred lines up as badly as the real far side does.
facts.source_title: Our Monte Carlo (scripts/mc.py; 200,000 area-weighted land samples, 12,000 random rotations, seed 42)
facts.quote: COMPUTED: "observed_antipodal_overlap": 0.13053, "null_mean": 0.2861258870833333, "null_sd": 0.08142226072875793, "frac_null_le_observed": 0.0115
facts.caveat: This describes how unusual the arrangement is. It does NOT prove a cause, and the 1875 tetrahedral theory that 'explained' it was wrong. Present it as 'unusual', never 'impossible'. Most of the effect comes from the poles: the north polar ocean sits opposite the south polar continent.

facts.claim: Splitting Earth's whole surface by what lies opposite: about 4% is land opposite land, 46% is ocean opposite ocean, and 50% is land opposite ocean (or the reverse). Under chance the mixed share would be about 41%.
facts.spoken_form: Half of the planet's surface is land that faces ocean, or ocean that faces land, on the opposite side.
facts.source_title: Our computation
facts.quote: COMPUTED: "land_land_frac_surface": 0.03756149963602683, "water_water_frac_surface": 0.4626050590534681, "land_water_frac_surface": 0.24991672065524204 (×2 for both directions = 0.4998)
facts.caveat: The mixed share counts both ends of each land–ocean pair. Expected under independence: 2 × 0.287 × 0.713 = 0.41.

facts.claim: The Arctic Ocean and Antarctica are about the same size. Arctic Ocean: about 14.06M km² (5.4M sq mi), or 15.56M km² if the Norwegian Sea is included (CIA). Antarctica: 14.2M km² (5.5M sq mi) including ice shelves (CIA). Our Natural Earth versions: Arctic with marginal seas but without the Norwegian Sea, 13.9M km²; Antarctica grounded, 12.3M km², or 13.8M km² with ice shelves.
facts.spoken_form: The ocean at the top of the world and the continent at the bottom are almost exactly the same size, about five and a half million square miles each.
facts.source_title: Wikipedia 'Arctic Ocean' (citing The New York Times Almanac 2007, p.455); CIA World Factbook 'Arctic Ocean' and 'Antarctica' (archived JSON mirror)
facts.quote: "The Arctic Ocean occupies a roughly circular basin and covers an area of about 14,056,000 km2, almost the size of Antarctica." CIA Antarctica: "14.2 million sq km (285,000 sq km ice-free, 13.915 million sq km ice-covered) (est.)"; CIA Arctic Ocean: "15.558 million sq km ... includes ... Norwegian Sea"
facts.caveat: Both areas depend on definition: ocean boundaries, and whether Antarctica includes its ice shelves. Say 'about the same size', not 'exactly'.

facts.claim: About 68% of Antarctica sits exactly opposite the Arctic Ocean and its marginal seas. The other 32% sits opposite Arctic land: Greenland 14.5% of Antarctica's area, Canada's Arctic 12.2%, Russia's Siberian Arctic 4.8%, Alaska 0.2%, Svalbard 0.1%.
facts.spoken_form: More than two-thirds of Antarctica sits directly opposite the Arctic Ocean. The rest lines up with Greenland, Arctic Canada and Siberia.
facts.source_title: Our computation (Natural Earth 50m land + admin-0 + 10m marine polygons, 0.1° and 0.05° agree)
facts.quote: COMPUTED: "frac_opposite_water": 0.6816498408667161, "frac_opposite_arctic_broad": 0.6814926940651801, opposite_land_by_country {"Greenland": 0.14537, "Canada": 0.12240, "Russia": 0.04754, "United States of America": 0.00221, "Norway": 0.00082}
facts.caveat: 'Arctic Ocean' here means Natural Earth's Arctic Ocean polygon plus the Arctic marginal seas (Barents, Kara, Laptev, East Siberian, Chukchi, Beaufort, Greenland, Lincoln, Baffin Bay, the Northwest Passage channels and others). All of Antarctica's opposite-water lies in that set. Using grounded Antarctica gives 68.2%; with ice shelves, 68.9% is opposite water.

facts.claim: About 90% of the deep central Arctic Ocean basin sits directly opposite Antarctica. That is Natural Earth's 'Arctic Ocean' polygon, about 5.2M km² (2.0M sq mi). For the whole Arctic Ocean including marginal seas (13.9M km²) the figure is 60%.
facts.spoken_form: Stand almost anywhere on the ice of the central Arctic Ocean, and nine times out of ten the far side of the planet is solid Antarctica.
facts.source_title: Our computation
facts.quote: COMPUTED: arctic_core {"area_km2": 5156547.752397676, "frac_opposite_antarctica": 0.9048101089008218}; arctic_broad {"area_km2": 13927357.107221708, "frac_opposite_antarctica": 0.5997368544198994}
facts.caveat: The figure depends on the definition: 90% for the central basin, 60% for the IHO-style ocean with all its seas. Name which one on screen ('central Arctic Ocean'). Uses grounded Antarctica; counting ice shelves would raise it slightly.

facts.claim: The poles are mirror images. North of the Arctic Circle the surface is 63% water; south of the Antarctic Circle it is 58% land, or 65% counting ice shelves. Within 10° of the poles it is starker: north of 80°N is only 10% land, while south of 80°S is 89% land, and 100% once ice shelves are counted.
facts.spoken_form: Near the North Pole, nine-tenths of the surface is ocean. Near the South Pole, it's essentially all land and ice. The two ends of the planet are photographic negatives.
facts.source_title: Our computation (Natural Earth 50m land + 50m Antarctic ice shelves)
facts.quote: COMPUTED: lat_gt_80 {"north_land_frac": 0.09882828536500568, "south_land_frac": 0.8903505002542378, "south_land_or_shelf_frac": 1.0}; arctic_circle_cap "water_frac": 0.6305486661009635; antarctic_circle_cap "land_frac": 0.5789759767472918, "land_or_shelf_frac": 0.6505382808274416
facts.caveat: Floating sea ice counts as ocean and ice shelves as noted. Ellesmere Island and northern Greenland make up the 10% land north of 80°N.

facts.claim: The seabed under the North Pole is about 4,261 m (13,980 ft, about 2.6 mi) deep, as measured by the Mir-1 submersible in 2007. At the South Pole the surface stands about 2,835 m (9,301 ft) above sea level, on ice about 2,700 m (about 9,000 ft) thick.
facts.spoken_form: At the North Pole, the sea floor is two and a half miles down. At the South Pole, you're standing almost two miles up, on a sheet of ice that's well over a mile and a half thick.
facts.display: N. POLE: −13,980 FT · S. POLE: +9,301 FT
facts.source_title: Wikipedia 'Arktika 2007' (Mir-1 dive); NSF 'Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station'; AMRDC (Univ. Wisconsin) South Pole Station page
facts.quote: Arktika 2007: "MIR-1 began its dive at 9:28 Moscow Time and at 12:08 reached the seabed 4261 m below the North Pole. MIR-2 ... reached the seabed 4302 m down." NSF: "Sits atop the Antarctic ice sheet at an elevation of approximately 2,835 meters (9,301 feet) above sea level." AMRDC: "Antarctica's nearly featureless ice sheet, which is about 2,700 meters (9,000 feet) thick at that location."
facts.caveat: The two Mir submersibles measured 4,261 m and 4,302 m; USS Nautilus (1958) gave 4,087 m. Say 'about two and a half miles'. The 2,700 m ice converts to about 8,860 ft, but AMRDC rounds to 9,000 ft. Cross-check the depth against IBCAO/ETOPO 2022 when building the cross-section.

facts.claim: Three pairings account for about 99% of all land that sits opposite land. South America ↔ East and Southeast Asia: 57% (southern cone ↔ China/Mongolia, Amazon/Andes ↔ Malay Archipelago and Indochina). Antarctica ↔ Arctic lands (Greenland, the Canadian Arctic, Siberia): 41%. New Zealand ↔ Spain/Portugal/Morocco: 1.7%.
facts.spoken_form: Almost all the land that lines up with other land comes in just three pairs: South America with East Asia, Antarctica with the Arctic, and New Zealand with Spain.
facts.source_title: Our computation (scripts/regions.py); cross-check Wikipedia 'Antipodes on Earth'
facts.quote: PUBLISHED: "The largest antipodal land masses are the Malay Archipelago, antipodal to the Amazon basin and adjoining Andean ranges; east China and Mongolia, and small sections of southeast Russia, antipodal to Argentina and Chile; and Greenland and the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, antipodal to East Antarctica." COMPUTED pair shares: Antarctica side 0.4073; South America side 0.2834×2 = 0.567; New Zealand side 0.0168
facts.caveat: Shares are of the 19.2M km² (7.4M sq mi) of land-on-land surface, counting both sides of each pair. The remaining ~1% is islands: Hawaii ↔ Botswana, Fiji and Samoa ↔ West Africa, Kerguelen ↔ Montana/Canada, and others.

facts.claim: Largest single antipodal pairs, by country: Argentina ↔ China ≈ 2.02M km² (781,000 sq mi); Greenland ↔ Antarctica ≈ 1.78M km² (688,000 sq mi); Canada ↔ Antarctica ≈ 1.50M km² (579,000 sq mi); Russia ↔ Antarctica ≈ 0.58M km² (225,000 sq mi); Brazil ↔ Indonesia ≈ 0.50M km² (192,000 sq mi). The biggest unbroken block is southern South America (Argentina/Chile/Bolivia) ↔ China/Mongolia: about 1.16M sq mi on each side.
facts.spoken_form: The biggest match on Earth: a chunk of Argentina and Chile over a million square miles across lines up almost perfectly with China and Mongolia.
facts.source_title: Our computation (Natural Earth 50m admin-0, 0.1° and 0.05° agree within 0.2%)
facts.quote: COMPUTED top pairs: "Argentina China 2022k km2 781k sqmi"; "Greenland Antarctica 1782k km2 688k sqmi"; "Antarctica Canada 1500k km2 579k sqmi"; contiguous block {"km2": 2994311.96, "sqmi": 1156110.31, "side": ["Argentina","Chile","Bolivia"], "opposite": ["China","Mongolia","Russia","Hong Kong S.A.R."]}
facts.caveat: Areas are for ONE side of each pair. Greenland follows Natural Earth's ADMIN name; it is part of the Kingdom of Denmark. On equirectangular maps the polar pairs look far too large, so show them on the globe.

facts.claim: Borneo is the largest landmass whose entire far side is land: 100% of it is opposite the Amazon (Brazil, Venezuela, Colombia). Malaysia, the Philippines, Brunei, Taiwan, Singapore, Fiji, Samoa, Tonga and Vanuatu are also 100% opposite land. Indonesia as a whole is 67%.
facts.spoken_form: Borneo is the biggest island on Earth with land under every single square mile of its far side: the Amazon rainforest.
facts.source_title: Our computation; cross-check WorldAtlas (Sawe 2017) and Wikipedia 'Antipodes on Earth'
facts.quote: PUBLISHED: "The Borneo Island is largest mass of land with antipodes entirely located on land situated in the Amazon rain forest". COMPUTED landmass #7: {"km2": 736k, "frac_opposite_land": 1.0, "countries": ["Malaysia","Indonesia","Brunei"]}
facts.caveat: Wikipedia's list of countries entirely opposite land is Brunei, Fiji, Malaysia, Philippines, Samoa, Taiwan, Vanuatu. Our 50m run adds small states and territories (Singapore, Tonga, Palau, Niue). Antipodes of tiny islands are resolution-sensitive.

facts.claim: Australia is the largest landmass with no land at all on its far side: 0% of it is opposite land. Its antipodes are in the North Atlantic, about 71% in the open North Atlantic and 29% in the Sargasso Sea.
facts.spoken_form: Australia is the opposite: the biggest landmass with nothing but ocean on its far side. Dig through and you'd come up in the North Atlantic.
facts.source_title: Our computation; cross-check WorldAtlas (Sawe 2017)
facts.quote: PUBLISHED: "whereas the mainland in Australia is the largest landmass whose antipodes are found entirely in water." COMPUTED: Australia {"frac_opposite_land": 0.0, "opposite_water": {"North Atlantic Ocean": 0.7125, "Sargasso Sea": 0.2875}}
facts.caveat: Bermuda's antipode lies only about 20–30 miles off the coast near Perth, so 'nearly' hits. Do not claim Bermuda is opposite Australia.

facts.claim: No part of the United States is opposite China. 99.99% of the lower 48 is opposite the Indian Ocean, and all of Kansas is. The only exceptions in the lower 48 are tiny: about 300 sq mi of northern Montana opposite France's Kerguelen Islands, and two specks of southeastern Colorado opposite France's Île Amsterdam and Île Saint-Paul (10m data). Hawaii is opposite Botswana (98%) and Namibia; about 2% of Alaska is opposite Antarctica. The antipode of the 1918 geographic centre of the lower 48 (39°50′N 98°35′W, near Lebanon, Kansas) is 39°50′S 81°25′E, about 220 mi from Île Saint-Paul and about 2,000 mi from Perth.
facts.spoken_form: Dig straight down from the middle of Kansas and you pop out in the southern Indian Ocean, more than two hundred miles from the nearest speck of land, a tiny French island. Not China. Not even close.
facts.source_title: Our computation (Natural Earth 50m admin-1 US states; 10m countries for small islands); Wikipedia 'Geographic center of the United States' (1918 USC&GS survey)
facts.quote: PUBLISHED: "The geographic center of the 48 contiguous or conterminous United States, determined in a 1918 survey, is located at 39°50′N 98°35′W, about 2.6 miles northwest of the center of Lebanon, Kansas". COMPUTED: us_lower48 {"frac_opposite_land": 0.00010250692421523265, "opposite_water": {"INDIAN OCEAN": 0.9998974930757849}}; Hawaii {"frac_opposite_land": 1.0, "opposite": {"Namibia": 344, "Botswana": 15431}}; Île Amsterdam centroid 37.86S 77.53E -> antipode 37.86N 102.47W 'Colorado'
facts.caveat: 'Anywhere in America can't dig to China' is TRUE: no US point has a Chinese antipode. 'Kansas comes out in the Indian Ocean' is true for all of Kansas. Don't say 'all of the US comes out in ocean', because of Hawaii/Botswana, Alaska/Antarctica, Montana/Kerguelen and Colorado/Île Amsterdam. Distances are great-circle on a 6,371 km sphere.

facts.claim: Even from China you would usually hit ocean: only about 27% of China is opposite land (Argentina 22%, Chile 5%) and 73% is opposite the South Pacific and South Atlantic. Reversed, it works far better: 86% of Argentina is opposite land, 73% of it China; 95% of Chile is opposite land.
facts.spoken_form: And here's the twist. Even if you started in China, three times out of four you'd surface in the ocean. The people who can actually dig to China are Argentinians.
facts.source_title: Our computation (Natural Earth 50m admin-0 + 10m marine polygons)
facts.quote: COMPUTED: China {"frac_opposite_land": 0.26623113728655823, "opposite_land": {"Argentina": 0.2157, "Chile": 0.0484}, "opposite_water": {"South Pacific Ocean": 0.5826, "South Atlantic Ocean": 0.1486}}; Argentina {"frac_opposite_land": 0.8615759746393423, "opposite_land": {"China": 0.7263, "Mongolia": 0.097, "Russia": 0.0367}}
facts.caveat: Percentages are by area, not population. China's population-weighted antipodes also fall largely in Argentina.

facts.claim: New Zealand ↔ Spain: 60% of New Zealand is opposite land (53% Spain, 6% Portugal, 1% Morocco), and the North Island is almost 100% opposite land. 28% of Spain is opposite New Zealand. One-sided pair area: about 141,000 km² (54,000 sq mi).
facts.spoken_form: New Zealand is the rare country that can dig to somewhere: most of it lines up with Spain.
facts.source_title: Our computation; cross-check Wikipedia 'Antipodes on Earth'
facts.quote: PUBLISHED: "the antipodes of most of New Zealand's North Island lie in Spain." COMPUTED: New Zealand {"frac_opposite_land": 0.6028675581919517, "opposite_land": {"Spain": 0.5287, "Portugal": 0.0584, "Morocco": 0.0121}}; landmass North Island {"frac_opposite_land": 0.999}

facts.claim: The Pacific Ocean alone is larger than all of Earth's land combined. NOAA: more than 155M km² (60M sq mi). CIA, including marginal seas: 168.7M km² (65.1M sq mi), against total land of 148.9M km² (57.5M sq mi).
facts.spoken_form: The Pacific alone is bigger than every continent put together, with room to spare.
facts.source_title: NOAA Ocean Exploration, 'How big is the Pacific Ocean?' (2013, updated 2020); CIA World Factbook 'Pacific Ocean' (archived JSON mirror)
facts.quote: "With a surface area of more than 155 million square kilometers (60 million square miles), this ocean basin is larger than the landmass of all the continents combined." CIA: "168.723 million sq km"
facts.caveat: The size of the margin depends on how the Pacific is bounded (with or without marginal seas). Keep it to 'with room to spare' and avoid exact leftover comparisons.

facts.claim: All of mainland South America lies east of Detroit. Its westernmost point, Punta Pariñas in Peru, is at 81.34°W (4.68°S); Detroit is at 83.05°W.
facts.spoken_form: And every inch of mainland South America is east of Detroit.
facts.source_title: Our computation (westernmost vertex of the South American mainland south of 7°N in Natural Earth 10m land); Wikipedia 'Detroit' coordinates
facts.quote: COMPUTED: "westernmost SA mainland (lat<7): lon -81.3376 lat -4.6783". Wikipedia Detroit: {{Coord|42|19|54|N|83|2|45|W}}
facts.caveat: The claim is for the mainland only; the Galápagos and other islands lie further west. Detroit's westernmost city limits are at about 83.29°W, so the margin is about 1.7° of longitude, roughly 85–120 mi depending on latitude.

result.notes:
METHOD: Every computed number can be reproduced from the scripts in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/script/research-numbers/scripts/: rast.py (rasteriser), basic.py, full.py, hemi.py, mc.py, plateau.py, regions.py, usisl.py. Outputs are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/script/research-numbers/out/ (full_0.1.json, full_0.05.json, hemi_50m.json, hemi_shelves.json, hemi_10m.json, antipode_overlay_equirect.png). Method notes are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/script/research-numbers/NOTES_method.txt.
- Rasterising: cell-centre sampling with an even-odd scanline fill and exact spherical cell areas. This reproduces the reference antipode.py result exactly: 0.1307 of land at 0.1°.
- Convergence: across grids from 0.5° to 0.025° and data from 110m to 10m, land is 28.70–28.87% of the surface. Land with land opposite is 13.0–13.3% of land, or 13.45% with ice shelves. Land-on-land is 3.74–3.83% of the surface, or 3.9% with ice shelves. The Northern Hemisphere holds 68.07–68.15% of land, or 67.4% with ice shelves.
- Natural Earth land EXCLUDES Antarctic ice shelves (1.55M km²) and the Caspian, and INCLUDES lakes. That is why it shows 146.6M km² against the CIA's 148.9M.

CORRECTIONS / WARNINGS FOR THE WRITER:
(1) The water-hemisphere centre is NOT at the Antipodes Islands.
  - The 1945 Boggs centre (47°13′S 178°28′E) is about 45 mi from the Bounty Islands and about 170 mi from the Antipodes Islands.
  - The modern optimum (IGN's Affholder 2003, and our run) puts the land centre in the sea about 30 mi SE of Tarragona, Spain (40.8°N 1.7°E). The water centre then falls about 270 mi east of NZ's North Island.
  - The maximum is so flat that Nantes, Île Dumet and Tarragona all give 81.2% within 0.05 points.
  - Script-safe wording: 'centred on western Europe' and 'the empty Pacific just off New Zealand'.
(2) The brief's 'actual ~13–15%': all our variants give 13.0–13.5%. WorldAtlas's 15% looks high and gives no method. Use 'about one in eight' or 'about thirteen percent'.
(3) The brief's 'under 5% of Earth': confirmed at 3.8%. 'Less than four percent' is also defensible, and published figures run from 3% (Spilhaus 1991) to 4.4% (WorldAtlas).
(4) 'Can't dig to China from anywhere in America' is TRUE: no US point is opposite China. But not every US point is opposite ocean: Hawaii ↔ Botswana, 2% of Alaska ↔ Antarctica, a sliver of Montana ↔ Kerguelen, and specks of SE Colorado ↔ Île Amsterdam/Saint-Paul. All of Kansas is opposite the Indian Ocean.
  - Bonus twist: 73% of China is itself opposite ocean, while 73% of Argentina is opposite China.
(5) Present the Monte Carlo 'about one in a hundred random spins' as descriptive, never as proof of a cause. It fits the S5 tetrahedron beat: the pattern is real and unusual, but the 1875 explanation was wrong.
(6) The Arctic ↔ Antarctica overlap depends on definition. 68% of Antarctica is opposite the Arctic Ocean with its seas; 90% of the central Arctic basin is opposite Antarctica. Say which one on screen.
(7) Our equirectangular overlay PNG inflates Greenland and Antarctica. For any visual comparison of the polar match, use the globe or an equal-area view.

PRIMARY SOURCES:
- Berget 1913 (archive.org OCR): the land hemisphere holds 115.4M km² of 144.1M km² (80.1%) and is 45.5% land; the water hemisphere is 88.7% water, 'neuf fois plus d'eau que de terres émergées'.
- Affholder (IGN), CFC No.176 (2003): a scanned PDF we read page by page. It finds two near-equal maxima, Brittany (47.41°N 2.49°W) and the Mediterranean (40.68°N 1.59°E). The difference between them is 0.04%.
- Boggs 1945 is paywalled (J. Geography 44(9):345); we cite it via Wikipedia.

facts.claim: In Novum Organum (1620), Book II, Aphorism 27, Francis Bacon wrote that the New World and the Old World are both broad toward the north and narrow and pointed toward the south.
facts.spoken_form: In sixteen twenty, Francis Bacon wrote that the Old World and the New are both 'broad and expanded toward the north, and narrow and pointed toward the south.'
facts.display: 1620 · BACON: "NARROW AND POINTED TOWARD THE SOUTH"
facts.source_title: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum, ed. Joseph Devey (New York: P. F. Collier & Son, 1902), Book II, Aphorism XXVII. Project Gutenberg eBook #45988
facts.quote: Again, the New and Old World are both of them broad and expanded toward the north, and narrow and pointed toward the south.
facts.caveat: This is Devey's translation. The standard Spedding translation reads: "Again, there is the Old and New World; both of which are broad and extended towards the north, narrow and pointed towards the south." (Works, vol. VIII, Boston 1863, p. 235; archive.org/details/worksoffrancisba08bacouoft/page/235). 'Old World' here effectively means Africa, Bacon's southward-tapering part of it. Bacon gives no cause. He lists it as an example of 'Conformable Instances' (resemblances in nature).

facts.claim: Bacon's original 1620 Latin calls the southern ends 'angusti et acuminati' (narrow and sharpened to a point). The passage is on p. 232 of the 1620 London first edition.
facts.spoken_form: In his original Latin, the southern ends are 'angusti et acuminati': narrow, and sharpened to a point.
facts.source_title: Bacon, Novum Organum II.27, Latin text in The Works of Francis Bacon, ed. Spedding, Ellis & Heath, vol. I (Boston: Brown & Taggard, 1861), p. 418. First edition: Instauratio Magna (London: J. Bill, 1620), p. 232
facts.quote: Item Novus et Vetus Orbis ; in eo quod utrique orbes versus septentriones lati sunt et exporrecti, versus austrum autem angusti et acuminati.
facts.caveat: I found the 1620 first-edition page by searching archive.org's OCR of instauratiomagna00baco (leaf index 247, printed p. 232; archive.org/details/instauratiomagna00baco/page/n247). The 1620 typeface OCRs badly, so the clean Latin quoted here is Spedding's. 'Acuminati' literally means 'made sharp/pointed'.

facts.claim: Bacon's 'not … mere accident' phrase refers to Africa and South America having similar isthmuses and capes. It sits in the sentence just before the narrow-to-the-south remark and is not a comment on the taper itself.
facts.spoken_form: Bacon's famous 'not by accident' line is actually about Africa and South America having matching capes and necks of land. The pointing-south remark comes in the very next breath.
facts.display: "NOT TO BE ATTRIBUTED TO MERE ACCIDENT"
facts.source_title: Bacon, Novum Organum II.27, Devey ed. (Collier 1902), Gutenberg #45988
facts.quote: similar instances are not to be neglected, in the greater portions of the world’s conformation; such as Africa and the Peruvian continent, which reaches to the Straits of Magellan; both of which possess a similar isthmus and similar capes, a circumstance not to be attributed to mere accident.
facts.caveat: The Latin is 'quod non temere accidit'. Spedding translates it 'which can hardly be by accident' (Works VIII p. 235). The 'NOT AN ACCIDENT' thumbnail is fair as Bacon's words in the same passage. The script should not claim Bacon called the drip itself non-accidental; safe wording is 'in the same breath'. Bacon's 'Peruvian continent' means South America.

facts.claim: Bacon made the observation twice in the same 1620 volume. The second time is in the Parasceve (Aphorism IX), and there he adds that the seas have the opposite shape (narrow to the north) and that the oceans run north–south.
facts.spoken_form: He said it twice. In the same sixteen twenty volume, Bacon notes again that the land is narrow and pointed toward the south and wide toward the north, and that the seas are the exact opposite.
facts.display: SAID TWICE IN 1620: LAND NARROWS SOUTH, SEA NARROWS NORTH
facts.source_title: Bacon, Parasceve ad Historiam Naturalem et Experimentalem, Aphorism IX, transl. in The Works of Francis Bacon (Spedding, Ellis, Heath), vol. VIII (Boston: Taggard & Thompson, 1863), p. 369
facts.quote: Fourthly, it would not be amiss to intersperse observations occasionally, as Pliny hath done ; as in the history of Earth and Sea, that the figure of the earth (as far as it is yet known) compared with the seas, is narrow and pointed towards the south, wide and broad towards the north ; the figure of the sea contrary : — that the great oceans intersect the earth in channels running north and south, not east and west ; except perhaps in the extreme polar regions.
facts.caveat: The OCR reads 'Pliny hap done', which I have corrected to 'hath'. The Latin is on p. 21 of the Parasceve in the 1620 first edition (archive.org instauratiomagna00baco, leaf index 388). Bacon offers it only as a sample 'observation', with no theory. James Dwight Dana repeats the land/ocean interlock in 1863 (see P19).

facts.claim: In the same aphorism, Bacon lists as an open question whether a Southern Continent exists at all. Antarctica, the landmass the drips point toward, was not sighted until January 1820, two centuries later.
facts.spoken_form: In that same passage, Bacon lists an unanswered question: is there even a Southern Continent, or only islands? Nobody would lay eyes on Antarctica for another two hundred years.
facts.display: 1620: "WHETHER THERE IS ANY SOUTHERN CONTINENT" → FIRST SEEN 1820
facts.source_title: Bacon, Parasceve, Aphorism IX, in Works vol. VIII (Boston 1863), p. 368; Wikipedia, 'Antarctica' (history section)
facts.quote: as in the history of Earth and Sea, whether the Caspian ebbs and flows, and at how many hours' interval ; whether there is any Southern Continent, or only islands ; and the like.
facts.caveat: The 1820 date comes from Wikipedia 'Antarctica': Bellingshausen 'recorded seeing an ice shelf on 27 January' 1820, and Bransfield 'discovered the tip of the Antarctic peninsula on 30 January 1820'. Who saw it first is disputed (Bellingshausen, Bransfield or Palmer), so say 'first seen in 1820'. Good ironic payoff for S1/S7.

facts.claim: Bacon did not propose the jigsaw fit of Africa and South America or continental drift. A 1965 Geological Magazine note calls that attribution a careless misreading: Bacon compared corresponding coasts and the shared southward taper, not facing coasts.
facts.spoken_form: Here's the myth: Bacon did not predict continental drift. A geographer called that story 'evidently false', the product of 'a careless reading of the text'.
facts.source_title: G. L. Davies, 'Francis Bacon and Continental Drift', Geological Magazine 102(4): 347 (August 1965), doi:10.1017/S0016756800053498
facts.quote: The attribution of the idea to Bacon is evidently false, however, and it arises only from a careless reading of the text. ... he points out that the Old and New Worlds both taper southwards, and that Africa and South America display a further general similarity in their outlines. Here he does not seem to have been comparing the opposed coasts of the two continents, but rather their corresponding coasts.
facts.caveat: N. A. Rupke, 'Continental Drift before 1900', Nature 227: 349–350 (1970) is also reported to reject Bacon as a drift precursor, but I could not open its text. Britannica and many popular sites still list Bacon among early observers of the Atlantic fit, so expect comments; this note is the rebuttal.

facts.claim: Bacon's own 19th-century editor flagged the same point: Humboldt, not Bacon, noted that the facing Atlantic coasts correspond; Bacon compared the corresponding coasts.
facts.spoken_form: Even Bacon's Victorian editor pointed it out: Bacon was comparing matching coastlines, not two puzzle pieces.
facts.display: EDITOR, 1858: "NOT THE OPPOSITE BUT THE CORRESPONDING COASTS"
facts.source_title: Editorial footnote to Novum Organum II.27 in The Works of Francis Bacon, ed. Spedding, Ellis & Heath, vol. I (Boston 1861; London ed. 1858), p. 418, note 1
facts.quote: A. von Humboldt has pointed out the conformity of the opposite shores of the Atlantic — the approximate correspondence between the projections on each side and the recesses on the other. But Bacon apparently compares not the opposite but the corresponding coasts of Africa and America.
facts.caveat: The footnote is unsigned. R. L. Ellis edited the Novum Organum in this edition, so 'Bacon's editor' is safe and 'Ellis' is likely but not certain.

facts.claim: The first known suggestion that the Americas were torn away from Europe and Africa came from the mapmaker Abraham Ortelius in 1596, not from Bacon.
facts.spoken_form: The first person to suggest the Americas had been torn away from Europe and Africa was a mapmaker, Abraham Ortelius, in fifteen ninety-six.
facts.source_title: USGS, This Dynamic Earth: The Story of Plate Tectonics, 'Historical perspective'
facts.quote: this notion was first suggested as early as 1596 by the Dutch map maker Abraham Ortelius in his work Thesaurus Geographicus . Ortelius suggested that the Americas were "torn away from Europe and Africa . . . by earthquakes and floods"
facts.caveat: This is about drift and the Atlantic fit, not the drip. Use it only to correct the Bacon myth. The USGS page does not mention Bacon at all.

facts.claim: Over 2,000 years ago, Eratosthenes (as reported by Strabo) described Europe's south as three jutting promontories: Iberia, Italy, and the Greek/Balkan one ending at Cape Malea.
facts.spoken_form: Over two thousand years ago, the Greek scholar Eratosthenes described southern Europe as three prongs jutting into the sea: Spain, Italy, and Greece.
facts.source_title: Strabo, Geography 2.4.8, transl. H. L. Jones (Loeb Classical Library, 1917), LacusCurtius edition
facts.quote: For Eratosthenes spoke of only three promontories: first, the promontory that juts down to the Pillars, on which is Iberia; secondly, that to the Strait of Sicily, on which is Italy; and, thirdly, that which ends at Cape Malea
facts.caveat: The ancient authors describe promontories but never state a 'points south' pattern. It was Humboldt (Cosmos, 1845, p. 291) who read Eratosthenes and Polybius as early noticers of the 'pyramidal terminations'. Script wording: 'already noticed the three prongs', not 'noticed the drip'. Eratosthenes' dates are c. 276–194 BC.

facts.claim: In 1778 Johann Reinhold Forster, naturalist on Captain Cook's second voyage, wrote that all the major southern points of land look alike: high, rocky, the end of a mountain range running north, with large islands to their east.
facts.spoken_form: In seventeen seventy-eight, Captain Cook's naturalist, Johann Reinhold Forster, noticed something stranger: every great southern tip looks the same. High, rocky, the end of a mountain chain, with a big island off to the east.
facts.source_title: Johann Reinhold Forster, Observations Made during a Voyage round the World (London: G. Robinson, 1778), section 'Lands', p. 13
facts.quote: All the remarkable Southern points of lands on our globe, have a great and striking similarity in regard to their conformation, and the situation of islands in their vicinity. They are all high and rocky; each seems to be the extremity of a range of high mountains running northward. All have to the eastward one or more large islands.
facts.caveat: I have modernized the long-s spellings ('fimilarity' becomes 'similarity'). Forster's examples (pp. 12–14) are Cape Froward/Cape Horn with Tierra del Fuego, Staten Land and the Falklands to the east; the Cape of Good Hope with Madagascar; Cape Comorin with Ceylon; and New Holland's (Tasmania's) high rocky point with New Zealand. So Forster counted Australia as a south-pointer.

facts.claim: Forster said the pattern was too consistent to be accidental, and he blamed a violent flood from the south-west.
facts.spoken_form: His explanation? Too many coincidences to be an accident. So, he suggested, a giant flood came roaring in from the south-west and sculpted every one of them.
facts.display: FORSTER'S CAUSE: "A VIOLENT FLOOD FROM THE SOUTH-WEST"
facts.source_title: J. R. Forster, Observations Made during a Voyage round the World (London 1778), p. 13
facts.quote: So many coinciding circumstances seem, not to be merely accidental, but rather to proceed from one and the same general cause. I do not pretend to point out this first cause, but cannot help suspecting, that a violent flood coming from the south-west has produced this striking identity of conformation in these lands
facts.caveat: Long-s spellings are modernized. The theory is wrong (see P12). It makes a good comic Explorer beat: a giant wave 'sanding down' the continents.

facts.claim: Forster's flood theory was accepted by notable contemporaries such as the explorer Peter Simon Pallas. By 1849 the geographer Arnold Guyot wrote that modern geology forbids adopting it.
facts.spoken_form: Some of the top scientists of the day bought it. Seventy years later, a geographer wrote that modern geology forbids us to adopt it.
facts.display: 1849 · GUYOT: GEOLOGY "FORBID[S] US TO ADOPT IT"
facts.source_title: Arnold Guyot, The Earth and Man, transl. C. C. Felton (Boston: Gould, Kendall & Lincoln, 1849), pp. 20–21
facts.quote: This hypothesis, bold as it is ingenious, was admitted by several of the most distinguished contemporaries of Forster. Pallas, among others, the celebrated northern traveller, inclines to receive this general cataclysm from the south-west ... Seductive as this idea is at the first glance, it is scarcely necessary to say that all that modern geology has taught us upon the structure of the mountains, their rise, and the composition of the soil, forbid us to adopt it.
facts.caveat: This is Guyot's account of Pallas, a secondary report; I did not check Pallas's own text. The page numbers are those of the 1849 Boston edition.

facts.claim: In 1817 the philosopher G. W. F. Hegel listed 'the compact spreading of land in the north' and 'the sharp tapering of the parts towards the south' among Earth's basic features, and tied them to Earth's axis and magnetic axis.
facts.spoken_form: Even the philosopher Hegel weighed in, in eighteen seventeen: land spread out in the north, sharply tapering to the south. His culprit? Earth's magnetism.
facts.source_title: G. W. F. Hegel, Encyclopaedia of the Philosophical Sciences (Heidelberg text, 1817), §263, transl. Steven A. Taubeneck (Continuum, 1990), via Marxists Internet Archive, 'Hegel's Philosophy of Nature III'
facts.quote: Standing in closer relation to these axes and their polarisation is the distribution of sea and land: the compact spreading of land in the north, the division and sharp tapering of the parts towards the south, the further separation into an old and a new world
facts.caveat: In the 1830 edition this is §339, so cite '1817, §263'. Hegel links it to the axes 'and their polarisation' (the preceding sentence names 'the inclination of its axis to the orbit and the magnetic axis'). 'Blamed magnetism' is a fair, slightly simplified summary.

facts.claim: By the mid-1800s the pattern had been extended to peninsulas. The philosopher Henrik Steffens, as reported by Guyot in 1849, listed Greenland, California (Baja), Florida, Scandinavia, Spain, Italy, Greece, India, Indochina, Korea and Kamchatka as all having 'their points turned towards the south'.
facts.spoken_form: By the eighteen-forties, someone had already made the list you saw at the start: Greenland, Baja California, Florida, Scandinavia, Italy, Greece, India, Korea, Kamchatka. All with 'their points turned towards the south.'
facts.display: 1849: "ALL THEIR POINTS TURNED TOWARDS THE SOUTH"
facts.source_title: Arnold Guyot, The Earth and Man, transl. C. C. Felton (Boston 1849), p. 22, summarizing Henrik Steffens
facts.quote: He remarks, first, that the lands expand and come together towards the north, while they separate and narrow down to points in the south. Now this tendency is marked, not only in the principal masses of the continents, but also in all the important peninsulas which detach themselves from it. Greenland, California, Florida, in America ; Scandinavia, Spain, Italy, and Greece, in Europe ; the two Indies, Corea, Kamtschatka, in Asia, have all their points turned towards the south.
facts.caveat: Guyot's wording is certain. I did not check Steffens's original German, probably his Anthropologie (1822). 'The two Indies' means India and Indochina/Malay Peninsula. 'California' means Baja. 'Spain' as a south-pointer is doubtful because Iberia is blocky. This makes an excellent callback to the cold-open list.

facts.claim: In Cosmos (vol. 1, 1845), Alexander von Humboldt called the 'pyramidal configuration of all the southern extremities of continents' a real physical resemblance, crediting Bacon and Forster.
facts.spoken_form: In eighteen forty-five, the most famous scientist alive, Alexander von Humboldt, called it 'the pyramidal configuration of all the southern extremities of continents', and gave Bacon and Forster the credit.
facts.source_title: Alexander von Humboldt, Cosmos, vol. 1, transl. E. C. Otté (Harper & Brothers 1858 ed.), pp. 290–291. Project Gutenberg #14565
facts.quote: The pyramidal configuration of all the southern extremities of continents belongs to the 'similtudines physicae in configuratione mundi', to which Bacon already called attention in his 'Novum Organon', and with which Reinhold Foster, one of Cook's companions in his second voyage of circumnavigation, connected some ingenious considerations.
facts.caveat: The transcription's typos ('similtudines', 'Foster') are kept verbatim. German original, Kosmos Bd. 1 (1845): 'Die pyramidale Gestaltung aller südlichen Endspitzen der Continente gehört unter die similitudines physicae in configuratione Mundi, auf welche schon Baco von Verulam im Neuen Organon aufmerksam machte'. Elsewhere (p. 47) Humboldt calls it a 'law' that 'determines the nature of climates', which overstates it.

facts.claim: Humboldt noted that the pattern repeats at smaller scale in Arabia, India and Malacca (the Malay Peninsula) and in Spain, Italy and Greece.
facts.spoken_form: And he saw it repeat in miniature: Arabia, India, the Malay Peninsula, then Spain, Italy and Greece.
facts.source_title: Humboldt, Cosmos, vol. 1 (Otté transl., 1858 Harper ed.), p. 291. Project Gutenberg #14565
facts.quote: The pyramidal terminations of the great continents are variously repeated on a smaller scale, not only in the Indian Ocean and in the peninsulas of Arabia, Hindostan, and Malacca, but also, as was remarked by Eratosthenes and Polybius, in the Mediterranean, where these writers had ingeniously compared together the forms of the Iberian, Italian, and Hellenic peninsulas.
facts.caveat: Arabia's tip points roughly south-east, not cleanly south. Holden (1976) also calls it a 'subdrip'.

facts.claim: Humboldt noticed that Eurasia's farthest-south and farthest-north points lie on almost the same meridian (Malacca and Cape Taimura). Modern coordinates confirm it: Tanjung Piai (southernmost mainland Eurasia, 103.51°E) and Cape Chelyuskin (northernmost mainland Eurasia, 104.25°E) are less than one degree of longitude apart and about 5,280 miles apart north to south.
facts.spoken_form: Humboldt spotted something even weirder. The southernmost point of mainland Asia and the northernmost point are on almost the exact same line of longitude: less than one degree apart, and over five thousand miles from each other.
facts.source_title: Humboldt, Cosmos vol. 1 (Otté transl.), p. 291; Wikipedia 'Tanjung Piai' and 'Cape Chelyuskin' (coordinates); our haversine computation
facts.quote: It is also a remarkable circumstance that the greatest extension toward the south falls in the Old Continent, under the same meridian in which the extremest projection toward the north pole is manifested. This will be perceived on comparing the Cape of Good Hope and the Lagullas Bank with the North Cape of Europe, and the peninsula of Malacca with Cape Taimura in Siberia.
facts.caveat: Coordinates (Wikipedia): Tanjung Piai 1.266°N 103.511°E, 'the most southern point of mainland Eurasia'; Cape Chelyuskin 77.733°N 104.25°E, 'the northernmost point of the Eurasian continent'. Δlon = 0.74°; great-circle distance 8,503 km (5,283 mi). Humboldt's Africa/Europe pair is much looser (Cape Agulhas 20.0°E vs Nordkinn 27.65°E), so use only the Asia pair. Show it on screen as a 'bonus coincidence', not as evidence for the drip.

facts.claim: Mary Somerville's bestselling Physical Geography (1848) said that almost all peninsulas tend to the south, while the continents' northern edges are broken and ragged, with very few exceptions.
facts.spoken_form: By eighteen forty-eight it was in the bestselling geography textbook of its day. Mary Somerville wrote that almost all the peninsulas tend to the south.
facts.display: 1848 · SOMERVILLE: "ALMOST ALL THE PENINSULAS TEND TO THE SOUTH"
facts.source_title: Mary Somerville, Physical Geography, vol. 1 (London: John Murray, 1848), ch. 2, p. 33
facts.quote: The tendency of the land to assume a peninsular form is very remarkable; and it is still more so that almost all the peninsulas tend to the south, while to the north, with a very few exceptions, the two great continents terminate in a very broken line
facts.caveat: 'Bestselling' is a fair characterization (many editions through 1877) but is not sourced here. Script can say 'a hugely popular textbook' instead. Her portrait (Thomas Phillips, 1834) is public domain.

facts.claim: America's leading geologist, James Dwight Dana, wrote in his 1863 Manual of Geology that continents and oceans interlock: the land narrows southward and the oceans narrow northward, with the land's mass gathered around the Arctic.
facts.spoken_form: In eighteen sixty-three, America's top geologist put it in a single line: the continents narrow southward, the oceans narrow northward. They interlock, like fingers.
facts.source_title: James D. Dana, Manual of Geology (Philadelphia: Theodore Bliss & Co., 1863), p. 11 (§16) and p. 13 (§18)
facts.quote: The land is gathered about the Arctic, and reaches south in two great continental masses, the occidental and oriental ; but the latter, through Africa and Australia, has two southern prolongations, making in all three, corresponding to the three oceans. Thus the continents and oceans interlock, the former narrowing southward, the latter northward.
facts.caveat: I fixed the page numbers by reading the scan's running heads, because archive.org's page_numbers.json is off by one here. p. 13 adds: 'The land of the globe has been stated to lie with its mass to the north, about the Arctic, and to narrow as it extends southward into the waters of the Southern hemisphere. The mean southern limit of the continental lands is the parallel of 45°'. Dana also counts Australia as a southern prolongation.

facts.claim: Dana gave American readers a scale anchor: Africa's southern tip, at 34°51′S, mirrors the latitude of Tennessee's southern border, and South America's tip (Cape Horn, 56°S) mirrors Edinburgh or northern Labrador.
facts.spoken_form: Dana gave Americans a mirror test. Flip the globe, and Africa's southern tip lines up with the southern border of Tennessee.
facts.source_title: James D. Dana, Manual of Geology (1863), p. 13
facts.quote: South America reaches only to 56° S. (Cape Horn being in 55° 58'), which is the latitude of Edinburgh or northern Labrador; Africa to 34° 51' (Cape of Good Hope), nearly the latitude of the southern boundary of Tennessee, and 60 miles nearer the equator than Gibraltar
facts.caveat: Dana labels 34°51′ as the 'Cape of Good Hope', but that is the latitude of Cape Agulhas, Africa's true southern tip (Cape of Good Hope is 34.36°S). Tennessee's southern border is the 35th parallel. Cape Horn is on an island, so mainland South America ends at Cape Froward, 53.9°S (see P29).

facts.claim: Dana's 1863 textbook described each America as 'triangular in outline, with the widest part, or head, to the north', and said South America lies 'east of the meridian of Niagara Falls'. The first-edition scan prints 'west' where 'east' was meant, and an early reader corrected it by hand in the margin. The Niagara claim is also slightly off: the westernmost point of mainland South America (Punta Pariñas, 81.33°W) is west of Niagara Falls (79.07°W). The Detroit version (83.0°W) is the correct one.
facts.spoken_form: Even the eighteen sixty-three textbook got tangled up: it printed 'west' where it meant 'east', and some reader fixed it in pen. And its claim that all of South America is east of Niagara Falls? Not quite. It is east of Detroit, though.
facts.display: "WIDEST PART, OR HEAD, TO THE NORTH" · 1863
facts.source_title: James D. Dana, Manual of Geology (1863), p. 24 (archive.org scan, leaf n43); Wikipedia 'Punta Pariñas' and 'Niagara Falls' coordinates
facts.quote: moreover, South America is set so far to the west of North America (being east of the meridian of Niagara Falls) that each has an almost entire ocean-contour. Moreover, each is triangular in outline, with the widest part, or head, to the north.
facts.caveat: I checked the scan image myself: 'west' is printed and struck through, with 'east' written in the margin by hand. Punta Pariñas is 'the westernmost point in mainland South America, located at 04°40′45″S 81°19′35″W' (Wikipedia). Niagara Falls is 79.07°W. Optional fun visual; the core usable line is 'triangular … head to the north'.

facts.claim: William Lowthian Green's tetrahedral-Earth theory (1875) was summarized by the French geologist de Lapparent as predicting northern continents 'terminating in points, towards the south', an ocean at the North Pole and land at the South Pole.
facts.spoken_form: The tetrahedron theory seemed to predict it all: three northern continents, each ending in a point toward the south, an ocean at the North Pole, and land at the South Pole.
facts.display: TETRAHEDRON THEORY: CONTINENTS "TERMINATING IN POINTS, TOWARDS THE SOUTH"
facts.source_title: W. L. Green, Vestiges of the Molten Globe, Part II (Honolulu: Hawaiian Gazette, 1887), p. 7, quoting A. de Lapparent's summary of Green's theory
facts.quote: there would exist, in the Northern Hemisphere, three symmetrical continental projections, while the Arctic Pole would be the centre of the sea ; on the other hand, a continental protuberance will appear at the Antarctic Pole. And the northern continents, terminating in points, towards the south, as well as in the direction of the east, and of west, will leave oceans between them largely developed in the Southern Hemisphere
facts.caveat: This archive.org item is catalogued as 1875 but is actually PART II (1887). The passage is de Lapparent's French summary in English translation, as quoted by Green; the OCR 'appeai;' is corrected to 'appear'. The S5 researcher should cite Green's own 1875 Part I wording for the main claims. This is included only to show that the theory addressed the southward points.

facts.claim: The name 'continental drip' was coined as a joke by Ormonde de Kay Jr. in Horizon magazine (Winter 1973), at a time when plate tectonics was newly accepted.
facts.spoken_form: The pattern finally got its name in nineteen seventy-three, as a joke. A magazine writer called it 'continental drip'.
facts.source_title: Ormonde de Kay Jr., 'Continental Drip', Horizon 15 (Winter 1973): 118–119; reprinted in R. L. Weber (ed.), More Random Walks in Science (1982), pp. 201–203. Via Wikipedia 'Continental drip' and Morrison, ASBS Newsletter 68 (1991)
facts.quote: The observation was made by Ormonde de Kay in a 1973 tongue-in-cheek paper, which he introduced as "another earth-shaking new theory derived from simply looking at maps."
facts.caveat: I could not open the Horizon text itself (Google Books quota exhausted). The volume and pages come from Morrison's reference list in the Australian Systematic Botany Society Newsletter 68 (Sept 1991): 'de Kay, O. (1973) Continental drip. Horizon 15 (winter): 118-119.' Wikipedia lists de Kay's smaller drips as Baja, Florida, Europe's peninsulas except Jutland, the Malay Peninsula and Indochina.

facts.claim: In 1976 John C. Holden, co-author of the real 1970 Pangaea breakup reconstruction, published the parody 'Fake Tectonics and Continental Drip'. In it he declared all continents teardrop-shaped with points trending south, and cited his own real Dietz & Holden (1970) paper.
facts.spoken_form: Three years later, a real plate-tectonics mapmaker, John Holden, wrote the parody. All continents, he declared, are teardrops, 'with the pointed ends trending south indicating the directions from which they have come.'
facts.display: 1976 · HOLDEN: "TEAR-DROP SHAPED ... POINTED ENDS TRENDING SOUTH"
facts.source_title: John C. Holden, 'Fake Tectonics and Continental Drip', Journal of Irreproducible Results 22(2): 26–27 (1976); reprinted verbatim in Australian Systematic Botany Society Newsletter 68 (Sept 1991), pp. 21–22
facts.quote: However, the outlines of all continents are tear-drop shaped, with the pointed ends trending south indicating the directions from which they have come. This startling concept is called "continental drip", and is the essential concept of "Fake tectonics"
facts.caveat: The joke's half-truth ('indicating the directions from which they have come') is the real Gondwana answer, which is the S7 twist. Same text: 'A step in the right direction was made by Dietz and Holden (1970), when they recognized that there was only a "sudpolarfluchtkraft" (south polar fleeing force).' Holden lists Arabia as a 'subdrip', New Zealand as a 'drowned drip' and Ceylon and Antarctica as 'anti-drips'. The figure is copyrighted (JIR), so quote the text only.

facts.claim: Holden's parody predicted the drips would reunite as the supercontinent 'Pangooy' in a 'continental splash' at exactly 9:00 a.m. on a Tuesday in the year 1,786,379 AD. Antarctica is an 'anti-drip' that never joins because it sits 'at the top of the globe'.
facts.spoken_form: He even gave a date for the reunion: Tuesday morning, nine a.m., in the year one million, seven hundred eighty-six thousand, three hundred seventy-nine. The new supercontinent? 'Pangooy.'
facts.source_title: J. C. Holden, 'Fake Tectonics and Continental Drip', J. Irreproducible Results 22(2) (1976), reprinted in ASBS Newsletter 68 (1991), p. 21
facts.quote: Based on computer analyses of the northward vector sums for continents now in motion, this event will occur on Tuesday morning at 9:00 a.m. 1,786,379 A.D. The resulting new universal landmass (excluding Antarctica) is called "Pangooy", and the event is termed "continental splash"; the final coalescence of continental drips
facts.caveat: Pure parody. It works as a comic setup for the finale's real future-supercontinent models, but label it as a joke on screen. Also from the same text: 'The anti-drip of Antarctica is due to the fact that Antarctica, being situated at the top of the globe, has not yet made up its mind which way to flow'.

facts.claim: Vsauce's YouTube Short 'Why Does Earth Look 'Drippy'?' (published July 12, 2024; about 27.4 million views as of Nov 4, 2026) names the pattern continental drip and says it is 'really just a coincidence', attributing it to pareidolia/apophenia.
facts.spoken_form: A video with over twenty-seven million views called it 'really just a coincidence.'
facts.source_title: Vsauce, 'Why Does Earth Look 'Drippy'?' (YouTube Short, id 4bmrcZHi-0s), Jul 12, 2024. Auto-captions
facts.quote: it's called Continental drip and it's real Lee just a coincidence we just happen to be alive when Earth happens to look like this our brains have a tendency to find meaningful Connections in unrelated things it's called apophenia
facts.caveat: Quoted from YouTube auto-captions: 'real Lee' is how the captions render 'really'. The view count is 27,367,923 on 2026-11-04 (watch-page HTML); oEmbed confirms author 'Vsauce'. The brief's 'mostly a coincidence' is inaccurate; the Short says 'really just a coincidence'. Mention by name only, with no footage (production rule).

facts.claim: Hank Green posted a YouTube Short titled 'Why do all the continents point south?' on September 26, 2026 (about 2.59 million views by Nov 4, 2026).
facts.spoken_form: Just this fall, Hank Green asked the same question in under a minute.
facts.source_title: Hank Green, 'Why do all the continents point south?' (YouTube Short, id lghuDPPiiE8)
facts.quote: Why do all the continents point south? | Hank Green — publishDate "Sep 26, 2026" — "2,586,463 views"
facts.caveat: Title and author come from YouTube oEmbed; date and views from the watch-page HTML on 2026-11-04. I did not review its content (title and date only, per the task). Probably best not narrated. Related: vlogbrothers 'Continents are Dumb' (Sep 24, 2015) is a different video.

facts.claim: The cold-open tips are real southern terminations: Kanyakumari (India), Cape Farewell (Greenland), Cape Lopatka (Kamchatka), Tanjung Piai (Malay Peninsula, southernmost mainland Eurasia), Cape Matapan (mainland Greece), Cape Sable (mainland Florida/US) and Cabo San Lucas (Baja California).
facts.spoken_form: India. Greenland. Kamchatka. The Malay Peninsula. Greece. Florida. Baja. Each one ends in a point aimed south.
facts.display: TIPS: INDIA 8.1°N · GREENLAND 59.8°N · KAMCHATKA 50.9°N · MALAY 1.3°N · GREECE 36.4°N · FLORIDA 25.3°N · BAJA 22.9°N
facts.source_title: Wikipedia lead sections: 'Kanyakumari', 'Cape Farewell, Greenland', 'Cape Lopatka', 'Tanjung Piai', 'Cape Matapan', 'Cape Sable', 'Cabo San Lucas'
facts.quote: Kanyakumari ... is the southernmost tip of the contiguous Indian subcontinent / Cape Farewell is a headland on the southern shore of Egger Island ... As the southernmost point of the country / Cape Lopatka is the southernmost point of Kamchatka Peninsula / Tanjung Piai ... is the southernmost point of Peninsular Malaysia and thus the most southern point of mainland Eurasia / Cape Matapan is the southernmost point of mainland Greece / Cape Sable is the southernmost point of the United States mainland and mainland Florida / Cabo San Lucas ... is a resort city on the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula
facts.caveat: Coordinates (Wikipedia): Kanyakumari 8.088°N 77.539°E; Cape Farewell 59.773°N 43.923°W (on an island, Egger Island); Cape Lopatka 50.87°N 156.67°E; Tanjung Piai 1.266°N 103.511°E; Cape Matapan 36.389°N 22.483°E; Cape Sable 25.272°N 81.124°W; Cabo San Lucas 22.895°N 109.915°W. I did not fetch Korea's or Scandinavia's tips; take those from Natural Earth. For the red tip pops, a peninsula 'points south' only by its base-to-tip azimuth; show the method on screen in S8.

facts.claim: Two 'tip' myths. Africa's southern tip is Cape Agulhas, about 34 miles (55 km) farther south than the Cape of Good Hope. Cape Horn is on a small island, so mainland South America ends at Cape Froward.
facts.spoken_form: Quick myth-bust: the Cape of Good Hope is not the bottom of Africa. Cape Agulhas is, about thirty-four miles farther south. And Cape Horn isn't on the mainland at all; it's on an island.
facts.display: AFRICA'S TIP: CAPE AGULHAS (+34 MI SOUTH OF GOOD HOPE)
facts.source_title: Wikipedia: 'Cape Agulhas', 'Cape Horn', 'Cape Froward'
facts.quote: It is both the southernmost point of South Africa, the geographic southern tip of Africa ... It is approximately half a degree of latitude, or 55 kilometres (34 mi), farther south than the Cape of Good Hope. / Cape Horn is the southernmost headland of the Tierra del Fuego archipelago of southern Chile, and is located on the small Hornos Island. Although not the most southerly point of South America ... / Cape Froward is the southernmost point of mainland South America.
facts.caveat: Coordinates: Cape Agulhas 34.833°S 20.0°E; Cape of Good Hope 34.358°S 18.476°E; Cape Froward 53.893°S 71.306°W; Cape Horn 55.98°S 67.29°W. Several historical sources (Forster, Dana, Guyot) use 'Cape of Good Hope' or 'Cape Horn' loosely. Use their quotes verbatim, but put the correct tip on the globe.

facts.claim: Real north-pointing counterexamples exist: Cape York Peninsula (Australia), the Antarctic Peninsula, Yucatán (extends north-east), Jutland (tip at Grenen in the north), the Taymyr Peninsula (Eurasia's northern tip) and Boothia/Murchison Promontory (the Americas' northernmost mainland point). Somerville in 1848 already allowed 'a very few exceptions'.
facts.spoken_form: Not everything drips. Australia's Cape York, Mexico's Yucatán, Denmark's Jutland, Siberia's Taymyr: all point north. And the Antarctic Peninsula has no choice; from the South Pole, every direction is north.
facts.display: POINT NORTH: CAPE YORK · YUCATÁN · JUTLAND · TAYMYR · ANTARCTIC PEN.
facts.source_title: Wikipedia lead sections: 'Cape York (Queensland)', 'Antarctic Peninsula', 'Yucatán Peninsula', 'Jutland', 'Taymyr Peninsula', 'Murchison Promontory'
facts.quote: Cape York ... is the northernmost point of the mainland of Australia. / The Antarctic Peninsula ... is the northernmost part of mainland Antarctica. / The peninsula extends towards the northeast / It stretches from the Grenen spit in the north / The Taymyr Peninsula ... forms the northernmost part of the mainland of Eurasia. / Murchison Promontory ... is the northernmost mainland point of the Americas and of Canada.
facts.caveat: 'Points' depends on how you measure; use base-to-tip azimuth in S8 and show it. Historical writers (Forster 1778, Humboldt 1845, Holden 1976) counted Australia as a south-pointing drip because of Tasmania's 'high rocky point', so 'Australia points north' is a framing choice: it has a north-pointing peninsula but a south-tapering outline. Eurasia as a whole has no single southern taper; it ends in several southern prongs (Arabia, India, Indochina/Malaya). Arabia points roughly SE. The Antarctic Peninsula is a geometric necessity, so present it as a joke ('anti-drip'), not as evidence.
