result.notes:
Scope: the drip pattern itself and the history of people noticing it. My working notes and downloaded primary texts are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/script/research-pattern/ (ledger_notes.txt lists the line ranges in dl/).

Corrections and flags for the brief and script:
1) Bacon's 'not to be attributed to mere accident' refers to the Africa/Peru 'similar isthmus and similar capes'. The taper sentence follows it as a separate 'Again…'. The brief's S1 wording ('called the Africa/South America likeness not … accident') is correct; just don't stretch it to 'called the drip not an accident'.
2) NEW: Bacon states the taper TWICE in the 1620 volume, in Novum Organum II.27 and again in Parasceve Aph. IX, where he adds 'the figure of the sea contrary'. In the same Parasceve aphorism he lists as an open question 'whether there is any Southern Continent, or only islands'. Antarctica wasn't seen until 1820. This is a strong ironic callback for S1 to S7: the drips point at the continent Bacon didn't know existed.
3) The myth-bust that Bacon did not predict drift is backed by Davies 1965 (Geol. Mag. 102:347) and by the Spedding-edition editor's footnote. The real first 'torn apart' idea is Ortelius 1596 (USGS).
4) The history chain is now fully sourced to primary texts: Eratosthenes/Strabo (promontories, medium) → Bacon 1620 → Forster 1778 (southern tips all high, rocky, with islands to the east; cause 'a violent flood coming from the south-west'; Pallas agreed) → Hegel 1817 (blamed Earth's axes/magnetism) → Humboldt 1845 ('pyramidal configuration of all the southern extremities'; credits Bacon and Forster) → Guyot/Steffens 1849 → Somerville 1848 → Dana 1863 ('continents and oceans interlock, the former narrowing southward') → Green/Lapparent tetrahedron → de Kay 1973 (name) → Holden 1976 (parody). Steffens's 1849 list (Greenland, California, Florida, Scandinavia, Spain, Italy, Greece, the two Indies, Corea, Kamtschatka) is almost exactly our cold-open list: 'someone made this list 175 years ago.'
5) Vsauce Short: 'Why Does Earth Look 'Drippy'?', Jul 12, 2024, 27,367,923 views. It says 'really just a coincidence', NOT 'mostly'. Fix the brief's S-intro framing to 'called it a coincidence', which is accurate. Hank Green Short: 'Why do all the continents point south?', Sep 26, 2026, 2,586,463 views.
6) Dana 1863 says South America lies 'east of the meridian of Niagara Falls'. That is wrong: Punta Pariñas (81.33°W) is west of Niagara (79.07°W). Keep the brief's Detroit version (83.0°W), which is correct. The scan also misprints 'west' for 'east', corrected by a reader's pen in the margin; optional gag.
7) Bonus verified 'sounds fake' fact (from Humboldt, checked with modern coordinates): the southernmost and northernmost points of mainland Eurasia (Tanjung Piai 103.51°E, Cape Chelyuskin 104.25°E) are less than 1° of longitude apart, about 5,283 miles apart north to south.
8) Tip myths: Africa's tip is Cape Agulhas, not the Cape of Good Hope (34 mi farther south). Cape Horn is on an island, and mainland South America ends at Cape Froward. Put the correct points on the globe even when quoting old sources that say 'Cape of Good Hope'.
9) Counterexamples: Cape York, the Antarctic Peninsula, Yucatán (NE), Jutland, Taymyr and Boothia/Murchison point north. Arabia points SE. Eurasia has no single taper. Forster, Humboldt and Holden all counted Australia as south-pointing via Tasmania, so the 'Australia points north!' comments can be pre-empted as a framing issue.
10) Green: the archive.org item labelled 1875 is actually Part II (Honolulu, 1887), which quotes de Lapparent's summary. The S5 researcher should cite Part I (1875) directly.

Could not verify: the text of the Geological Society 'Ask a Geologist: Why do most peninsulas point south' page (it now redirects, and web.archive.org is blocked); de Kay's Horizon text itself (Google Books quota exhausted, so I used the Wikipedia quote plus Morrison 1991's citation, Horizon 15(winter):118–119); Steffens's German original; and Rupke 1970's text (paywalled). Wikimedia API rate-limited further portrait lookups (Humboldt, Dana, Guyot, Hegel). Those portraits are all pre-1900 and almost certainly public domain, but check each file page.

facts.claim: In 1875 William Lowthian Green argued that Earth's cooling crust was collapsing toward a tetrahedron. He said this one shape explained five things: why most land is in the north, why three continents end in pyramid-like points aimed south, why an ocean surrounds the North Pole, why land usually lies opposite water, and why a three-cornered continent sits on the South Pole.
facts.spoken_form: In eighteen seventy-five, a man named William Lowthian Green said one shape explained everything: most land up north, three continents pointing south, an ocean on top of the world, a continent at the bottom, and land always opposite water. The shape was a four-cornered pyramid. A tetrahedron.
facts.source_title: Green, W. L. (1875). Vestiges of the Molten Globe, as Exhibited in the Figure of the Earth, Volcanic Action and Physiography, Part I. London: Edward Stanford, pp. 6-7 (archive.org scan)
facts.quote: First. Why most of the land of the globe should be in the Northern Hemisphere ... Second. We see why there should be three continents mainly in the Northern Hemisphere, with a pyramidal projection to each, pointing into the Southern Ocean. Third. We see why there should be a polar basin and an Arctic ocean surrounding the North Pole. Fourth. We perceive why, as has often been remarked by physical geographers, there should always be water on the opposite side of the globe to which there is land ... we find a three-cornered continent occupying the South polar regions
facts.caveat: Quote lightly cleaned of OCR errors (e.g. 'soUd'). Green's 'three continents' are double continents (Europe-Africa, North-South America, Asia-Australia), with Antarctica as the fourth corner. 'Land opposite water' was a generalisation with exceptions (e.g. Spain/New Zealand).

facts.claim: Green was not an academic: the title page lists him as Minister of Foreign Affairs to the King of the Sandwich Islands (Hawaii). He first proposed in 1857, in the Edinburgh New Philosophical Journal, that the pointed southern ends of the continents had a physical cause, and he illustrated it with a bent card dipped in water.
facts.spoken_form: Green wasn't a professor. He was the foreign minister of the Kingdom of Hawaii. And he'd been obsessed with those pointy southern tips since eighteen fifty-seven, when he demonstrated them with a bent card dipped in water.
facts.source_title: Green, W. L. (1875). Vestiges of the Molten Globe, title page and Preface (archive.org scan)
facts.quote: WILLIAM LOWTHIAN GREEN, MINISTER OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS TO THE KING OF THE SANDWICH ISLANDS. ... In 1857, 'The Edinburgh New Philosophical Journal' contained a paper in which I suggested the view that the pyramidal form of the outline of the southern extremities of the continents of the globe was the result of the conical superficial figure of the reliefs of the land entering the ocean ... by slightly arching a card, or by bending it with a ridge along the middle ... and holding it with the edges just at the surface of the water
facts.caveat: This is how Green describes himself in his own book. In 1857 he blamed the points on the crust dipping south under the ocean; the full tetrahedron argument came in 1875. Wikipedia describes him as an English-born merchant who became a Hawaiian cabinet minister.

facts.claim: The tetrahedron idea went mainstream. In 1899 geologist J. W. Gregory presented it to the Royal Geographical Society. He argued that a shrinking, hard-shelled Earth must tend toward a tetrahedron because, among regular solids, it holds the least volume for a given surface. He also stated that North America is exactly antipodal to the Indian Ocean, and the Arctic Ocean to Antarctica.
facts.spoken_form: This wasn't a fringe idea. In eighteen ninety-nine, a leading geologist told the Royal Geographical Society that a shrinking Earth had to squeeze toward a tetrahedron, the shape that wraps the most surface around the least volume. He even noted that North America sits exactly opposite the Indian Ocean.
facts.display: A SHRINKING EARTH BECOMES A PYRAMID
facts.source_title: Gregory, J. W. (1899). The Plan of the Earth and Its Causes. The Geographical Journal 13(3): 225-250 (archive.org scan of the March 1899 issue)
facts.quote: Now, among the regular geometrical figures with approximately equal axes, the tetrahedron is that which contains the smallest volume for a given surface. Hence every hard-shelled body which is diminishing in size, owing to internal contraction, is constantly tending to become tetrahedral in form ... we should find that the whole of that continent is exactly antipodal to the Indian ocean ... and the Arctic ocean is precisely antipodal to the antarctic land.
facts.caveat: OCR typos corrected ('figitres', 'fornu'). Gregory also called the 'triangular shape of the geographical units ... with the bases to the north' a textbook fact. B. K. Emerson's 1900 paper in the GSA Bulletin, 'The tetrahedral earth and the zone of the intercontinental seas' (11:61-106), shows the idea had US support too.

facts.claim: By 1918 a children's magazine was telling readers that scientists expected Earth to become a tetrahedron. It cited the polar discoveries (an ocean at the North Pole, a continent at the South Pole) as confirmation.
facts.spoken_form: By nineteen eighteen, a children's magazine was telling kids that one day the Earth would turn into a pyramid, and that the great polar explorers had proved it.
facts.display: KIDS WERE TAUGHT: EARTH BECOMES PYRAMID
facts.source_title: 'What The World May Come To', My Magazine, May 1918 (transcription hosted by Forgotten Futures)
facts.quote: Men of science believe that in millions of years the earth will lose the shape of a globe and become a sort of pyramid or tetrahedron. ... such is actually the case, as we know from the discoveries of Nansen, Peary, Scott, and Shackleton.
facts.caveat: Transcription on a hobbyist site; I did not check the original scan, and no author is credited. Fine as colour, but don't overclaim: say 'a children's magazine', not 'schools taught'.

facts.claim: The tetrahedral theory was abandoned because it depended on a cooling, shrinking Earth. Once radioactive decay was found to heat the interior, contraction theory lost its engine, and continental drift and later plate tectonics explained the continents' layout instead. The tetrahedron plays no role in modern geology.
facts.spoken_form: So what killed it? The whole idea needed a cooling, shrinking Earth. Then scientists discovered radioactivity heating the planet from inside, and the shrinking engine stalled. Drifting continents explained the map better, and the pyramid quietly vanished from geology.
facts.source_title: Wikipedia: 'Tetrahedral hypothesis' and 'Geophysical global cooling' (secondary; primary: Holmes, A. 1925, Geological Magazine; Holmes 1944, Principles of Physical Geology, p. 32)
facts.quote: the tetrahedral shape plays no special role in modern theories ... After radioactive decay was discovered, it was realized it would release heat inside the planet. This undermines the cooling effect upon which the shrinking planet theory is based.
facts.caveat: Both sources are secondary (two Wikipedia articles). Arthur Holmes (1925, Geological Magazine) wrote that geologists rejected the thermal contraction theory as inadequate by itself. Even Gregory (1899) had to answer the objection that Earth is measurably an oblate spheroid, not a tetrahedron. Say 'faded out' rather than give a single year.

facts.claim: The name 'continental drip' was coined as a joke by writer Ormonde de Kay Jr. in Horizon magazine (Winter 1973), and later reprinted in More Random Walks in Science (1982, pp. 201-203). It spoofed plate tectonics, which was then brand new.
facts.spoken_form: The name came in nineteen seventy-three, as a joke. A magazine writer called it continental drip, a fake theory you could prove just by staring at a map.
facts.source_title: Wikipedia: 'Continental drip', citing de Kay, O. Jr., 'Continental Drip', Horizon (Winter 1973), in Weber, R. L. (ed.), More Random Walks in Science (1982), pp. 201-203
facts.quote: The observation was made by Ormonde de Kay in a 1973 tongue-in-cheek paper, which he introduced as "another earth-shaking new theory derived from simply looking at maps."
facts.caveat: I did not see the original Horizon text; the anthology's contents list does include 'Continental drip'. Wikipedia lists his examples as Baja, Florida, and all of Europe's peninsulas except Jutland.

facts.claim: In 1976 John C. Holden published the parody 'Fake Tectonics and Continental Drip' in the Journal of Irreproducible Results 22(2): 26-27. It claimed every continent is teardrop-shaped, with its point aimed at where it came from. FAKE stood for 'Final Answers for the Knowledge of Earth tectonics'.
facts.spoken_form: Three years later, a geologist named John Holden ran with the joke in a science humor journal. Every continent, he wrote, is a teardrop, and the point shows the direction it came from.
facts.source_title: Holden, J. C. (1976). Fake tectonics and continental drip. Journal of Irreproducible Results 22(2): 26-27; reprinted with permission in Austral. Syst. Bot. Soc. Newsletter 68 (Sept 1991), pp. 20-21
facts.quote: However, the outlines of all continents are tear-drop shaped, with the pointed ends trending south indicating the directions from which they have come. This startling concept is called "continental drip", and is the essential concept of "Fake tectonics", the acronym for Final Answers for the Knowledge of Earth tectonics.
facts.caveat: Read directly from the 1991 authorised reprint. Holden signed as 'Mazama Institute of Geotectonic Redundancies, Winthrop, Washington' (a joke affiliation). The JIR figure is copyrighted, so recreate it rather than reproduce it.

facts.claim: Holden's gags: because drips flow down, maps must be upside down (south should be on top); Antarctica is an 'anti-drip' that can't decide which way to flow; and the continents will re-merge as 'Pangooy' in a 'continental splash' on a Tuesday at 9:00 a.m. in 1,786,379 A.D.
facts.spoken_form: His punchline: drips always flow down, so our maps are upside down. Antarctica can't decide which way to drip. And all the continents will splash back together on a Tuesday, at nine in the morning, in the year one million, seven hundred eighty-six thousand, three hundred seventy-nine.
facts.source_title: Holden (1976), JIR 22(2): 26-27, reprinted in Austral. Syst. Bot. Soc. Newsletter 68 (1991)
facts.quote: the south pole should be at the top of the globe and the north pole on the bottom because, as we all know, drips should always flow down. ... Antarctica, being situated at the top of the globe, has not yet made up its mind which way to flow ... this event will occur on Tuesday morning at 9:00 a.m. 1,786,379 A.D. The resulting new universal landmass (excluding Antarctica) is called "Pangooy", and the event is termed "continental splash"
facts.caveat: This is satire, so label it clearly as the joke. Under the owner's few-numbers rule, the year can go on a gag card instead of being spoken.

facts.claim: The joker was a real Pangaea mapper. With Robert S. Dietz, Holden co-authored 'Reconstruction of Pangaea: Breakup and dispersion of continents, Permian to Present' (Journal of Geophysical Research 75(26): 4939-4956, 1970). His parody cites that real paper and Wegener's real 'pole-flight' idea. Its 'the point shows where it came from' line matches the real reconstructions, in which the southern tips sat against Antarctica.
facts.spoken_form: Here's the twist. The man who wrote the joke had drawn the real maps of Pangaea breaking apart, six years earlier. And his joke cited them. The punchline was the answer all along.
facts.display: THE JOKER DREW THE REAL MAPS
facts.source_title: Holden (1976) parody text (ASBS 1991 reprint); Dietz, R. S. & Holden, J. C. (1970), JGR 75(26): 4939-4956, doi:10.1029/JB075i026p04939
facts.quote: Actually, fake tectonics can be traced back to the early historical development of continental drift, when Wegener (1929) referred to the continents' flight away from the poles, or "polarfluchtkraft". A step in the right direction was made by Dietz and Holden (1970), when they recognized that there was only a "sudpolarfluchtkraft" (south polar fleeing force).
facts.caveat: JGR citation verified via Crossref. Dietz & Holden also published 'The Breakup of Pangaea' in Scientific American (Oct 1970). The reprint spells the coinages without umlauts ('sudpolarfluchtkraft', 'sudpolarfluchttrofeln'); Wikipedia uses the umlauted forms. 'The punchline matches the real answer' is our framing.

facts.claim: Wegener started from the same map shapes Bacon had noticed. In a letter to his future wife (December 1910) he asked whether South America's east coast fits Africa's west coast as if the two had once been joined.
facts.spoken_form: In nineteen ten, a young German weather scientist wrote to his future wife: doesn't South America fit against Africa, as if they were once joined? This is an idea I'll have to pursue.
facts.display: 'AS IF THEY HAD ONCE BEEN JOINED'
facts.source_title: NASA Earth Observatory / NASA Science, 'Alfred Wegener' (biography feature)
facts.quote: "Doesn't the east coast of South America fit exactly against the west coast of Africa, as if they had once been joined?" wrote Wegener to his future wife in December 1910. "This is an idea I'll have to pursue."
facts.caveat: English translation. An AWI article (Polarforschung 2005) dates the letter to January 1911, so say 'around 1910'.

facts.claim: Wegener presented continental drift on 6 January 1912 in Frankfurt and published the book in 1915. Because of World War I, it went unnoticed outside Germany until the 1922 third edition was translated.
facts.spoken_form: In January nineteen twelve, Alfred Wegener stood up in Frankfurt and told geologists the continents move. Three years later he wrote the book. Then a world war buried it.
facts.source_title: NASA Earth Observatory / NASA Science, 'Alfred Wegener'
facts.quote: Just a few months later, on January 6, 1912, Wegener startled a meeting of the Geological Association in Frankfurt with his radical theory. ... published in 1915. Because of the First World War, Wegener's book went unnoticed outside Germany. In 1922, however, a third (revised) edition was translated into English, French, Russian, Spanish, and Swedish
facts.caveat: Book title: Die Entstehung der Kontinente und Ozeane. USGS (This Dynamic Earth) adds that Ortelius had already suggested in 1596 that the Americas were 'torn away from Europe and Africa'.

facts.claim: Wegener was ridiculed. The president of the American Philosophical Society called drift 'utter, damned rot', another American said accepting it meant forgetting 70 years of learning, and Wegener could not get a professorship at any German university.
facts.spoken_form: The reaction was brutal. One society president called it utter, damned rot. Another scientist said believing it meant forgetting everything geologists had learned in seventy years.
facts.source_title: NASA Earth Observatory / NASA Science, 'Alfred Wegener'
facts.quote: "Utter, damned rot!" said the president of the prestigious American Philosophical Society. "If we are to believe [this] hypothesis, we must forget everything we have learned in the last 70 years and start all over again," said another American scientist. ... Because of this abuse, Wegener could not get a professorship at any German university.
facts.caveat: These quotes are widely repeated, but I did not check the primary sources. The '70 years' line is usually credited to R. T. Chamberlin at the AAPG New York symposium (15 Nov 1926; proceedings published 1928). Don't name the speakers on screen without a primary source. Graz (Austria) made Wegener a professor in 1924.

facts.claim: The main objection was the missing force. Wegener's candidates, a centrifugal 'flight from the poles' and tidal forces, were too weak. In his 1929 edition he admitted, 'The Newton of drift theory has not yet appeared.' Mantle convection, which he also discussed, is today's leading candidate.
facts.spoken_form: Critics had one killer question: what could possibly push a continent? Wegener guessed Earth's spin and tides. Both were far too weak. He admitted it himself: the Newton of drift theory has not yet appeared.
facts.display: 'THE NEWTON OF DRIFT ... NOT YET APPEARED'
facts.source_title: NASA Earth Observatory / NASA Science, 'Alfred Wegener'
facts.quote: His major problem was finding a force or forces that could make the continents "plow around in the mantle," as one critic put it. Wegener tentatively suggested two candidates: centrifugal force caused by the rotation of the Earth, and tidal-type waves in the Earth itself ... "The Newton of drift theory has not yet appeared."
facts.caveat: The rotation-based force is Wegener's 'Polflucht' (flight from the poles), the idea Holden parodied. Harold Jeffreys showed these forces were far too small.

facts.claim: Wegener died on the Greenland ice sheet in November 1930. The last photo shows him leaving the mid-ice station Eismitte on 1 November 1930, his 50th birthday. His body was found on 12 May 1931; his companion Rasmus Villumsen was never found.
facts.spoken_form: On his fiftieth birthday, Wegener left a camp in the middle of the Greenland ice. He never made it back. They found his body the next May, carefully buried in the snow by his companion, who vanished into the ice.
facts.source_title: NASA Earth Observatory / NASA Science, 'Alfred Wegener'
facts.quote: The last photo of Alfred Wegener and Rasmus Villumsen, taken on 1 November 1930 (Wegener's 50th birthday) as they were leaving the "Eismitte" Station. ... On May 12, 1931, they found Wegener's body. ... Though a long, exhaustive search was made, the faithful Greenlander's body was never found.
facts.caveat: The exact date of death is unknown (mid to late November 1930); the presumed cause is heart failure from overexertion. The photos on the NASA page are (c) AWI, not public domain.

facts.claim: The proof came from the seafloor. From the 1950s on, magnetometers found 'zebra' stripes of normal and reversed magnetism running parallel to the mid-ocean ridges, mirrored on both sides. Vine and Matthews (Nature, September 1963) explained them as seafloor spreading, 33 years after Wegener's death.
facts.spoken_form: The proof was hiding on the ocean floor: stripes of magnetized rock, mirrored on both sides of the mid-ocean ridges, like a tape recording of new seafloor being made. It was published in nineteen sixty-three, thirty-three years after Wegener died.
facts.source_title: USGS, This Dynamic Earth, 'Developing the theory'; Vine, F. J. & Matthews, D. H. (1963), Magnetic Anomalies Over Oceanic Ridges, Nature 199: 947-949
facts.quote: By explaining both the zebralike magnetic striping and the construction of the mid-ocean ridge system, the seafloor spreading hypothesis quickly gained converts and represented another major advance in the development of the plate-tectonics theory.
facts.caveat: Vine-Matthews citation verified via Crossref (Nature 199(4897): 947-949, Sept 1963). Lawrence Morley reached the same idea independently, and Harry Hess proposed seafloor spreading in 1962. '33 years' = 1963 minus 1930.

facts.claim: In reconstructions of Gondwana, Antarctica is the centrepiece, with South America, Africa, India and Australia fitted around it. Geologists have called it the 'keypiece' of Gondwana since Du Toit's 1937 book.
facts.spoken_form: Run the clock back and the southern continents lock together into one supercontinent, Gondwana. At its heart sits Antarctica. Geologists call it the keypiece.
facts.source_title: Dalziel, I. W. D. (2013). Antarctica and supercontinental evolution: clues and puzzles. Earth and Environmental Science Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh 104: 3-16 (abstract via Crossref)
facts.quote: Antarctica has been known as the "keypiece" of the Gondwana supercontinent since publication of Du Toit's 1937 classic book Our Wandering Continents.
facts.caveat: NASA's Wegener feature adds that once Africa, Antarctica, Australia and India are put back together as Gondwanaland, the Permo-Carboniferous glacial deposits 'clustered neatly around the South Pole'.

facts.claim: Gondwana began tearing apart in the Jurassic. Huge Karoo-Ferrar lava floods around 183 million years ago came first. The first ocean crust between Africa and Antarctica formed about 155 million years ago, and South America and Africa had fully split from Antarctica by the Early Cretaceous (chron M14N).
facts.spoken_form: It started in the age of dinosaurs. About a hundred and fifty-five million years ago, the first sliver of new ocean opened between Africa and Antarctica.
facts.source_title: Jokat, W., Boebel, T., Konig, M. & Meyer, U. (2003). Timing and geometry of early Gondwana breakup. Journal of Geophysical Research 108(B9), doi:10.1029/2002JB001802
facts.quote: In the Riiser-Larsen Sea/Mozambique Basin, the first oceanic crust between Africa and Antarctica formed around 155 Ma. ... At chron M14N, South America and Africa finally were split off the Antarctic continent.
facts.caveat: Ages depend on which magnetic timescale is used. Duncan et al. (1997, JGR 102: 18127) date the Karoo lavas to 183 +/- 1 Ma and write that 'Seafloor spreading and dispersion of east and west Gondwana followed some 10-20 m.y. afterward.' Each piece broke off at a different time, tens of millions of years apart.

facts.claim: The South Atlantic opened from south to north, like a zipper. Rifting began in the south in the Late Jurassic. Seafloor spreading started in the southern segment around 138-127 million years ago, and the last connection near the equator broke around 104-103 million years ago.
facts.spoken_form: And the Atlantic between Africa and South America unzipped from the bottom up. The south tore open first. The last seam, near the equator, didn't let go for another twenty-five million years or so.
facts.display: THE ATLANTIC UNZIPPED SOUTH TO NORTH
facts.source_title: Torsvik, T. H. et al. (2009). A new scheme for the opening of the South Atlantic Ocean and the dissection of an Aptian salt basin. Geophys. J. Int. 177: 1315-1333; Heine, C., Zoethout, J. & Muller, R. D. (2013). Kinematics of the South Atlantic rift. Solid Earth 4: 215-253
facts.quote: Rifting began in the south in the late Jurassic ... incorporating south-to-north opening of the ocean [Torsvik 2009] ... Final break-up between South America and Africa occurred in the conjugate Santos-Benguela margin segment at around 113 Ma and in the equatorial Atlantic domain between the Ghanaian Ridge and the Piaui-Ceara margin at 103 Ma. [Heine 2013]
facts.caveat: 'Zipper' is our metaphor. In detail the opening was diachronous and happened in phases; within the central segment, Heine et al. find break-up began first in the Sergipe-Alagoas segment (in the north). Heine dates the start of normal seafloor spreading in the southern segment to around 127 Ma, with spreading beginning in isolated compartments in the far south around 138 Ma. The Torsvik quotes are extracted clauses because the full sentence is over 125 characters. Jokat 2003 dates the first South Atlantic oceanic crust to chron M9N (~130 Ma).

facts.claim: When Gondwana broke up, Antarctica stayed almost still while the other pieces moved away. Africa and Australia moved at 2-4 cm (about 1-1.5 inches) a year. India raced at 18-20 cm (about 7-8 inches) a year in the Late Cretaceous, then slowed to about 5 cm a year after hitting Asia about 50 million years ago. One proposed reason: India's lithospheric root is only about 100 km deep, against 180-300 km for its siblings.
facts.spoken_form: Antarctica barely moved. Everyone else left. And India sprinted, up to about eight inches a year, several times faster than Africa or Australia, until it slammed into Asia.
facts.source_title: Kumar, P. et al. (2007). The rapid drift of the Indian tectonic plate. Nature 449: 894-897 (abstract via Europe PMC)
facts.quote: Plate reconstructions based on palaeomagnetic data suggest that the Indian plate attained a very high speed (18-20 cm yr(-1) during the late Cretaceous period) subsequent to its breakup from Gondwanaland, and then slowed to approximately 5 cm yr(-1) after the continental collision with Asia approximately 50 Myr ago. The Australian and African plates moved comparatively less distance and at much lower speeds of 2-4 cm yr(-1) (refs 3-5). Antarctica remained almost stationary.
facts.caveat: The speeds come from paleomagnetic reconstructions; later work (e.g. van Hinsbergen et al. 2011) finds similar peaks (~15-18 cm/yr). The thin-root explanation is the authors' hypothesis. India separated from Madagascar about 88 Ma (Storey et al. 1995, Science 267: 852).

facts.claim: A 2022 paper argues the cause runs the opposite way to what you'd guess. South America was already wedge-shaped when Gondwana split, and that southward taper controlled how the South Atlantic opened, making the opening asymmetric and faster and wider in the south. The paper treats the taper as a starting condition and does not explain where it came from.
facts.spoken_form: One recent study flips the question around. It argues South America's wedge shape didn't come from the Atlantic opening. The wedge was already there, and it steered how the ocean opened, wider and faster in the south.
facts.source_title: Gao, D. (2022). Continental tapering of South America caused asymmetric non-uniform opening of the South Atlantic Ocean. Communications Earth & Environment 3: 278, doi:10.1038/s43247-022-00587-3
facts.quote: Here I use geological and geophysical data to inform analytical modelling, revealing that westward drifting and southward tapering of the South American continent have controlled the asymmetry and the non-uniformity in South Atlantic opening. ... The splitting of the supercontinent to the tapering continent of South America set the initial boundary condition for South Atlantic opening.
facts.caveat: The high confidence is about what the paper says, not that the question is settled. It is a single-author analytical model (West Virginia University), and it also claims its mechanism 'undermines the classical theory of thermal convection and upwelling as active drivers', which is a minority position. Cite it only in the direction taper -> opening. Owner override: no citation in the video; say 'one recent study'.

facts.claim: The best expert answer we found: the southward points of Africa, South America and India are largely a legacy of Gondwana's breakup. The pieces drifted apart but kept their orientation, so their points still aim toward the South Pole, where they were once joined to Antarctica. Australia, from the same breakup, 'points' north, and smaller peninsulas have no single explanation. We found no peer-reviewed study that sets out to explain the taper itself.
facts.spoken_form: So here's the honest answer most geologists would give. The big drips are scars. Africa, South America and India broke off a supercontinent built around Antarctica, and they still point back toward where they tore away. The small drips? No single answer.
facts.source_title: Geological Society of London, 'Ask a Geologist: Why Do Most Peninsulas Point South?', answered by Ted Nield (editor, Geoscientist), c. 2009
facts.quote: largely a legacy of the breakup of Gondwana ... drifted away from each other while preserving their general orientation, with the "point" directed to the South Pole ... to my eyes at least "points" north
facts.caveat: The GSL page now redirects. The quote fragments come from the search engine's index of the page, not a live read (web.archive.org was unreachable). Nield also says peninsulas 'can have no single geological explanation', and gives Cape York, Arnhem Land and the Kola Peninsula as examples that point north. 'No peer-reviewed study explains the taper' comes from our own literature search: Gao 2022 takes the taper as given.

facts.claim: Continents split along branching rifts that meet at triple junctions, and you can watch one happening now. In Afar, Ethiopia, a Y-shaped rift system is tearing Arabia away from Africa while Africa itself starts to split. Rifts that meet at angles cut continents into wedge-shaped pieces.
facts.spoken_form: You can watch a continent being cut into wedges right now. In Ethiopia, three cracks meet in a giant Y. One arm made the Red Sea, one the Gulf of Aden, and the third is slowly unzipping East Africa.
facts.display: AFAR: A CONTINENT CRACKING IN A 'Y'
facts.source_title: Geological Society of London, Plate Tectonics: 'Triple Junction: The Red Sea/East Africa'
facts.quote: The Afar region in Northern Ethiopia is the centre of a "Y" shaped rift system, where the continental lithosphere is being stretched and is splitting. ... The point in the Afar region where the boundaries of all three plates meet is called a Triple Junction.
facts.caveat: The Afar facts are solid. 'Rifts meeting at angles make wedges' is a geometric inference, not a published explanation of the southern tapers. Burke & Dewey (1973, J. Geol. 81: 406-433) proposed that mantle plumes generate rift-rift-rift junctions, and the Benue Trough in Nigeria is often called the failed third arm of the South Atlantic junction, but that model is debated.

facts.claim: Greenland's point has a different origin from the Gondwana tips. Greenland sits between two branches of North Atlantic rifting: the now-extinct Labrador Sea-Baffin Bay rift to the west (spreading from about 62 million years ago) and the North Atlantic to the east (breakup about 54-56 million years ago). Conventional models have Greenland drifting as its own plate in the Paleogene, which some geologists dispute.
facts.spoken_form: Greenland's point is a different scar. About sixty million years ago, it was caught between two cracks: one opening the Labrador Sea toward Canada, the other the Atlantic toward Europe. Both were wider in the south. The result is a wedge pointing south.
facts.source_title: Pulvertaft, T. C. R. & Dawes, P. R. (2011). North Atlantic spreading axes terminate in the continental cul-de-sacs of Baffin Bay and the Laptev Sea. Canadian Journal of Earth Sciences 48(3): 593-601 (GEUS abstract); see also Oakey & Chalmers (2012), JGR 117, doi:10.1029/2011JB008942
facts.quote: In conventional plate-tectonic models, an independent Greenland plate is supposed to have drifted in the Paleogene along a transform fault through Nares Strait that links the two branches of the North Atlantic spreading system.
facts.caveat: Pulvertaft & Dawes themselves argue against the independent plate. The ~62 Ma (chron 27) start of Labrador Sea spreading and the ~54-56 Ma NE Atlantic breakup come from search summaries of Oakey & Chalmers 2012 and NGU work, not from text I read verbatim. 'Both rifts widen south, making the wedge' is our interpretation (the geography does narrow northward at Davis/Nares Strait and Fram Strait). Labrador Sea spreading stopped in the Eocene-Oligocene (dates vary from 45 to 33 Ma).

facts.claim: Baja California has a separate, young cause. About 6 million years ago the Pacific-North America plate boundary moved into the Gulf of California, and since then the Pacific Plate has carried Baja at least 276 km (about 170 miles) away from mainland Mexico.
facts.spoken_form: Baja is a different story entirely. About six million years ago, the Pacific Plate grabbed it and started dragging it away from Mexico. It's moved at least a hundred and seventy miles so far, and it's still going.
facts.display: BAJA: TORN AWAY ~6 MILLION YEARS AGO
facts.source_title: Oskin, M. & Stock, J. (2003). Pacific-North America plate motion and opening of the Upper Delfin basin, northern Gulf of California, Mexico. GSA Bulletin 115(10): 1173-1190 (Caltech abstract)
facts.quote: Addition of deformation from the continental margins of this basin indicates at least 276 +/- 13 km of Pacific-North America plate motion between coastal Sonora and the main gulf escarpment in Baja California since ca. 6 Ma ... but require that the Pacific-North America plate boundary became localized in the gulf at ca. 6 Ma.
facts.caveat: Rifting in a proto-Gulf began earlier (~12 Ma), and true seafloor spreading in some gulf basins began only ~3.5 Ma. Say 'about six million years ago' for the main tear. Current motion is roughly 45-50 mm/yr (about 2 in/yr).

facts.claim: Florida isn't a rift fragment at all. It is the exposed top of a huge carbonate platform: a tall underwater plateau of limestone and dolomite 2-6 km (about 1.25-3.75 miles) thick. Reef organisms built it in warm, shallow seas like today's Bahamas while its basement slowly sank, between about 180 and 60 million years ago.
facts.spoken_form: And Florida? It's not a drip at all. It's the top of a gigantic reef. Up to nearly four miles of limestone, built by tiny sea creatures in warm shallow water, like the Bahamas today.
facts.display: FLORIDA: UP TO ~4 MILES OF REEF ROCK
facts.source_title: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Gulf of Mexico 2018 expedition log (1 May): the Florida Escarpment
facts.quote: The Florida Escarpment is the western edge of a large carbonate platform that encompasses the Florida Peninsula. The platform is a tall underwater plateau (Figure 3) composed of carbonate rocks that were produced by biological organisms in warm, shallow, and tropical waters, very similar to the modern islands of the Bahamas. ... a platform of limestone and dolomite rock, with intermittent salt layers, that is between two and six kilometers (~1.25 and 3.75 miles) thick.
facts.caveat: The dry-land outline of the peninsula is set mainly by sea level on top of the platform, and the platform is much wider than the peninsula. NOAA's Figure 3 is 'courtesy of A. Hine, 2009', so it is not public domain.

facts.claim: Under Florida's limestone is basement rock that started out in Gondwana, next to West Africa (or South America). Its zircon ages match African and South American mountain-building events. That piece stayed attached to North America when Pangaea split.
facts.spoken_form: But dig under the limestone and there's a twist. Florida's deepest bedrock started out on the other side of the Atlantic, next to West Africa, as a piece of Gondwana that got left behind.
facts.source_title: Mueller, P. A. et al. (1994). Precambrian zircons from the Florida basement: A Gondwanan connection. Geology 22: 119-122 (USGS publication record)
facts.quote: clearly places the basement of Florida in Gondwanaland proximal to the West African and/or Trans-Amazonian-San Luis cratons
facts.caveat: Clause-level quote (the full sentence is over 125 characters). The Suwannee terrane joined North America while Pangaea was assembling (Paleozoic) and stayed when the Atlantic opened. Say 'next to West Africa', not 'a piece of Africa'.

facts.claim: Is there a deep reason the land piled up in the north? One leading model says mantle convection alternates between two patterns. When continents are scattered it is lopsided ('degree-1': one hemisphere upwelling, the other sinking); when a supercontinent exists it is two-sided ('degree-2'). Today's mantle is largely the two-sided kind, with superplumes under Africa and the Pacific, so there is no evidence of a one-sided mantle forcing land north today. The current northern bias is best treated as a snapshot of drifting plates.
facts.spoken_form: Is something deep inside Earth pushing the land north? Some models say the mantle can churn lopsided, up on one side and down on the other. But today's mantle isn't built that way. Most likely, this is just one frame of a very slow movie.
facts.source_title: Zhong, S., Zhang, N., Li, Z.-X. & Roberts, J. H. (2007). Supercontinent cycles, true polar wander, and very long-wavelength mantle convection. Earth and Planetary Science Letters 261: 551-564
facts.quote: mobile-lid mantle convection ... is characterized by either a spherical harmonic degree-1 planform with a major upwelling in one hemisphere and a major downwelling in the other hemisphere when continents are absent, or a degree-2 planform with two antipodal major upwellings when a supercontinent is present. ... Our model suggests that the largely degree-2 structure for the present-day mantle with the Africa and Pacific antipodal superplumes, is a natural consequence of this dynamic process
facts.caveat: Abstract read from a repository mirror (geologyscience.ru) of the Elsevier abstract. 'No evidence that a one-sided mantle is forcing land north today' is our inference, not the paper's claim; there is no consensus deep cause. In the late Paleozoic, Gondwana sat over the South Pole (NASA). Kumar 2007 notes that Antarctica stayed put while Africa, India and Australia moved away. Geoscience Australia says Australia's plate 'travels around seven centimetres each year' (to the north-east).

facts.claim: Real geology does have drips. Under California's southern Sierra Nevada, the dense root of the mountains has been peeling off and sinking into the mantle as a 'drip' beneath the Great Valley. This Rayleigh-Taylor instability began 10 to 3 million years ago.
facts.spoken_form: Here's the strangest part. Continental drip started as a joke, but geologists have since found real drips. Under California's Sierra Nevada, the heavy root of the mountains is peeling off and sinking slowly into the Earth.
facts.display: REAL DRIP: UNDER THE SIERRA NEVADA
facts.source_title: Zandt, G. et al. (2004). Active foundering of a continental arc root beneath the southern Sierra Nevada in California. Nature 431: 41-46 (abstract via Europe PMC)
facts.quote: The removal appears to have initiated between 10 and 3 Myr ago with a Rayleigh-Taylor-type instability, but with a pronounced asymmetric flow into a mantle downwelling (drip) beneath the adjacent Great Valley.
facts.caveat: These drips sink downward into the mantle and have nothing to do with continents pointing south. Frame them as an ironic twist, not an explanation.

facts.claim: In 2009, seismologists found a cold blob of lithosphere dripping into the mantle beneath central Nevada. It is about 100 km wide and at least 500 km tall (about 60 by 300 miles), and was described as 'honey dripping off a spoon'. The lead scientist admitted he had long been 'anti-drip'.
facts.spoken_form: And under Nevada sits a drip about sixty miles wide and at least three hundred miles tall, like honey sliding off a spoon. The scientist who found it admitted he'd been anti-drip his whole career.
facts.display: NEVADA DRIP: 60 MI WIDE, 300+ MI DEEP
facts.source_title: ScienceDaily / NSF-ASU release (26 May 2009) on West, J. D., Fouch, M. J., Roth, J. B. & Elkins-Tanton, L. T. (2009). Vertical mantle flow associated with a lithospheric drip beneath the Great Basin. Nature Geoscience 2: 439-444
facts.quote: A lithospheric drip can be envisioned as honey dripping off a spoon, where an initial lithospheric blob is followed by a long tail of material. ... a large cylindrical mass 100 km wide and at least 500 km tall (about 60 by 300 miles). "As a general rule, I have been anti-drip since my early days as a scientist," admits Fouch.
facts.caveat: This is a press release about a peer-reviewed paper (Crossref: Nat. Geosci. 2: 439-444, doi:10.1038/ngeo526). The team thinks the drip started 15-20 million years ago and has little surface effect. The interpretation has been debated.

facts.claim: In Turkey's Central Anatolia, a 2024 study links the rapidly sinking Konya Basin to a lithospheric drip inside a rising plateau. A 2022 study by the same group attributes basins on the Andes' Puna Plateau (e.g. the Arizaro Basin) to similar dripping.
facts.spoken_form: Turkey has one too. A basin in the middle of a rising plateau is sinking, and lab models suggest a drip of rock is pulling it down from below.
facts.display: TURKEY: A BASIN PULLED DOWN FROM BELOW
facts.source_title: Andersen, A. J., Gogus, O. H., Pysklywec, R. N., Sengul Uluocak, E. & Santimano, T. (2024). Multistage lithospheric drips control active basin formation within an uplifting orogenic plateau. Nature Communications 15 (abstract via Europe PMC); Andersen et al. (2022), Communications Earth & Environment 3: 150
facts.quote: Using scaled laboratory (analogue) experiments we show that the active formation of the Konya Basin may be accounted for by the descent of a mantle lithospheric drip causing local circular-shaped surface subsidence. We interpret that the Konya Basin is developing through a secondary drip pulse that is contemporaneous with broad plateau uplift caused by a larger-scale lithospheric drip since the Miocene.
facts.caveat: The subsidence is measured (GNSS/InSAR); the drip is an interpretation based on models ('may be accounted for'). The 2022 Andes abstract says 'the formation of the Arizaro Basin and nearby Central Andean basins are caused by symptomatic lithospheric dripping events' (from analogue models).

result.notes:
The full ledger, with the same 30 facts, is saved as JSON at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/script/research-science/facts_ledger.json. Downloaded primary texts are under /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/script/research-science/dl/ (gao/gao.txt, heine/heine.txt, green/green.txt, gregory/gj.txt, holden/asbs.txt, wegener/nasa.txt, usgs/*.txt).

THE HONEST ANSWER, AS A STORY:
(1) Big drips = scars of Gondwana. Antarctica was the 'keypiece'. The first ocean crust between Africa and Antarctica formed ~155 Ma. The South Atlantic opened south to north (rifting began in the south in the Late Jurassic; the last link broke at the equator ~103 Ma). Antarctica 'remained almost stationary' while India sprinted (~8 in/yr). The points face where the pieces tore away (expert answer: Ted Nield, GSL). Rifts that meet at triple junctions (Afar today) cut wedges; that last link is our inference.
(2) Gao 2022 only says taper -> asymmetric opening. It takes the taper as given and is a contrarian, single-author model. We found NO peer-reviewed paper explaining why the southern continents taper. Say 'nobody has a single tidy answer'.
(3) Small drips have separate causes: Baja (the Pacific Plate grabbed it ~6 Ma, 170+ mi), Florida (a reef platform up to ~4 mi thick, with Gondwanan bedrock beneath), Greenland (between two rifts, ~60 Ma; the independent-plate model is debated).
(4) North-heavy land: there is no evidence of a deep one-sided (degree-1) mantle driving it today (Zhong 2007: today's mantle is degree-2), so call it a snapshot. This is a medium-confidence inference.

BEST STORY BEATS:
- Gregory (1899) already said that North America is exactly antipodal to the Indian Ocean. That ties directly to the brief's S3 'dig from Kansas' beat.
- Green was Hawaii's foreign minister and demonstrated the tips with a bent card in water (1857).
- A 1918 children's magazine said Earth would become a pyramid and cited Scott and Shackleton (medium confidence).
- Holden's joke says 'pointed ends ... indicating the directions from which they have come'. That is essentially the real answer, and the parody cites Dietz & Holden 1970 plus Wegener's 'polarfluchtkraft'. Verified from the 1991 authorised reprint; JIR 22(2): 26-27.
- Real lithospheric drips exist (Sierra Nevada, Nature 2004; under Nevada, 60 x 300+ mi, 'honey dripping off a spoon', scientist was 'anti-drip'; Konya Basin, Turkey 2024; Puna, Andes 2022). They drip DOWN, not south, so use them as the ironic closer for S8 or the finale.

UNVERIFIED / CAVEATS:
- de Kay 1973: original not seen (via Wikipedia).
- Nield GSL page now redirects; the quote comes from the search index; archive.org's Wayback Machine was blocked.
- Wegener ridicule quotes come from NASA (secondary), and the speakers are not verified.
- Torsvik quotes are clause-level.
- Wegener's letter is dated Dec 1910 (NASA) vs Jan 1911 (AWI).
- Baja: plate boundary localized ~6 Ma, but some spreading began ~3.5 Ma.
- Greenland timing comes from search summaries.
- I could not retrieve the Scotese 2021 land-fraction-through-time figures (403), so I avoided specific past northern/southern land percentages. MinuteEarth's '70% of land south at Pangaea' is unsourced, so don't use it.
- Florida claim: say 'next to West Africa', not 'a piece of Africa'.

FEW-NUMBERS OVERRIDE: suggested hero numbers from this ledger are India ~8 in/yr, Baja ~6 million years / 170 mi, the Nevada drip at 300 miles, and 1875/1912/1930 as story dates. Everything else can be told as images.

Andes drip is folded into the Anatolia fact. Kamchatka, Korea, Italy and Scandinavia were searched but not ledgered for lack of space: Kamchatka is a volcanic arc over Pacific subduction made of accreted terranes; the Sea of Japan back-arc opened ~18-15 Ma; Italy is shaped by Adria rollback and counterclockwise rotation; the Norwegian margin broke up ~54 Ma. All of these need sourcing before use.

facts.claim: Pangaea Proxima, first named 'Pangaea Ultima', is Christopher Scotese's future-supercontinent model. In it the Atlantic stops widening and closes, and the Americas rejoin Europe and Africa in about 250 million years. It is a model scenario, not a prediction.
facts.spoken_form: One model, from geologist Christopher Scotese, has the Atlantic slamming shut and America crashing back into Africa in about two hundred fifty million years.
facts.source_title: Pangaea Proxima (Wikipedia, citing Scotese 2003/2021, Williams & Nield, New Scientist 2007). Cross-check: NASA APOD 2 Oct 2000, 'Pangea Ultima: Earth in 250 Million Years?' (Credit & Copyright: C. R. Scotese, PALEOMAP)
facts.quote: This potential configuration, hypothesized by Christopher Scotese in November 1982, earned its name from its similarity to the ancient Pangaea supercontinent.
facts.caveat: The 1982 date comes only from Wikipedia; the primary Paleomap page (scotese.com) was unreachable. The 250-Myr timescale and the Atlantic closing are confirmed by APOD 2000 and Scotese's own Paleomap material. Scotese's maps are copyrighted, so redraw the configuration with the engine and label it 'MODEL'.

facts.claim: Scotese first called the future supercontinent 'Pangaea Ultima' ('Last Pangaea'). He later renamed it 'Pangaea Proxima' ('Next Pangaea') because 'Ultima' suggested it would be the last supercontinent ever.
facts.spoken_form: He first called it Pangaea Ultima, the last Pangaea. Then he renamed it, because the planet clearly isn't done.
facts.source_title: Pangaea Proxima (Wikipedia, lead section, citing Williams & Nield 2007)
facts.quote: could imply that it would be the last-ever supercontinent
facts.caveat: No date for the rename is known. The 2023 Farnsworth study still uses the name 'Pangea Ultima' for this configuration, so both names are in use and the narration should pick one.

facts.claim: Novopangaea was proposed by Roy Livermore in the late 1990s. Today's motions continue: the Atlantic keeps opening and the Pacific closes. The Americas hit Antarctica, which is drifting north, and then hit Africa-Eurasia. Davies, Green & Duarte (2018) rate it the most likely of the four scenarios.
facts.spoken_form: In the model most of these geologists bet on, nothing changes direction. The Pacific closes, and the Americas crash into Antarctica.
facts.source_title: Davies, Green & Duarte, 'What planet Earth might look like when the next supercontinent forms – four scenarios' (Bangor University / The Conversation, 27 Nov 2018), summarizing Global and Planetary Change 169:133–144 (2018). Proposer: Novopangaea (Wikipedia).
facts.quote: Of these four scenarios we believe that Novopangea is the most likely.
facts.caveat: 'Most likely' is the opinion of three authors, not a consensus. The Livermore/late-1990s attribution comes from Wikipedia, so treat it as medium. Spellings vary: Novopangaea and Novopangea.

facts.claim: Amasia: Yale researchers (Mitchell, Kilian & Evans, Nature, 9 Feb 2012) model the Arctic Ocean and Caribbean closing first, with the Americas meeting Eurasia near the North Pole in 50–200 million years. A different Amasia model from Curtin University (Huang et al., National Science Review, 2022) forms it by closing the Pacific in 200–300 million years.
facts.spoken_form: Another model sends everything north. The Arctic Ocean vanishes, and America meets Asia practically at the North Pole.
facts.source_title: Yale News, 'Next supercontinent forms: Arctic Ocean, Caribbean will vanish first' (8 Feb 2012); Phys.org/Curtin University (30 Sep 2022)
facts.quote: You'd have the Americas meeting Eurasia practically at the North Pole.
facts.caveat: The 50–200 Myr figure was Mitchell speaking to Yale News; the paper itself gives no date. The name 'Amasia' was coined earlier by Paul F. Hoffman (Wikipedia). The 2012 and 2022 Amasias are different models with the same name. Yale: Antarctica may stay separate.

facts.claim: Aurica (Duarte, Schellart & Rosas, Geological Magazine, 2016): both the Atlantic and the Pacific close, a new ocean opens across Asia, and Australia ends up at the centre. The name joins Australia and America.
facts.spoken_form: A third model closes both oceans at once and puts Australia in the middle of everything. Its name is Australia plus America: Aurica.
facts.source_title: Bangor University / The Conversation (27 Nov 2018); Duarte, Schellart & Rosas, Geological Magazine 155:45–58, doi:10.1017/S0016756816000716; Aurica (Wikipedia) for the name
facts.quote: it would be at the centre of the new continent as East Asia and the Americas close the Pacific from either side
facts.caveat: It requires new subduction zones in the Atlantic, which the authors say may already be starting off SW Iberia, but this is speculative. The name's derivation is from Wikipedia and Portuguese press, so medium.

facts.claim: The next supercontinent has been suggested to form in about 200–250 million years. All four named supercontinents are competing computer and geological model scenarios, and the authors call them speculative.
facts.spoken_form: Geologists think the next supercontinent arrives in about two hundred to two hundred fifty million years. They just can't agree on what it looks like.
facts.source_title: Davies, Green & Duarte, Bangor University news (27 Nov 2018)
facts.quote: It has been suggested that the next supercontinent will form in 200-250 million years.
facts.caveat: The time range depends on the model; Amasia's estimates run from 50 to 300 million years. Ronald Blakey (quoted in The Atlantic, 2013) calls projections beyond about 100 million years 'very, very speculative'. Present all four maps as labelled models.

facts.claim: Farnsworth et al. 2023 (Nature Geoscience) simulated the 'Pangea Ultima' supercontinent about 250 million years from now. Only 8–16% of land stayed habitable for mammals, with widespread temperatures of 40–50 °C (104–122 °F). The model assumes humans stop burning fossil fuels.
facts.spoken_form: One study ran the climate on that future supercontinent. Only about one-tenth of the land stayed livable for mammals, with heat over a hundred and twenty degrees.
facts.source_title: University of Bristol press release, 'New research reveals extreme heat likely to wipe out humans and mammals in the distant future' (25 Sep 2023), on Farnsworth et al., Nature Geoscience 16:901–908, doi:10.1038/s41561-023-01259-3
facts.quote: only somewhere between 8% and 16% of land would be habitable for mammals
facts.caveat: This is one study using one geography, Scotese's Ultima/Proxima. Brief rule: say 'one study'. Other quotes: 'Widespread temperatures of between 40 to 50 degrees Celsius', and Mills: 'this assumes that humans will stop burning fossil fuels'. It projects heat stress, not proven extinction.

facts.claim: Where the US ends up depends on the model. Proxima/Ultima: back against Europe and Africa. Amasia: up against Asia over the Arctic. Novopangaea: the Americas hit Antarctica, then Africa-Eurasia. Aurica: the Americas and East Asia close around Australia.
facts.spoken_form: So which continent does America crash into? Depending on the model: Africa, Asia, Antarctica, or Australia. Pick your neighbor.
facts.display: US crashes into: Africa? Asia? Antarctica? Australia?
facts.source_title: Davies, Green & Duarte, Bangor University news (27 Nov 2018); Yale News (2012)
facts.quote: leading to a reforming of Pangea as the Americas, Europe and Africa are brought back together
facts.caveat: This is a synthesis of four model descriptions; each map must be labelled 'MODEL'. The 'pick your neighbor' joke is fine as long as the four-way uncertainty is clear.

facts.claim: USGS: tectonic plates move at roughly the rate your fingernails grow, and GPS can track that motion to within a fraction of a millimetre per year.
facts.spoken_form: Continents move about as fast as your fingernails grow.
facts.source_title: USGS FAQ, 'How fast do tectonic plates move?'
facts.quote: Tectonic plates move roughly at the same rate that your fingernails grow.
facts.caveat: This is an approximation; plate speeds range from under 1 inch to about 6 inches a year. A 1988 NASA JPL release made the same fingernail comparison.

facts.claim: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge spreads about 2.5 cm (about 1 inch) per year. The fastest ridge, the East Pacific Rise near Easter Island, spreads more than 15 cm (about 6 inches) per year. The slowest, the Arctic Ridge, spreads less than 2.5 cm per year.
facts.spoken_form: The Atlantic widens by about an inch a year. Parts of the Pacific floor race along at six.
facts.source_title: USGS, This Dynamic Earth, 'Understanding plate motions'
facts.quote: The rate of spreading along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge averages about 2.5 centimeters per year (cm/yr), or 25 km in a million years.
facts.caveat: These are full spreading rates (both sides combined). The figures are long-term averages from magnetic stripes. Same page: 'The Arctic Ridge has the slowest rate (less than 2.5 cm/yr), and the East Pacific Rise... has the fastest rate (more than 15 cm/yr).'

facts.claim: Fingernails grow about 3.47 mm a month (about 1.6 inches a year) and toenails about 1.62 mm a month (about 0.8 inches a year). This is a small study of 22 healthy American young adults.
facts.spoken_form: Your fingernails grow about an inch and a half a year. Your toenails, less than half that.
facts.source_title: Yaemsiri et al., 'Growth rate of human fingernails and toenails in healthy American young adults', J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 24(4):420–423 (2010)
facts.quote: average fingernail growth rate was faster than that of toenails (3.47 vs. 1.62 mm/month, P < 0.01)
facts.caveat: Conversions are computed (3.47 mm × 12 = 4.16 cm/yr = 1.64 in; 1.62 mm × 12 = 1.94 cm/yr = 0.77 in). The sample of n=22 is small, and growth varies with the person and the finger.

facts.claim: The two US science agencies pick different nails. NOAA says land masses move about 1.5 cm (0.6 inches) a year on average, 'about the rate that human toenails grow'. USGS says fingernails.
facts.spoken_form: Even the government can't agree. One agency says continents move at fingernail speed. Another says toenails.
facts.source_title: NOAA National Ocean Service, 'What is plate tectonics?' (oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/tectonics.html); USGS FAQ
facts.quote: Earth's land masses move toward and away from each other at an average rate of about 1.5 centimeters (0.6 inches) a year. That's about the rate that human toenails grow!
facts.caveat: Both are fair, since they describe different averages. It is a joke beat, not a contradiction to fact-check. Do not name agencies on screen (owner override); 'one agency... another' works.

facts.claim: The Americas and Africa/Europe separate at about 4 cm (about 1.5 inches) a year, which is fingernail speed. A South Atlantic drilling site off South America and Africa (IODP U1558, about 31°S) records a half-spreading rate of about 19.5 mm/yr, a full rate of about 39 mm/yr.
facts.spoken_form: Africa and South America are still drifting apart, about an inch and a half every year. That's exactly fingernail speed.
facts.source_title: University of Southampton press release via EurekAlert (27 Jan 2021) on Wang et al., Nature, doi:10.1038/s41586-020-03139-x; IODP Expedition 390/393 Proceedings, Site U1558 (2024)
facts.quote: The plates attached to the Americas are moving apart from those attached to Europe and Africa by four centimetres per year.
facts.caveat: Rates vary along the ridge, from about 3 to 4 cm/yr in the South Atlantic and lower in the North Atlantic (about 2.4 cm/yr North America–Africa per UCSD Earthguide). Say 'about an inch or so, up to an inch and a half'. IODP quote: 'a slow half spreading rate of ~19.5 mm/y'.

facts.claim: COMPUTED: since Bacon noticed the fit in 1620 (406 years), the Atlantic has widened about 33–53 ft (10–16 m), roughly a school bus or more. And 250 million years at about 1.5 in/yr is about 6,200 miles (10,000 km), a quarter of the way around Earth.
facts.spoken_form: Since Bacon noticed the fit, the Atlantic has grown about a school bus wider. Give it two hundred fifty million years at fingernail speed, and that adds up to a quarter of the way around the planet.
facts.source_title: Computed from USGS This Dynamic Earth (2.5 cm/yr) and the Southampton/EurekAlert 2021 release (4 cm/yr)
facts.quote: This rate may seem slow by human standards, but because this process has been going on for millions of years, it has resulted in plate movement of thousands of kilometers.
facts.caveat: Pure arithmetic: 406 yr × 2.5–4 cm = 10.2–16.2 m (33–53 ft); 250e6 yr × 4 cm = 10,000 km = 6,214 mi = 25% of Earth's circumference. Real motion is not constant or straight-line, so use 'about'. A school bus is about 35–45 ft.

facts.claim: North-up is only a convention. Medieval European world maps put east at the top: the Hereford Mappa Mundi (c. 1300) shows Eden at the top, in the east, with Jerusalem at the centre. 'Orient(ation)' comes from the east-up habit.
facts.spoken_form: For centuries, European maps didn't even put north on top. They put east up, with the Garden of Eden at the top of the world.
facts.source_title: Hereford Cathedral, The Mappa Mundi (themappamundi.co.uk)
facts.quote: The earthly paradise, Eden, is represented by a circular island at the eastern extreme of the world (the top).
facts.caveat: The 'orient' etymology (Latin oriens, 'rising', meaning east) was not verified against a dictionary because etymonline returned 403. Avoid the etymology line or soften it. Dating is c.1300; Commons metadata says c.1250.

facts.claim: Al-Idrisi's world maps, made for King Roger II of Sicily and completed in 1154, put south at the top, following the Balkhi school.
facts.spoken_form: And one of the greatest maps of the Middle Ages, drawn for a king of Sicily, put south at the top.
facts.source_title: Library of Congress, Worlds Revealed blog, Carissa Pastuch, 'Al-Idrisi's Masterpiece of Medieval Geography' (Jan 2022)
facts.quote: Following the Balkhi School of Geography, the maps are oriented with the South at the top and Mecca at the center.
facts.caveat: The oldest surviving copy is c.1325 (BnF MS Arabe 2221); the 1154 original is lost. The Commons image (TabulaRogeriana.jpg) is Konrad Miller's 1929 composite, and the page asks users not to rotate it north-up.

facts.claim: In 1979, 21-year-old Australian Stuart McArthur published the south-up 'McArthur's Universal Corrective Map of the World', to answer 'the perpetual onslaught of Down Under jokes'.
facts.spoken_form: In nineteen seventy-nine, a twenty-one-year-old Australian got so sick of 'Down Under' jokes that he published a world map with Australia on top.
facts.source_title: South-up map orientation (Wikipedia, citing Wood, Kaiser & Abramms, Seeing Through Maps, 2006, pp. 50–51, and the ICA Commission on Map Design 2014); ABC News Australia (8 Aug 2020)
facts.quote: In 1979, twenty-one year old Australian Stuart McArthur published
facts.caveat: Sources differ on his age and status (college or high-school student). The 26 Jan 1979 (Australia Day) launch appears only in secondary sources. The map is still in copyright, so do NOT show it; rotate our own globe south-up instead. The 'Down Under jokes' wording is also in ABC 2020.

facts.claim: The most famous photo of Earth, Apollo 17's 'Blue Marble' (7 Dec 1972), was taken with the South Pole at the top. The version everyone knows was flipped north-up.
facts.spoken_form: Even the most famous photo of Earth was taken with Antarctica on top. It got flipped, because that's how we're used to seeing it.
facts.source_title: The Blue Marble (Wikipedia); Wikimedia Commons file 'Apollo 17 Blue Marble original orientation (AS17-148-22727).jpg' (NASA, public domain)
facts.quote: The original photograph was taken with the South Pole facing the top.
facts.caveat: Wikipedia's wording is somewhat inconsistent ('rotated with south pointing up relative to the capsule'). In zero-g the 'original orientation' is just how the camera was held, so say 'taken with Antarctica on top' and 'published flipped'. Strong visual: show both PD versions side by side.

facts.claim: Myth-bust: the Cape of Good Hope is NOT Africa's southern tip. That is Cape Agulhas, about 90 miles (150 km) east-southeast, which is also the official IHO boundary between the Atlantic and Indian Oceans.
facts.spoken_form: Ask anyone where Africa ends and they'll say the Cape of Good Hope. Wrong. The real tip is a quiet spot about ninety miles away called Cape Agulhas.
facts.display: Real tip of Africa: Cape Agulhas
facts.source_title: Cape of Good Hope (Wikipedia); Cape Agulhas (Wikipedia, citing IHO Special Publication 23, Limits of Oceans and Seas, 1953)
facts.quote: A common misconception is that the Cape of Good Hope is the southern tip of Africa.
facts.caveat: Same page: 'the southernmost point of Africa is Cape Agulhas about 150 kilometres (90 mi) to the east-southeast.' Agulhas is about 34 mi (55 km) farther south in latitude. Britannica was 403 and could not be checked directly; the facts are uncontroversial.

facts.claim: The Cape of Good Hope's marker makes a carefully worded claim: 'the most south-western point of the African continent', not the southernmost point.
facts.spoken_form: The sign at the Cape of Good Hope is very carefully worded. It doesn't say southernmost. It says most south-western.
facts.source_title: Atlas Obscura, 'Cape of Good Hope' (search excerpt); 22places.com; German Wikivoyage ('südwestlichste Punkt Afrikas')
facts.quote: The marker found at the Cape of Good Hope is slightly more contrived: the most southwestern point of the African continent.
facts.caveat: Atlas Obscura returned 403 to the fetcher; the quote is from the search-engine excerpt, so the exact engraved text was not seen. Commons has photos of the sign (CC BY-SA). Check the sign text in the photo before quoting it on screen.

facts.claim: Bartolomeu Dias, the first European to round it (1488), named it the 'Cape of Storms'. King John II of Portugal renamed it the 'Cape of Good Hope', an early rebrand driven by hope of a sea route to India.
facts.spoken_form: And its original name? The Cape of Storms. A king renamed it the Cape of Good Hope. History's first rebrand.
facts.display: Cape of Storms → Cape of Good Hope
facts.source_title: Cape of Good Hope (Wikipedia, citing Britannica's Bartolomeu Dias entry)
facts.quote: Bartolomeu Dias on 12 March 1488, who named it the "Cape of Storms"
facts.caveat: Who renamed it is not fully settled: most sources say John II, and some say Dias himself. Say 'Portugal renamed it' to be safe. Dates differ slightly (late 1487 / early 1488). Calling it 'history's first rebrand' is a joke, not a factual claim.

facts.claim: 'Agulhas' means 'needles'. The Portuguese named it the Cape of Needles because around 1500 the compass needle there pointed exactly at true north. So the southern tip of Africa is named after a needle pointing north.
facts.spoken_form: Its name means Cape of Needles, because sailors' compass needles there pointed perfectly north. Africa's southern tip is named after pointing north.
facts.source_title: Cape Agulhas (Wikipedia, citing Patricia Seed on the coincidence of magnetic and true north)
facts.quote: the direction of magnetic north (and therefore the compass needle) coincided with true north in the region
facts.caveat: Some sources (Britannica, as cited in search results) give a second explanation: needle-like reefs and rocks. Hedge it: 'the best-known story is…'. Magnetic declination there is very different today.

facts.claim: Cape Horn is not named for a horn shape. It is named after the Dutch town of Hoorn, home and sponsor of the expedition that first rounded it on 29 January 1616. The expedition's second ship, also called Hoorn, had burned down while its hull was being scorched clean.
facts.spoken_form: Cape Horn isn't shaped like a horn. It's named after a Dutch town called Hoorn. The explorers' other ship, also called the Hoorn, had accidentally burned down while they were cleaning it.
facts.source_title: New Netherland Institute, 'Cape Horn: How a Trading Monopoly, a Disenchanted Wealthy Merchant, and Two Dutch Explorers Put it on the Map'
facts.quote: During a refit, the Hoorn was lost, having caught fire while her weed-fouled hull was being scorched clean.
facts.caveat: Same page: 'On January 29, 1616, the Eendracht rounded "Kaap Hoorn."' Some sources say the name honours both the town and the ship; the town is the primary namesake. Explorers: Willem Schouten and Jacob Le Maire.

facts.claim: Cape Horn sailor tradition: a sailor who had rounded the Horn could wear a gold loop earring and eat with one leg on the table. National Geographic also lists the nickname 'tailbone of the Americas'.
facts.spoken_form: Sailors who survived rounding Cape Horn earned the right to wear a gold earring and eat with one foot on the table. Some call it the tailbone of the Americas.
facts.source_title: National Geographic Travel, 'Bottoms Up on Cape Horn, Chile'; Cape Horn (Wikipedia)
facts.quote: wear a gold loop earring and to dine with one leg on the table
facts.caveat: This is sea lore and tradition, not a documented rule; sources disagree on which ear. Wikipedia: 'Traditionally, a sailor who had rounded the Horn was entitled to wear a gold loop earring'. Frame it as 'tradition says'. No reliable source was found for 'record winds at Cape Horn', so that line was dropped; NatGeo says only that the latitude's winds are the 'furious fifties'.

facts.claim: Cape Horn is not on the South American mainland. It sits on Hornos Island, which was only found to be an island in 1624, and it is not even South America's southernmost point; Águila Islet is farther south.
facts.spoken_form: And the famous tip of South America? It's on an island. And it's not even the southernmost point.
facts.display: Cape Horn: an island, not the tip
facts.source_title: Cape Horn (Wikipedia)
facts.quote: Although not the most southerly point of South America (which is Águila Islet) ... it was only in 1624 that the Horn was discovered to be an island
facts.caveat: Águila Islet is in the Diego Ramírez Islands, far offshore; the mainland's southern tip is Cape Froward (not verified here). The Commons photo '00 4479 Cape Horn.jpg' wrongly describes Cape Horn as the mainland tip, so ignore that caption.

facts.claim: Kanyakumari (Cape Comorin) is the southern tip of mainland India, but India's southernmost point is Indira Point on Great Nicobar Island. In the 2004 earthquake and tsunami, that tip sank about 4.25 m (14 ft).
facts.spoken_form: India's southern tip on the mainland is Kanyakumari. But the country's true southernmost point is on an island, and in two thousand four, it sank about fourteen feet.
facts.source_title: Indira Point (Wikipedia); Kanyakumari (Wikipedia)
facts.quote: the southernmost tip subsided 4.25 metres (13.9 ft) after the earthquake
facts.caveat: This is a Wikipedia-level source. The 'lighthouse now underwater' claims are from aggregator sites and could not be confirmed. Since the drip's India tip is Kanyakumari, use this only as a side gag, or skip it.

facts.claim: Greenland, one of the drip's tips and where Wegener died, was named as a marketing move. Erik the Red said people would be keener to settle there if the land had an attractive name.
facts.spoken_form: Greenland got its name from a Viking marketing campaign. Erik the Red said people would want to move there if it had a nice name.
facts.source_title: Eirik the Red's Saga, tr. J. Sephton (1880), Project Gutenberg #17946
facts.quote: men will desire much the more to go there if the land has a good name.
facts.caveat: The quote is verbatim from the saga translation; the saga is literature written about 200 years later, so say 'according to the saga'. Some argue southern Greenland's coast is genuinely green in summer; Snopes covers this.

facts.claim: Florida's famous 'Southernmost Point' buoy in Key West is not the continental US's southernmost point, and not even Key West's. The real one is Ballast Key, a private island about 10 miles (16 km) away.
facts.spoken_form: Florida's famous Southernmost Point marker? Not the southernmost point. The real one is a private island ten miles away.
facts.source_title: Southernmost Point Buoy (Wikipedia, citing the City of Key West buoy history and others)
facts.quote: neither the true southernmost point of the continental US nor of Key West
facts.caveat: Key West's own true southern tip is on US Navy (Truman Annex) land, about 900 ft farther south. The buoy was installed 10 Sep 1983. 'Continental US' here means the contiguous 48 states.

facts.claim: Green's 1875 book draws the 'normal form of a continent' as a three-lobed triangle (Figure 1) and labels a figure 'Tetrahedral collapse of Earth's crust in the southern hemisphere' (Figure 5), with S. America, Africa and Australia at the corners of a six-faced tetrahedron.
facts.spoken_form: In his eighteen seventy-five book, Green drew what he called the normal shape of a continent: a triangle pointing south.
facts.display: Green, 1875: 'the normal form of a continent'
facts.source_title: W. Lowthian Green, Vestiges of the Molten Globe (London: E. Stanford, 1875), archive.org scan (Oxford copy, Google-digitized), p. 5–6 and Figures 1, 4, 5
facts.quote: This figure represents the normal form of a continent in its simplest development, namely, as a regular trilobed mass.
facts.caveat: Figure pages: Figure 1 = scan leaf n17; Figures 4–5 = n39; Figures 7–10 (globes) = n56–n57. archive.org marks the scan 'NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT'. The folded Plates I–II are cut off in this scan. 300-dpi renders are saved in .../research-future-visuals/assets/.

facts.claim: In 1858 Antonio Snider-Pellegrini published a two-panel map showing the Americas and Africa fitted together and then pulled apart: the first known illustration of the Atlantic opening.
facts.spoken_form: In eighteen fifty-eight, a Frenchman drew the Americas and Africa snapped together like puzzle pieces. Then he pulled them apart.
facts.source_title: Wikimedia Commons, File:Antonio Snider-Pellegrini Opening of the Atlantic.jpg (from La Création et ses mystères dévoilés, Paris, 1858)
facts.quote: First known illustration of the Opening of the Atlantic Ocean, by Antonio Snider-Pellegrini, 1858.
facts.caveat: He tied the split to the Biblical Flood, so do not present him as a proto-plate-tectonics scientist. He was an American-born geographer working in Paris; 'a Frenchman' is loose, so prefer 'a geographer in Paris'.
