LEDGER BACKUP: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/script/research-future-visuals/ledger_future_visuals.json (compact). Green 1875 figure renders at 300 dpi are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/script/research-future-visuals/assets/ (green1875_pdfpage-18.png = Fig 1; -40.png = Figs 4–5; -57/-58.png = globe Figs 7–10). The full PDF is in dl/green/green.pdf.

KEY TAKEAWAYS FOR THE SCRIPT:
(1) Future finale: there are four labelled MODELS. Proxima (Scotese; Atlantic closes; ~250 Myr). Novopangaea (Livermore; Pacific closes; called 'most likely' by Davies/Green/Duarte 2018). Amasia (Mitchell 2012, Americas meet Eurasia at the North Pole, 50–200 Myr; an alternative Curtin 2022 version closes the Pacific, 200–300 Myr). Aurica (Duarte 2016, Australia + America). The hero number is Farnsworth 2023: only 8–16% of land livable for mammals, in ONE study using the Ultima/Proxima geography. 'Which continent does America crash into?' has four answers: Africa, Asia, Antarctica, Australia. Good comedic beat that stays honest.
(2) Plate speed: USGS says fingernails, NOAA says toenails (joke beat). Atlantic ~1 in/yr; Americas vs Africa/Europe ~1.5 in/yr, which is exactly fingernail speed (~1.6 in/yr). Computed lines: since Bacon (1620), about a school bus wider (33–53 ft); 250 Myr at fingernail speed is about 6,000 miles, a quarter of the way around Earth.
(3) North-up is a habit. Hereford c.1300 is east-up, al-Idrisi 1154 is south-up, McArthur 1979 put 'Australia on top', and the Blue Marble was shot south-up and flipped. So 'pointing south' is real geometry, but 'dripping DOWN' only exists because we hang maps north-up. The Explorer could rotate the globe and the drip 'drips up'.
(4) Strongest TRUE comedy facts:
- Cape Agulhas, not Good Hope, is Africa's tip.
- Good Hope's sign hedges with 'most south-western point'.
- Cape of Storms was rebranded as Good Hope.
- Agulhas means 'Cape of Needles' because compasses there pointed true north, so Africa's tip is named for pointing NORTH.
- Cape Horn is named for the Dutch town of Hoorn, and the expedition's ship 'Hoorn' burned while being cleaned.
- Cape Horn is on an island and isn't South America's southernmost point.
- Rounding the Horn earned a gold earring and one foot on the table.
- Greenland was named as Erik the Red's sales pitch.
- Key West's 'Southernmost Point' buoy isn't.
- India's true southern tip sank about 14 ft in 2004.
'Record winds at Cape Horn' is DROPPED: no reliable record figure was found.

CAVEATS / ACCESS ISSUES:
- Wikimedia's API and upload.wikimedia.org returned HTTP 429 (rate limit, probably shared IP). Licences were verified by reading each Commons File: page instead. Direct URLs were built from the standard md5 path, which is confirmed for the Blue Marble files via the API. Downstream downloads should use a descriptive User-Agent, pause a few seconds between files, and retry on 429.
- Britannica, Atlas Obscura, raremaps, etymonline, the ICA mapdesign site and scotese.com were blocked or unreachable, so a few items rest on Wikipedia or search excerpts (marked medium).
- The IHO S-23 1953 PDF is an image scan with no text layer.

LICENSING:
- Prefer the PD (NASA/old) assets. The CC BY / CC BY-SA photos (Agulhas marker, Good Hope sign and view, Cape Horn photo, Cape Comorin) need attribution. Per the owner override (no on-screen credits), put the credits in the YouTube description: author, licence link, 'cropped/animated'.
- The Novum Organum Houghton file is the 1645 edition. Use Instauratio_Magna_1620.jpg for the 1620 beat.
- Do NOT use the McArthur map or the Scotese future maps (copyrighted); recreate them in the engine.
- Per the owner override, spoken text must not cite agencies or journals. The 'one agency says fingernails, another says toenails' gag works without naming them.

title_options: Why the Continents All Point South (It's Not Just Luck)
Earth Looks Like It's Dripping. Here's the Real Reason
The 400-Year-Old Mystery in the Shape of the Continents
Why Earth's Land Drips South (It's NOT the Spin)
Your Map Never Told You Why the Continents Point South
The Real Reason Earth Looks Like It's Melting
thumbnail_concepts: CAN'T UNSEE IT (UNSEE in red, white text on black boxes): a dark Blue Marble globe tilted ~60 deg to show its underside; South America, Africa and India glow hero-orange #FF5A36; white curved drip-arrows run down from their tips into a pulsing yellow ring on Antarctica. Pair with title 1 or 6.

NOT AN ACCIDENT (NOT in red; Bacon's own words from the same 1620 passage): the same tilted globe, with a torn sepia strip of the 1620 Novum Organum page (public domain) across one corner and 'acuminati' underlined in orange. Pair with title 3.

ALL POINT HERE (HERE in red): a Gondwana jigsaw in which South America, Africa, India and Australia are extruded slabs pulled apart from a red-ringed Antarctica, with one fat white arrow aimed at the ring. Use as the third arm of a 3-way test, paired with title 2 or 4.

chapters.title: Why does Earth look like it's melting?
Why did geologists laugh at Wegener?
Where is the drip going next?

segments.text: Spin a globe, and Earth looks like it's {m:melt}melting.
segments.visual: FRAME 1 = THUMBNAIL IN MOTION: photoreal globe (Blue Marble, desaturated 30%, navy #0A1A2E ocean) tilted ~60 deg to show the underside, slowly spinning. South America, Africa and India already glow hero-orange #FF5A36 with bloom. At {m:melt} white curved drip-arrows draw down from their tips toward a pulsing yellow #FFD23F ring on Antarctica.
sfx: low whoosh as the globe turns
segments.music: Cold open: pulsing low synth bed, tense and minimal, starts on frame 1.

segments.text: {m:sam}South America, {m:afr}Africa, {m:ind}India. {m:grl}Greenland, {m:fla}Florida, {m:baja}Baja, {m:kam}Kamchatka.
segments.visual: Camera swings across the globe; each southern tip pops hero-orange with a white draw-on outline exactly on its marker: {m:sam} Cape Froward, {m:afr} Cape Agulhas (NOT the Cape of Good Hope), {m:ind} Kanyakumari, {m:grl} Cape Farewell, {m:fla} Cape Sable, {m:baja} Cabo San Lucas, {m:kam} Cape Lopatka. One small leader-line label at a time, fading as the next pops. One event every ~0.8 s.

segments.text: Every point aims {m:south}south, like somebody left the planet out in the sun.
segments.visual: Pull out: all seven tips glow at once; at {m:south} short yellow arrows point south from each. Hard cut to EXPLORER GAG 1: the low-poly Explorer stands on a tiny Little-Prince Earth right on Africa's southern tip; Interact clip as he leans out and reaches under the tip as if to catch a falling drop; HitRecieve_2 clip as he nearly slips; Run_Back clip to safety.
segments.humor: Narration: 'left the planet out in the sun'. Explorer gag 1: tries to catch the drip, nearly falls off Africa (Interact, HitRecieve_2, Run_Back).
sfx: short cartoon fall whistle as he wobbles

segments.text: {m:twothirds}Two-thirds of all land sits north of the equator. So do nearly {m:nine}nine in ten people.
segments.visual: Back to the photoreal globe. At {m:twothirds} a glowing equator line slices it; northern land brightens, southern land dims; whip to a NORTH/SOUTH split bar with a counter rolling to 68%. At {m:nine} the bar refills with night-lights dots and the counter rolls to 'about 9 in 10'.

segments.text: You'd think Earth's {m:spin}spin did this. It's far too weak. A video with tens of millions of views called it {m:coin}just a coincidence.
segments.visual: At {m:spin} the globe spins fast under curved white spin-arrows; the continents do not budge; a small 'SPIN FORCE' gauge twitches and sags to near zero. At {m:coin} a spinning coin graphic flips in front of the globe.

segments.text: It isn't. {m:not}Not entirely.
segments.visual: The coin freezes in mid-air and cracks in two at {m:not}. Music drops out for half a second before 'It isn't'.
segments.music: Music cut 0.5 s, then the bed returns heavier.

segments.text: So why do the continents point south? By the end, you'll see the answer written in their {m:shapes}shapes.
segments.visual: Slow push-in on the tilted globe; the drip-arrows redraw and converge on Antarctica's yellow ring. Kinetic headline lands at {m:shapes}.
onscreen: WHY DO THE CONTINENTS POINT SOUTH?

segments.text: Along the way: why you can't dig to China from {m:usa}anywhere in America. A half of the planet that's {m:water}eighty-nine percent water.
segments.visual: Teaser montage, ~2 s each, nothing explained: at {m:usa} a glowing line punches straight through the globe from the United States and exits into open ocean with a '?'; at {m:water} a hemisphere cap glows cyan #3DE3FF and a counter flashes 89% for one second.

segments.text: A theory from {m:t1875}eighteen seventy-five that predicted all of it, and was dead wrong. And the last one: the continent your country is going to {m:crash}crash into. Eventually.
segments.visual: At {m:t1875} a one-second sepia flash of Green's 1875 tetrahedron figure (PD) as the globe briefly morphs into a pyramid. At {m:crash} flash the final reveal for ~1 s without explanation: North America (white tracked marker) sliding across a shrinking future ocean toward a ghosted neighbor labelled MODEL. Hard cut to black on 'Eventually'.
segments.humor: 'Eventually.' undercuts the doom.
sfx: impact hit on the cut to black

segments.text: First, the bad news: you're not the first person to notice. {m:bacon}Not even close.
segments.visual: Hard cut from black to sepia: an old print frame fills the screen; at {m:bacon} the 1620 Instauratio Magna engraved title page (galleon between the Pillars of Hercules, PD) fades in with a slow Ken Burns push.
segments.humor: Self-aware 'bad news' for the viewer.
segments.music: Switch to felt piano + soft strings for the history.

segments.text: In sixteen twenty, Francis Bacon wrote that the Old World and the New are both 'broad and expanded toward the north, and {m:narrow}narrow and pointed toward the south.'
segments.visual: Ken Burns on Francis Bacon's portrait (Paul van Somer I, 1617, PD). The quote types on in two lines. At {m:narrow} cross-dissolve to the globe where the tapers of South America and Africa glow orange.

segments.text: In his Latin: {m:acum}acuminati. Sharpened to a point. And once wasn't enough; he wrote it twice, in the same book.
segments.visual: Macro Ken Burns across the 1620 first-edition page 232 (PD scan); at {m:acum} the word 'acuminati' gets a hand-drawn orange underline. A second 1620 page (Parasceve p. 21, PD) slides in beside it and a 'x2' stamp lands.
segments.humor: 'Once wasn't enough' (he repeats himself).

segments.text: And in the very same breath, he said Africa and South America's matching capes were {m:accident}'not to be attributed to mere accident.'
segments.visual: Globe: Africa and South America highlighted side by side; their southern capes pulse. At {m:accident} a sepia quote card slides in.
onscreen: "NOT TO BE ATTRIBUTED TO MERE ACCIDENT"

segments.text: Then he wrote down an open question: is there even a {m:southcont}southern continent down there? Nobody would lay eyes on Antarctica for two more centuries. Remember that.
segments.visual: Camera dives to the bottom of the globe at {m:southcont}; Antarctica is hidden under a blank white fog with a hand-lettered '?'. A sepia year ticker flicks 1620 -> 1820 and the fog thins, then the shot freezes on the '?'.

segments.text: Now, you may have heard that Bacon predicted continental drift. {m:scratch}He didn't.
segments.visual: Animated jigsaw: South America rotates to snap into Africa's coast; at {m:scratch} it freezes mid-snap and a red JUICE CHECK stamp slams down.
segments.humor: Record-scratch myth-bust.

segments.text: He wasn't snapping Africa and South America together like puzzle pieces. He was saying they're the {m:same}same shape, side by side.
segments.visual: Rewind the jigsaw; instead Africa and South America sit side by side in the same orientation at {m:same}, matching tapers outlined in white. Brief Ken Burns on the 1861 edition page 418 footnote (PD scan), underline 'corresponding coasts'.

segments.text: So Bacon saw the drip, but couldn't explain it. For a very long time, neither could anyone else. And boy, did they try.
segments.visual: Sepia montage: PD book pages (Forster 1778, Somerville 1848, Guyot 1849) slide in and stack over the slowly turning globe, one every ~1.5 s.
segments.humor: 'Boy, did they try.'

segments.text: Captain Cook's naturalist, Johann Reinhold Forster, noticed that every great southern tip looks alike: high, rocky, the end of a {m:mtn}mountain chain.
segments.visual: Ken Burns on J. R. Forster's engraved portrait (Bause after Graff, PD). Cut to the globe: Cape Froward, Cape Agulhas, Kanyakumari and Tasmania's southern point glow; at {m:mtn} white lines trace the mountain chains running north from each tip.

segments.text: His explanation? A giant flood came {m:wave}roaring in from the south-west and carved every one of them. Some of the top scientists of the day bought it. Geology did not.
segments.visual: EXPLORER GAG 2: tiny-Earth diorama; at {m:wave} a flat stylized blue wave graphic sweeps in from the south-west; the Explorer sprints out of its path (Run_Right clip), then Roll clip as it passes; behind the wave the tips 'sharpen'. Cut to Forster 1778 p. 13 (PD scan) with 'a violent flood' underlined. On 'Geology did not', the wave graphic deflates.
segments.humor: Explorer gag 2: outruns Forster's imaginary flood (Run_Right, Roll). Dry tag: 'Geology did not.'

segments.text: Even Alexander von Humboldt, the most famous scientist alive, called the southern tips {m:pyr}'pyramidal.'
segments.visual: Sepia kinetic quote card over the globe. At {m:pyr} thin white triangle outlines snap onto the southern ends of South America, Africa and India (planting the 'pyramid' idea for Chapter 3).

segments.text: And by the {m:list}eighteen-forties, someone had written down almost the exact list you saw at the start: Greenland, Baja, Florida, India, Kamchatka. 'All their points turned towards the south.'
segments.visual: Ken Burns on Guyot 1849 p. 22 (PD scan). At {m:list} cut to the cold-open globe angle and re-pop Greenland, Baja, Florida, India, Kamchatka in the same rhythm and with the same thump as 0:04. The quote types on last.
onscreen: "ALL THEIR POINTS TURNED TOWARDS THE SOUTH"
sfx: same tip-pop thump x5 as the cold open

segments.text: Then, in the nineteen-seventies, the pattern got its name, as a {m:joke}joke. A magazine writer called it {m:drip}'continental drip': a fake theory you could prove just by staring at a map.
segments.visual: Typewriter card on cream paper (generic, no real magazine branding). At {m:joke} a coffee-stained sheet slides in. At {m:drip} 'CONTINENTAL DRIFT' types out, then the 'FT' is struck through and a 'P' typed over it: DRIP.
segments.humor: DRIFT gets retyped as DRIP on screen.
segments.music: Light, playful pizzicato under the joke.

segments.text: Three years later, a geologist took that joke even further. Hold on to him. He matters more than you'd think.
segments.visual: A second typewriter sheet slides in behind the first; its byline is blurred out; a yellow ring circles the blur; slow push-in.

segments.text: Because the shapes are only clue number one. Clue number two is on the {m:far}far side of the planet.
segments.visual: The globe whips around and dives under; at {m:far} a cyan line from the North Pole pierces straight through the planet's center and out the bottom.
segments.music: Riser into Chapter 2; switch to the pulsing synth + strings data bed.

segments.text: Start at the very top of the world. The {m:np}North Pole isn't land. It's ocean. Stand on the ice there, and the sea floor is about {m:depth}two and a half miles beneath your boots.
segments.visual: Chapter card (2 s). Camera rises over the Arctic: photoreal sea ice on dark water, pulsing marker 'NORTH POLE' at {m:np}. At {m:depth} the globe slices open into a cross-section under the pole and a depth ruler drops from the ice to the sea floor.
sfx: deep rumble as the ruler drops

segments.text: Now go to the bottom. At the {m:sp}South Pole, you're standing almost two miles up, on a sheet of ice more than a mile and a half thick.
segments.visual: Cross-section flips to the South Pole at {m:sp}: sea-level line near the bottom, a tall white ice column rising almost two miles above it, bedrock beneath. A tiny Explorer figure (Idle_Neutral) stands on top for scale.

segments.text: The two ends of the planet are {m:neg}photographic negatives. Ocean on top. A continent at the bottom.
segments.visual: Split screen: polar view of the Arctic (dark ocean ringed by land) beside a polar view of Antarctica (white land ringed by ocean). At {m:neg} the Arctic view color-inverts into the Antarctic one like a photo negative.
onscreen: OCEAN ON TOP. LAND AT BOTTOM.

segments.text: And they're almost the same size. {m:drag}Drag the Arctic Ocean down onto Antarctica, and the sizes nearly match.
segments.visual: At {m:drag} the Arctic Ocean outline (cyan) lifts off the globe and is dragged at true size down onto Antarctica (orange); the two areas settle almost on top of each other.

segments.text: But here's the part that doesn't make sense. They don't just match. They {m:line}line up. Most of Antarctica sits directly opposite the Arctic Ocean, on the exact other side of the Earth.
segments.visual: Globe turns semi-transparent. At {m:line} a glowing yellow axis runs straight through the planet's center from the Arctic Ocean to Antarctica; Antarctica flipped to its antipode lands on the Arctic Ocean and the overlap flashes yellow.
segments.music: Cut the bed 0.5 s before 'line up'.

segments.text: And it's not just the poles. All over the planet, land and ocean seem to {m:avoid}avoid each other. Which brings us to a classic American playground myth.
segments.visual: Pull back to the whole globe. At {m:avoid} a one-second teaser of the antipode overlay: flipped land in cyan slides away from real land like repelling magnets. Kinetic headline lands.

segments.text: If you dig straight down, you'll reach {m:china}China. Let's test it. Start in Kansas, right at the center of the lower forty-eight, and {m:dig}dig.
segments.visual: At {m:china} China lights orange on the far side of the globe. Marker drops on the geographic center of the lower 48 near Lebanon, Kansas. EXPLORER GAG 3 at {m:dig}: the Explorer on the Kansas marker of the tiny Earth plays Interact on a loop as a digging motion, dirt particles flying. Cutaway (Three.js, under 15 s): a glowing tunnel line runs through the planet's layers with a progress bar (no numbers).
segments.humor: Explorer gag 3: digs to China (Interact loop).

segments.text: You come out in the {m:indian}southern Indian Ocean. The nearest land is a tiny French island, more than two hundred miles away.
segments.visual: At {m:indian} the tunnel exits into open blue water; the Explorer tumbles out (Roll clip) with a splash and bobs alone (Idle clip); camera pulls up to show empty ocean, a tiny dot labelled 'Ile Saint-Paul' far off.
segments.humor: Explorer gag 3 payoff: pops out into empty ocean (Roll, Idle).

segments.text: Not China. Not even close. In fact, there isn't a single spot in the United States that sits opposite {m:china2}China.
segments.visual: All of the United States (incl. Alaska and Hawaii) flipped to its antipode in cyan; China in orange. At {m:china2} they don't touch anywhere; JUICE CHECK stamp.

segments.text: Even if you started in China, three times out of four you'd surface in the ocean. The people who can actually dig to China? {m:arg}Argentinians.
segments.visual: China flipped to its antipode: most of it lands on blue South Pacific/South Atlantic, a sliver on Argentina and Chile. At {m:arg} Argentina lights orange and its flipped outline lands squarely on China; a Kenney mini character pops up on Argentina and plays emote-yes.
segments.humor: Punchline: 'Argentinians.' (Kenney mini emote-yes)

segments.text: Now flip {m:flipall}every continent to the far side of the planet and lay it over the original. Only about {m:eighth}one-eighth of the land has land on the other side.
segments.visual: Full antipode overlay on the globe at {m:flipall}: real land grey, flipped land cyan, overlaps flash yellow (South America / East Asia, Antarctica / Arctic, New Zealand / Spain). At {m:eighth} hero counter rolls to '1 IN 8'.

segments.text: That's less than half of what you'd expect if the continents had been {m:random}sprinkled at random.
segments.visual: Side by side: left globe with the same continents scattered at random (label RANDOM), lots of yellow overlap; right, the real Earth with little yellow (label REAL). At {m:random} two bars grow; the REAL bar stops at less than half.

segments.text: So try a puzzle. Slice the Earth into {m:half}two halves, any way you like, and cram as much land as you can into one of them.
segments.visual: At {m:half} a translucent cyan hemisphere dome sweeps around the globe; the land inside it flickers brighter and dimmer as it searches.

segments.text: The winner is centered on {m:europe}western Europe. It scoops up most of the world's land. And it's still {m:still}more than half water.
segments.visual: Dome settles centered on western Europe, between Brittany and the Spanish coast, at {m:europe}; land inside glows. Music cuts 0.5 s; at {m:still} the ocean inside the dome floods cyan.

segments.text: There is no way to cut this planet in half and get a half that's mostly land.
segments.visual: Fast montage: the dome jumps to five other centers (Asia, Africa, the Americas, Antarctica, Australia); each time a red 'MOSTLY WATER' tag flashes.

segments.text: Now flip the globe {m:flip}over. The other half is {m:p89}eighty-nine percent water, centered in the empty Pacific just off New Zealand.
segments.visual: Globe whips 180 deg at {m:flip}; the opposite dome goes deep cyan; at {m:p89} hero counter climbs to 89%; New Zealand is a small orange sliver near its center.

segments.text: The Pacific alone could swallow {m:drop}every continent on Earth, with room to spare.
segments.visual: From {m:drop}, every continent is dragged at true size and dropped into the Pacific one by one with a heavy thunk. EXPLORER GAG 4: the Explorer rides the last one (Australia) in, lands, looks around at all the leftover blue (Idle_Neutral), then waves at camera (Wave clip).
segments.humor: Explorer gag 4: surfs the last continent into the Pacific, waves from the leftover room (Idle_Neutral, Wave).

segments.text: Ocean on top, land at the bottom. Land that avoids land. It's a planet that looks strangely {m:lop}lopsided, and the drip is just the part you can see.
segments.visual: Callback montage, ~1 s each: pole negative, antipode overlay, water half. At {m:lop} return to the tilted drip globe from the cold open (core question restated ~40%).
onscreen: WHY DO THE CONTINENTS POINT SOUTH?

segments.text: Every week, Myth Juice takes one thing you were taught about the world and checks it against the map. If you want the next one, {m:sub}subscribe.
segments.visual: Picture keeps moving: slow orbit of the globe with the antipode overlay glowing. At {m:sub} a small animated subscribe button glows in the lower third. No freeze.

segments.text: Back in {m:g1875}eighteen seventy-five, one man thought he'd found a single shape that explained all of it.
segments.visual: Sepia wipe. At {m:g1875} a 3D tetrahedron wireframe slowly rotates inside a translucent globe.
segments.music: Riser; switch to curious felt piano + pizzicato for Chapter 3.

segments.text: His name was William Lowthian Green. He wasn't a professor. He was the {m:hawaii}foreign minister of the Kingdom of Hawaii.
segments.visual: Chapter card (2 s). Ken Burns on the title page of Green's 1875 'Vestiges of the Molten Globe' (PD scan). At {m:hawaii} the line 'MINISTER OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS TO THE KING OF THE SANDWICH ISLANDS' gets an orange highlight; quick cut to a pulsing marker on Hawaii.
segments.humor: Reveal: the theorist was Hawaii's foreign minister.

segments.text: And he'd been obsessed with those pointy southern tips for years. He even demonstrated them with a {m:card}bent card dipped in water.
segments.visual: Small 3D diorama: an arched white card lowered onto a still water surface at {m:card}; where its edges touch the water, the wet outline tapers into a point. Cross-dissolve to Green's 1875 Figure 1, 'the normal form of a continent' (PD), a south-pointing three-lobed triangle.

segments.text: His big idea: the Earth was cooling, shrinking, and slowly collapsing toward a {m:tet}tetrahedron. A four-cornered pyramid.
segments.visual: Three.js (under 20 s across this and the next two segments): at {m:tet} the translucent globe slowly morphs toward a tetrahedron, continents stretched over its faces. EXPLORER GAG 5: as the face under the Explorer tilts, he tumbles down it (Roll clip) to a corner and lands on a southern point (Idle_Neutral).
segments.humor: Explorer gag 5: slides off the pyramid Earth (Roll).

segments.text: It sounds ridiculous. But watch what it {m:pred}predicted. Most land in the north: {m:c1}check. Three continents ending in points aimed south: {m:c2}check.
segments.visual: Checklist, one line at a time (each replaces the previous; never more than two text elements on screen). At {m:c1} 'MOST LAND IN THE NORTH' + tick; at {m:c2} 'THREE CONTINENTS POINTING SOUTH' + tick. The tetrahedron rotates to show each feature as it's ticked.

segments.text: An ocean on top of the world: {m:c3}check. A continent at the bottom: {m:c4}check. Land sitting opposite water: {m:c5}check. One shape, every clue.
segments.visual: Continue one line at a time: {m:c3} 'OCEAN AT THE NORTH POLE' + tick; {m:c4} 'CONTINENT AT THE SOUTH POLE' + tick; {m:c5} 'LAND OPPOSITE WATER' + tick; then a '5 / 5' stamp.

segments.text: And it went {m:main}mainstream. By the turn of the century, a leading geologist was telling Britain's top geographers that a shrinking Earth had to squeeze toward a tetrahedron.
segments.visual: Ken Burns across the March 1899 journal's tetrahedron diagrams (Fig. 5, PD scan) with a warm vignette at {m:main}.

segments.text: He even pointed out that North America sits exactly opposite the {m:io}Indian Ocean. The same ocean you just dug into.
segments.visual: Globe: North America flipped to its antipode lands entirely in the Indian Ocean at {m:io}; the Explorer's Kansas tunnel line from Chapter 2 re-glows (callback).
segments.humor: Callback to the dig gag.

segments.text: By nineteen eighteen, a children's magazine was telling kids that one day, the Earth would turn into a {m:pyramid}pyramid.
segments.visual: Recreated sepia children's-page card (our own typography, no real masthead). Kenney mini characters sit cross-legged facing a chalkboard where a globe morphs into a pyramid at {m:pyramid}.
segments.humor: Kids being taught the pyramid Earth (Kenney minis sit).

segments.text: So, hang on. If it predicted all that, {m:how}how do we know it's wrong?
segments.visual: The tetrahedron freezes mid-turn; music drops out at {m:how}; a single question mark draws itself on one face.
segments.music: Silence 0.9 s.

segments.text: Because the whole idea needed a cooling, shrinking Earth. Then scientists discovered {m:rad}radioactivity, heating the planet from the inside, and the shrinking engine stalled.
segments.visual: Cutaway: at {m:rad} scattered glowing specks heat the interior orange, heat shimmer rising; the inward 'shrinking' arrows stall and reverse. EXPLORER GAG 6: the Explorer walks up to the tetrahedron (Walk clip) and kicks it (Kick_Right clip); it pops back into a round sphere.
segments.humor: Explorer gag 6: kicks the pyramid back into a ball (Kick_Right).

segments.text: The pyramid quietly vanished from geology. Green's checklist was real. He'd just pinned the clues on the wrong {m:suspect}suspect.
segments.visual: Green's 1875 globe engravings (Figs. 7-10, PD) drift away in sepia; the five ticks stay glowing. At {m:suspect} a red string-and-pin board links the five clues to a crossed-out tetrahedron.
segments.humor: Detective framing: 'wrong suspect'.

segments.text: The real culprit had been staring out of world maps for centuries. A mapmaker had floated it even before Bacon wrote his line. It just needed someone stubborn enough to say it out loud: the continents {m:move}move.
segments.visual: Old-map texture over the globe: the Atlantic coasts of South America and Africa glow. A sepia card for the mapmaker's 1596 idea. At {m:move} the two continents twitch apart.
segments.music: Riser into Chapter 4.

segments.text: Around nineteen ten, a young German weather scientist named Alfred Wegener wrote to his future wife. Doesn't South America fit against Africa, he asked, as if they had once been {m:joined}joined?
segments.visual: Chapter card (2 s). Ken Burns on the Alfred Wegener portrait (c. 1924-30, PD in US). At {m:joined} globe: South America slides east across the Atlantic and nestles against Africa.
onscreen: WHY DID GEOLOGISTS LAUGH AT WEGENER?
sfx: soft click as the coasts meet
segments.music: Chapter 4: hopeful strings that later turn cold.

segments.text: 'This is an idea I'll have to pursue.'
segments.visual: Handwritten-style letter card (our own typography) with the line; the fitted continents glow behind it.

segments.text: In January nineteen twelve, he stood up before a meeting of geologists and told them the {m:move}continents move. Then a world war buried his book.
segments.visual: At {m:move} every continent on the globe starts drifting slowly (label SIMPLIFIED). Then a dark fog rolls across the frame and a simple book silhouette marked 1915 sinks under it.

segments.text: When the rest of the world read it, the reaction was brutal. One society president called it {m:rot}'utter, damned rot.' No German university would make him a professor.
segments.visual: EXPLORER GAG 7: at {m:rot} a quote card slams into frame; the Explorer, standing beside the drifting globe, recoils as if hit by the words (HitRecieve clip). Then a row of simple university-door icons slam shut one by one.
segments.humor: Explorer gag 7: knocked back by an insult (HitRecieve).

segments.text: And critics had one killer question: what could possibly {m:push}push a continent? Wegener guessed Earth's spin, and tides. Both were far too weak.
segments.visual: At {m:push} a big '?' over the continents. Spin arrows and a tidal-bulge graphic push on a continent; the same 'SPIN FORCE' gauge from the cold open barely twitches (callback).
onscreen: SPIN AND TIDES: FAR TOO WEAK
segments.humor: Callback to the cold-open spin gauge.

segments.text: He admitted it himself. 'The Newton of drift theory has not yet appeared.'
segments.visual: Wegener portrait again, slow push toward the eyes; the quote types on.
onscreen: "THE NEWTON OF DRIFT ... NOT YET APPEARED"

segments.text: In nineteen thirty, Wegener was deep on the ice of {m:grl}Greenland. One of the drip's own tips.
segments.visual: At {m:grl} Greenland pops orange on the globe with the same tip-pop as the cold open; then a low DEM flyover skims across the white Greenland ice sheet toward its center (Three.js, ~15 s).
segments.music: Sparse cold drone and wind.

segments.text: On his {m:fifty}fiftieth birthday, he left a camp in the middle of the ice sheet with a Greenlander named Rasmus Villumsen.
segments.visual: Slow Ken Burns on the last photo of Wegener and Villumsen at Eismitte (1930, PD, AWI archive); hold at {m:fifty}.

segments.text: Neither of them made it back.
segments.visual: The photo slowly desaturates and dissolves into blank white snow.
segments.music: Music drops to silence; wind only.

segments.text: They found Wegener's body the next May, carefully buried in the snow. Villumsen was never found.
segments.visual: Flyover resumes over empty ice; a small marker on the ice sheet; light snowfall.

segments.text: Wegener never saw his idea proven. The proof was hiding on the {m:floor}ocean floor: stripes of magnetized rock, mirrored on both sides of the mid-ocean ridges, like a tape recording of new seafloor being made.
segments.visual: Cut from white ice to the dark ocean floor. At {m:floor} magnetic 'zebra' stripes (recreated, USGS-style) appear on both sides of a glowing mid-ocean ridge; new stripes emerge at the center and slide outward symmetrically like tape leaving a recorder.
segments.music: Slow warm swell returns.

segments.text: It came out {m:y33}thirty-three years after he died.
segments.visual: Year counter rolls 1930 -> 1963 at {m:y33}; the stripes lock into place.

segments.text: Today, satellites clock the continents moving at about the speed your {m:nail}fingernails grow. Or your toenails, depending on which government agency you ask.
segments.visual: Globe with GPS velocity arrows on the plates at {m:nail}; split-screen inset of a simple fingernail growing. On 'toenails' a second inset of a foot appears; the two insets are labelled AGENCY A / AGENCY B and glare at each other.
segments.humor: Fingernails vs toenails: the agencies disagree.

segments.text: So Wegener was right. The continents move. But that still doesn't explain the drip. Why would so many of them end up {m:point}pointing the same way?
segments.visual: Pull back to the tilted drip globe; the southern tips glow; at {m:point} a big '?' hangs over Antarctica (core question restated ~65%).
onscreen: WHY DO THEY ALL POINT SOUTH?

segments.text: To find out, you have to run the clock {m:rewind}backwards.
segments.visual: A time-scrub bar slides in along the bottom; at {m:rewind} its counter starts rolling backwards.
segments.music: Building swell begins.

segments.text: Rewind into the age of dinosaurs, and watch the southern continents slide home: {m:r_sam}South America, {m:r_afr}Africa, {m:r_ind}India, {m:r_aus}Australia.
segments.visual: Chapter card (2 s). Plate-reconstruction time-scrub on the globe (rotated Natural Earth polygons, labelled SIMPLIFIED), counter rolling back toward ~180 million years ago. Each piece glows as it's named and slides south toward Antarctica.
segments.music: Building swell continues.

segments.text: They lock together into one supercontinent: {m:gond}Gondwana. And at its heart sits {m:ant}Antarctica. Geologists call it the keypiece.
segments.visual: Pieces lock with a clunk at {m:gond}; at {m:ant} Antarctica pulses with a yellow ring at the center of the assembled Gondwana.

segments.text: Remember Bacon's open question? Is there even a southern continent? The drips were pointing at it {m:whole}the whole time.
segments.visual: Bacon's 1620 sepia question card fades in over Antarctica. At {m:whole} white arrows from every southern tip converge on the yellow ring.
segments.music: Music cut 0.5 s before 'the whole time', then swell.

segments.text: Now let the clock run forward. The first sliver of new ocean opens between {m:afant}Africa and Antarctica.
segments.visual: Counter starts running forward; at {m:afant} a thin blue line of new ocean cracks open between Africa and Antarctica.

segments.text: Then the Atlantic {m:zip}unzips from the bottom up. The south tears open first. The last seam, near the equator, hangs on for millions of years more.
segments.visual: At {m:zip} the South Atlantic opens like a zipper from its south end northward, a zipper-pull icon tracking the opening; the equatorial link holds, then snaps.
onscreen: THE ATLANTIC UNZIPS SOUTH TO NORTH

segments.text: And then everyone leaves. Except {m:stay}Antarctica. It barely moves.
segments.visual: Africa, South America, India and Australia drift away north. EXPLORER GAG 8: the Explorer stands alone on Antarctica and waves goodbye (Wave clip) as they leave.
segments.humor: Explorer gag 8: left behind on Antarctica, waving everyone off (Wave).

segments.text: India {m:sprint}sprints: up to about eight inches a year, several times faster than Africa or Australia, until it slams into Asia.
segments.visual: At {m:sprint} India streaks north with a glowing speed trail and a speed tag; it crashes into Asia with a shock ring.
onscreen: INDIA: UP TO ~8 INCHES A YEAR

segments.text: Now look at what's left behind. The pieces drifted apart, but they kept their orientation. Their points still {m:aim}aim back toward the South Pole, where they tore away.
segments.visual: Counter reaches TODAY; camera pulls back to the present-day tilted globe. At {m:aim} dotted ghost trails run from the tips of South America, Africa and India back to the yellow ring on Antarctica.
segments.music: Music cut 0.5 s before the next line.

segments.text: The big drips aren't drips at all. They're {m:scar}scars.
segments.visual: At {m:scar} the dotted trails turn into glowing seam lines, like healed scars across the oceans.
segments.music: Swell lands on 'scars'.

segments.text: Which brings us back to that joke. The geologist who took 'continental drip' further was named John {m:holden}Holden.
segments.visual: The 1976 typewriter sheet from Chapter 1 returns; at {m:holden} its blurred byline un-blurs to JOHN C. HOLDEN.
segments.music: Playful pizzicato returns.

segments.text: Writing for a science humor journal, he declared that every continent is a {m:tear}teardrop, with the pointed end showing the direction it came from.
segments.visual: At {m:tear} the continents on the globe morph into cartoon teardrops (our own redraw, not the copyrighted figure), points aimed south.

segments.text: Drips always flow down, he reasoned, so our maps must be upside down. And one day, the continents would splash back together into a supercontinent called {m:pangooy}'Pangooy.' On a Tuesday. At nine in the morning.
segments.visual: Globe flips upside-down for a beat; then the teardrops slosh together at {m:pangooy} into one goofy blob (Antarctica left out). Gag card slides in with the date.
segments.humor: The Tuesday 9 a.m. date (year on card, not spoken).

segments.text: {m:twist}Here's the twist. Six years earlier, the very same John Holden had helped map, for real, how Pangaea broke apart.
segments.visual: Music cuts at {m:twist}. Split screen: left, our own serious Pangaea-breakup reconstruction (labelled 1970, SIMPLIFIED); right, the joke teardrop map (our redraw). A yellow line links the two with the same name.

segments.text: His joke even cited his own real work. 'The point shows where it came from' wasn't just a punchline. It was basically the {m:answer}answer.
segments.visual: The joke map's south-pointing teardrops slide over the Gondwana scar lines and line up with them; at {m:answer} the yellow ring on Antarctica flares.
segments.music: Swell, then hold.

segments.text: Now, the honest part, because we're not going to fake you a tidy answer. Not everything drips.
segments.visual: Hard switch to a clean data look: a grid of 12 peninsula tiles (Natural Earth outlines), each with a compass needle showing its base-to-tip direction.
segments.music: Lighter, curious bed.

segments.text: Australia's {m:york}Cape York points north. So do Mexico's Yucatán, Denmark's Jutland and Siberia's Taymyr. And the Antarctic Peninsula has no choice. From the South Pole, every direction is {m:north}north.
segments.visual: From {m:york} the tiles for Cape York, Yucatán, Jutland and Taymyr swing their needles grey-north one by one. At {m:north} a top-down view over the South Pole with arrows radiating outward in every direction, all labelled N.
segments.humor: 'From the South Pole, every direction is north.'

segments.text: Some smaller drips have stories all their own. Several million years ago, the Pacific Plate grabbed {m:baja}Baja and started dragging it away from Mexico. It's still going.
segments.visual: Ken Burns on the NASA astronaut photo of Baja California's delta (PD). Then globe: at {m:baja} Baja highlighted, a Pacific Plate arrow pulls it northwest as the Gulf of California widens.

segments.text: {m:fla}Florida isn't a drip at all. It's the top of a gigantic reef platform: miles of limestone built by tiny sea creatures. And under all that limestone sits bedrock that started out next to {m:wafr}West Africa.
segments.visual: At {m:fla} Florida highlighted; a cross-section reveals a thick pale limestone platform under the peninsula, wider than the peninsula itself. At {m:wafr} a deep basement layer glows and a dotted arc traces back across the Atlantic to West Africa.
onscreen: ITS BEDROCK: BORN NEXT TO AFRICA

segments.text: Even 'down' is our own invention. The most famous photo of Earth ever taken was shot with {m:bm}Antarctica on top. It got flipped, because that's how we're used to seeing it.
segments.visual: At {m:bm} the Apollo 17 Blue Marble in its original south-up orientation (PD), then it rotates 180 deg into the familiar north-up version. EXPLORER GAG 9: the tiny Earth flips south-up; the Explorer runs (Run_Back clip) to stay on top as it turns, then stands still (Idle_Neutral) while the drips now seem to drip upward.
segments.humor: Explorer gag 9: hamster-wheels on the flipping globe (Run_Back, Idle_Neutral).

segments.text: And Africa's southern tip isn't even the {m:gh}Cape of Good Hope. The sign there is very carefully worded: not 'southernmost', but 'most south-western.'
segments.visual: Ken Burns on the Cape of Good Hope sign-board photo (CC BY-SA, credit in description) at {m:gh}; orange underline on the sign's wording; a map marker hops from Good Hope to Cape Agulhas.
segments.humor: The lawyerly sign.

segments.text: The real tip is Cape {m:agul}Agulhas. The best-known story says the name means 'needles,' because sailors' compass needles there pointed true north. So Africa's southern tip is named after pointing north.
segments.visual: NASA ASTER satellite view of Cape Agulhas (PD) at {m:agul}; a compass-needle graphic spins and settles pointing north right at Africa's southern tip.
segments.humor: Africa's southern tip, named after pointing north.

segments.text: So, the verdict. The big drips are history: scars from a supercontinent that tore apart around {m:v_ant}Antarctica. The small drips have no single answer. And some of it is probably just us, connecting dots.
segments.visual: Brand verdict stamp. At {m:v_ant} scar lines glow on South America, Africa and India; the small drips flicker each with its own icon; then a dotted constellation line connects random tips and fades.

segments.text: As for all that land piled up in the north, there's no clear sign of a deep force dragging it there. Most likely, it's a {m:snap}snapshot of where the drifting pieces happen to be right now.
segments.visual: Cutaway into the mantle: two broad warm upwellings (schematic, under Africa and the Pacific) glow; no one-sided arrow pointing north. At {m:snap} a camera-shutter flash freezes the globe inside a white photo frame.

segments.text: And here's one more irony. 'Continental drip' started as a joke, but geologists have since found {m:realdrip}real drips. Under Nevada, a cold blob of rock is sinking into the Earth like honey off a spoon. The scientist who found it admitted he'd been 'anti-drip' since his early days.
segments.visual: Cross-section under the western United States (schematic, labelled SIMPLIFIED). At {m:realdrip} a cold blue blob with a long tail stretches down from beneath Nevada into the mantle; a small inset of honey sliding off a spoon mirrors its shape. On 'anti-drip', a quote card pops.
segments.humor: The scientist who found a real drip had been 'anti-drip'.
segments.music: Riser into the finale.

segments.text: So where is the drip going? Since Bacon wrote his line, the Atlantic has grown about a {m:bus}school bus wider.
segments.visual: Chapter card (2 s). Mid-Atlantic ridge diagram; at {m:bus} a yellow school-bus silhouette slides into the widening gap.
onscreen: WHERE IS THE DRIP GOING NEXT?
segments.humor: School-bus scale for 400 years of drift.
segments.music: Finale: epic but restrained build.

segments.text: Give it a couple hundred million years, and geologists think a new supercontinent will form. They just can't agree on what it looks like. So here are the four main {m:models}models.
segments.visual: Time-scrub runs forward; four empty panels each labelled MODEL slide in at {m:models}; the United States carries a white tracked marker.

segments.text: One: the Atlantic {m:prox}slams shut, and America crashes back into Africa in about two hundred fifty million years. Pangaea Proxima.
segments.visual: Panel 1 (our own redraw from Natural Earth polygons, labelled MODEL): at {m:prox} the Atlantic closes; the US marker bumps into Africa.

segments.text: Two: the Pacific closes instead, and the Americas hit {m:novo}Antarctica first. Novopangaea. One team's favorite bet.
segments.visual: Panel 2 (MODEL): the Pacific shrinks; at {m:novo} the Americas meet a north-drifting Antarctica.

segments.text: Three: the Arctic Ocean vanishes, and America meets {m:asia}Asia practically at the North Pole. Amasia.
segments.visual: Panel 3 (MODEL): camera over the North Pole; at {m:asia} North America and Asia close in over the vanishing Arctic Ocean.

segments.text: Four: both oceans close at once, and Australia ends up in the middle of everything. Australia plus America: {m:aurica}Aurica.
segments.visual: Panel 4 (MODEL): Atlantic and Pacific both shrink; Australia ends up at the center; at {m:aurica} the name assembles from AU + RICA.

segments.text: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia. Pick your {m:neighbor}neighbor. In a way, Holden's continental splash really is coming. Just not on a Tuesday.
segments.visual: EXPLORER GAG 10 (part 1): the Explorer stands on North America of the tiny Earth with four color-coded arrows to the four candidates; at {m:neighbor} he runs toward one (Run_Left clip), stops, runs toward another (Run_Right clip), stops, then stands undecided (Idle). On 'Tuesday', the Pangooy gag card flashes back for half a second.
segments.humor: Explorer gag 10a: can't decide which continent to crash into (Run_Left, Run_Right, Idle). 'Just not on a Tuesday.'

segments.text: One study ran the climate on one of these future supercontinents. Only about {m:tenth}one-tenth of the land stayed livable for mammals.
segments.visual: Schematic heat-map overlay (labelled MODEL) spreads red across the Proxima-style supercontinent; only thin cooler fringes remain; at {m:tenth} hero counter '~1 IN 10'. EXPLORER GAG 10 (part 2): in the heat shimmer the Explorer stands wilting (Idle_Neutral), then collapses in a comic faint (Death clip).
segments.humor: Explorer gag 10b: faints in the future heat (Death).

segments.text: In every one of these futures, the map we know gets rearranged. The drip is just a fingerprint: a mark of where the pieces have been.
segments.visual: The four model panels shrink into a filmstrip; the camera returns to the opening tilted globe angle and the drip-arrows re-trace toward Antarctica (callback to frame 1).

segments.text: Four hundred years ago, Bacon said the likeness of Africa and South America wasn't an accident. He was {m:half}half right. And nobody knows yet which future wins.
segments.visual: Bacon's 1620 sepia quote card ('NOT TO BE ATTRIBUTED TO MERE ACCIDENT') fades in over the globe; at {m:half} half its words glow gold, half fade; a '?' hovers over the four-model filmstrip.

segments.text: Every map you've ever seen is one {m:frame}frame of a very slow movie.
segments.visual: Music cuts to silence. The globe shrinks into a single frame on a filmstrip that slowly scrolls past, frame after frame of drifting continents. One felt piano note at {m:frame}.
segments.music: Silence plus one piano note on 'frame'.

segments.text: So which neighbor are you betting on? Africa, Antarctica, Asia or Australia. {m:oneword}One word, in the comments.
segments.visual: Four color-coded arrows from North America to the four candidates pulse in turn; at {m:oneword} a comment-bubble icon pops.

segments.text: But one continent isn't waiting around. Right now in {m:afar}Ethiopia, three cracks meet in a giant Y, and one of them is slowly unzipping East Africa.
segments.visual: Fast fly-down from space to the Afar region; at {m:afar} a glowing Y of three rift lines (Red Sea, Gulf of Aden, East African Rift) draws on; the southern arm pulses and creeps south.
segments.music: Low tension riser.

segments.text: What happens when Africa splits in two? That's Part Two, right {m:here}here. And if you want to watch the map keep changing, subscribe.
segments.visual: END SCREEN (last ~15 s, starting with the previous line): the Afar Y keeps glowing and widening behind; video tile 'MYTH JUICE #2: SPLIT IN TWO' at {m:here}; subscribe button glows on 'subscribe'; visuals keep moving to the final frame.
segments.music: Hold the riser under the end screen, cut on the last frame.

result.verdict:
RETENTION AUDIT (I timed the script at 2.6 words/s: 2,383 spoken words, 16:06 total. Chapter lengths: ch1 3:12, ch2 3:07, ch3 1:47, ch4 1:59, ch5 4:02, ch6 2:00. The timing table is at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/script/retention-auditor/timing_2.6wps.txt.)

The structure is strong:
- The thumbnail is in motion from frame 1, and the promise lands at 0:30.
- The cold open works as a Short.
- The China payoff comes at 27%, and the jaw-drop (the poles as photographic negatives) at about 3:40.
- The Wegener death beat is real human stakes.
- The Holden twist at 73% genuinely reframes the 1976 plant.
- The cliffhanger is a real Part 2 bridge.

The draft leaks viewers in six places:
1. **1:04–1:42 (s011–s014):** four Bacon beats in a row over sepia stills. s012 (the Latin word plus "he wrote it twice") adds no story.
2. **5:50–6:11 (s042–s043):** a recap montage followed by the subscribe ask, about 21 s with no new information.
3. **7:50–8:50 (s056–s059):** the "reveal" is "the continents move", the one fact every viewer already knows, and it opens the most-covered story in the niche.
4. **12:02–14:06 (s086–s095), the biggest leak:** after the main answer (11:08) and the twist (12:00) comes 2 minutes of loosely linked trivia: the Good Hope sign, the south-up photo, the needles name, then "So, the verdict." at 83%, a hard ending signal with 2:47 still to run.
5. **15:12–15:46 (s104–s107):** four wrap-up beats in a row (fingerprint, Bacon callback, slow-movie line plus 1.2 s of silence, comment prompt). It reads as the end, so viewers leave before the end screen.
6. **Two teasers under-deliver.** "The continent your country will crash into" pays off as "four models, pick one", which can feel like bait. "A half that's 89% water" sounds obvious to a 25-year-old ("the Pacific, duh").

**Loop ledger check.** Of the 22 listed loops, 21 close and the 22nd (s108 to Part 2) is meant to stay open. Three closures are weak:
- s009→s102: the tease promises one continent; the payoff is four.
- s005→s061: spin as the cause of the drip vs spin as the force that pushes continents. Loose, but harmless.
- s020→s047: the "pyramidal" link is only visual and never spoken.

Three open loops are missing from the ledger:
- **(a) s029/s030/s036.** The script itself calls this "the part that doesn't make sense": Antarctica opposite the Arctic Ocean, land avoiding land, less than half of what chance predicts. It is never resolved. s094 covers only the land piled up in the north.
- **(b) s024.** It counts "clue number one / clue number two", and the count never continues.
- **(c) s023→s024.** The "Because…" line is a non-sequitur.

rewrites.new_text: {m:sam}South America. {m:afr}Africa. {m:ind}India.

Visual: Atlantic coasts twitch apart at {m:move}, then a 1-s Greenland tip-pop with the cold-open thump. Drop the vague unnamed 1596 mapmaker.

result.verdict:
Most of this script is well sourced. Nearly every number matches the ledger (two-thirds of land in the north, nearly nine in ten people, one in eight, 89%, about 2.5 miles down, nearly 2 miles up, 33 years, about 8 inches a year, Argentina and China, Kansas to Île Saint-Paul about 222 miles), and the Bacon wording follows the "same breath" caveat. Six statements are false or overstated and need fixing before narration lock:
(1) s030 says land and ocean "avoid each other". That is backwards: it is land that avoids land.
(2) s051 says all of North America is "exactly" opposite the Indian Ocean. Arctic Canada and Greenland are opposite Antarctica, and the video's own s035 overlay shows that.
(3) s054's "Then scientists discovered radioactivity" puts radioactivity after the 1899 and 1918 beats. It was discovered in 1896.
(4) s060's "No German university would make him a professor" is false. Hamburg made Wegener an außerordentlicher Professor in 1921. He never held a full chair in Germany.
(5) s076 has "the Atlantic" unzipping south first with the last seam at the equator. That is only true of the South Atlantic. The central Atlantic opened first, and the North Atlantic last, about 55 million years ago.
(6) s079, s080 and s093 state the Gondwana "scars" answer as settled fact. It rests on one medium-confidence expert answer and no peer-reviewed study, so it needs a story-style hedge. "Kept their orientation" also needs "roughly".
The smaller fixes are wording: "predicted" should be "explained"; "same shape" should be "alike"; Forster's "noticed" should be "claimed", and the shot should not put Agulhas under his "high and rocky" line; Baja moves "away from mainland Mexico"; Florida is a carbonate platform, not a reef; the Blue Marble is "one of" the most famous photos; one Nevada scientist, not "the" scientist; Holden did not cite de Kay; and "if" Africa splits, not "when". Checks I made: the Cape of Good Hope sign does read "most south-western point" (confirmed), Green was foreign minister in 1875 (confirmed), "carefully buried" is supported by NASA, and the Agulhas compass story is hedged correctly.

issues.problem: 'All over the planet, land and ocean seem to avoid each other' says the opposite of the fact. Land sits opposite ocean almost everywhere; what avoids land on the far side is other land (numbers-10, numbers-12). The visual itself shows flipped land repelling real land. Also, numbers-13 says most of the effect comes from the poles, so 'all over the planet' overstates it.
issues.fix: Say that land almost always has ocean, not land, on its far side. See rewrite.

issues.problem: 'North America sits exactly opposite the Indian Ocean' is false. numbers-21 has Canada opposite Antarctica over about 579,000 sq mi and Greenland opposite Antarctica over about 688,000 sq mi; only the lower 48 is about 99.99% opposite the Indian Ocean (numbers-24). Gregory's 1899 'exactly' was his own overstatement, and 'He even pointed out' endorses it. It also contradicts s035, whose overlay shows the Antarctica / Arctic-lands overlap. The visual ('lands entirely in the Indian Ocean') repeats the error.
issues.fix: Say 'most of North America'. On screen: 'MOST OF NORTH AMERICA <-> INDIAN OCEAN'. In the visual, the lower 48 and Mexico land in the Indian Ocean while Greenland and Arctic Canada land on Antarctica.

issues.problem: Chronology error. Coming after the 1899 (s050) and 1918 (s052) beats, 'Then scientists discovered radioactivity' places the discovery after 1918. Radioactivity was discovered in 1896, and radiogenic heat in rocks was recognised around 1903–1906; contraction theory faded over the following decades (Holmes 1925; science-5 says 'faded out', with no single year). The visual note 'shrinking arrows stall and reverse' would also suggest an expanding Earth, which is pseudoscience. Earth is still cooling slowly.
issues.fix: Say radioactivity was discovered around the turn of the century and the shrinking engine stalled over the following decades. In the visual, the arrows stall and fade but never reverse.

issues.problem: 'No German university would make him a professor' is contradicted by a reputable source. German Wikipedia: '1921 wurde er dort zum außerordentlichen Professor an der neu gegründeten Universität Hamburg berufen.' NASA's line ('could not get a professorship at any German university') is loose. What holds up: he never got a full chair in Germany, and Graz (Austria) gave him one in 1924 (science-12 caveat).
issues.fix: 'In Germany, he never landed a full professorship. It took a university in Austria to give him one.'

issues.problem: 'The Atlantic unzips from the bottom up... The last seam, near the equator' holds only for the South Atlantic (science-18, whose spoken_form says 'the Atlantic between Africa and South America'). The central Atlantic (North America–Africa) opened in the Jurassic, before the South Atlantic. The last part to open was the North Atlantic between Greenland and Europe, about 54–56 Ma (science-23), long after the equatorial seam broke around 103 Ma. As written it is false for 'the Atlantic'. The on-screen text repeats it.
issues.fix: Name the South Atlantic, between Africa and South America. On screen: 'THE SOUTH ATLANTIC UNZIPS NORTHWARD'.

issues.problem: The video's central answer is stated as settled fact ('they kept their orientation. Their points still aim back toward the South Pole'). The ledger rates it medium (science-21). It rests on one Ask-a-Geologist answer quoted from a search index, and we found no peer-reviewed study that explains the taper. The owner override requires uncertain science to be hedged in story terms. 'Kept their orientation' is too strong: Nield says 'general orientation', and South America and India rotated substantially during drift (the classic Bullard fit rotates South America about 57° relative to Africa). They tore away from Antarctica, which is at the pole only today.
issues.fix: Open with a hedge ('Here's the best explanation geologists have'), say 'roughly kept their orientation', and aim the trails at Antarctica rather than 'the South Pole'. s080 can stay as written once s079 carries the hedge.

issues.problem: The verdict again states 'The big drips are history: scars...' as fact (science-21 is medium). 'Some of it is probably just us, connecting dots' has no evidence in the ledger: pattern-26 is only Vsauce's opinion, and Somerville 1848 actually claims 'almost all' peninsulas tend south. 'Probably' asserts a likelihood the video never supports.
issues.fix: 'Most likely' for the scars, and 'may' for pattern-seeking. See rewrite.

issues.problem: 'A theory... that predicted all of it' overclaims. Green's theory was built to explain features already known, such as land massing in the north and the southern points (science-1 says 'explained'). Only the polar items were arguably confirmed later. The same overclaim recurs in s048 ('watch what it predicted') and s053 ('If it predicted all that').
issues.fix: s009: 'that seemed to predict all of it'. s048: 'watch what it explained'. s053: 'If it explained all that'.

issues.problem: 'Watch what it predicted': the checklist items were known observations the theory was designed around, not predictions.
issues.fix: 'But watch what it {m:pred}explained.'

issues.problem: 'If it predicted all that' carries the same predicted/explained overclaim.
issues.fix: 'So, hang on. If it explained all that, {m:how}how do we know it's wrong?'

issues.problem: 'They're the same shape' overstates Bacon. He wrote 'similar isthmus and similar capes', both broad to the north and narrow to the south (pattern-3, pattern-6). The on-screen 'SAME SHAPE.' repeats it.
issues.fix: 'shaped alike'. On screen: 'NOT PUZZLE PIECES. LOOKALIKES.'

issues.problem: 'Bacon saw the drip, but couldn't explain it' implies he tried and failed. Bacon offered no cause; he listed it as an example of a resemblance in nature (pattern-1 caveat).
issues.fix: 'So Bacon saw the drip, but never tried to explain it. For a very long time, nobody else could. And boy, did they try.'

issues.problem: 'Forster noticed that every great southern tip looks alike' turns Forster's generalisation into an observation the narration endorses. It is not true for every tip; Cape Agulhas, for example, is a low 'rocky headland'. Forster's 'high and rocky' cape was the Cape of Good Hope (pattern-10). The visual lights Cape Agulhas and draws a chain 'running north' from it, but the Cape Fold Belt runs east–west there.
issues.fix: 'claimed' instead of 'noticed'. For this beat only, highlight Forster's own example (Cape of Good Hope / Table Mountain chain) labelled as his pick, or drop the north-running chain line from the African tip.

issues.problem: 'A geologist took that joke even further' implies Holden built on de Kay. Holden's 1976 reference list (ASBS reprint) cites Deetz & Adams, Dietz & Holden, Morgan and Wegener, not de Kay. Morrison (1991) calls them two 'competing models', and Wikipedia says Holden made 'his own version'. s081 has the same problem.
issues.fix: 'Three years later, a geologist published his own version of the joke.' s081: 'The geologist behind the second continental drip joke was named John Holden.'

issues.problem: 'Just off New Zealand' is stretched. The 1945 centre is about 45 mi from the Bounty Islands but hundreds of miles from the main islands, and the modern optimum is about 270 mi east of the North Island. The numbers-9 caveat says to use 'near' or 'southeast of New Zealand'.
issues.fix: 'centered in the empty Pacific near New Zealand.'

issues.problem: 'The drip is just the part you can see' asserts that the drip and the antipodal lopsidedness share one cause. The ledger does not support that (numbers-13: 'does NOT prove a cause'), and s094 later says there is no deep force.
issues.fix: '...and the drip might be just the part you can see.'

issues.problem: 'The first sliver of new ocean opens between Africa and Antarctica' can be heard as the first ocean anywhere in Gondwana's breakup. Jokat (science-17) only says the first oceanic crust between Africa and Antarctica formed about 155 Ma. The West Somali Basin (Africa–Madagascar) may be as old or older, and its age is debated.
issues.fix: 'Cracks open, and new ocean starts seeping in between Africa and Antarctica.'

issues.problem: 'Dragging it away from Mexico': Baja is part of Mexico. The source says 'away from mainland Mexico' (science-24). The on-screen text has the same issue.
issues.fix: 'away from mainland Mexico'. On screen: 'BAJA: TORN FROM MAINLAND MEXICO'.

issues.problem: 'Reef platform' is geologically loose. NOAA (science-25) describes a carbonate platform of limestone and dolomite produced by organisms in warm, shallow water, which is not the same thing as a reef. A geology-literate viewer will object.
issues.fix: Use 'limestone platform'. On screen: 'FLORIDA: A GIANT LIMESTONE PLATFORM'.

issues.problem: 'The most famous photo of Earth ever taken' is a superlative. Wikipedia says 'one of the most reproduced images in history'. 'It got flipped, because that's how we're used to seeing it' gives a reason that no source in the ledger states (future-visuals-18 is medium).
issues.fix: 'One of the most famous photos of Earth ever taken... It got flipped to match the maps we're used to.'

issues.problem: Two problems. 'The scientist who found it': Fouch was one of four authors (West et al. 2009; the first author is West). 'A cold blob of rock is sinking' is stated flatly, but the science-29 caveat says the interpretation has been debated.
issues.fix: 'appears to be sinking' and 'One of the scientists who found it'.

issues.problem: 'Stayed livable' reads like an observed outcome. It is a model projection (8–16% habitable; one study).
issues.fix: 'would stay livable'.

issues.problem: 'What happens when Africa splits in two?' presents the split as certain. Rifts can fail (science-22 caveat: the Benue Trough is a 'failed arm'), and the ledger only says Africa 'starts to split'.
issues.fix: 'What happens if Africa splits in two?'

issues.problem: The visual note labels the last Wegener–Villumsen photo '(1930, PD, AWI archive)'. The ledger (science-14) and NASA credit it 'Photograph copyright Alfred-Wegener Institute'. The Commons mirror's PD-70 tag is doubtful because the credited authors (Loewe, Georgi) died in the 1970s.
issues.fix: Check the licence on the live Commons page, or clear it with AWI, before use. Otherwise use a verified-PD expedition image or a recreated still.

issues.problem: The visual says China's flip leaves only 'a sliver on Argentina and Chile'. The real figure is about 27% of China (numbers-25): a quarter, not a sliver. That matters because the line says 'three times out of four'.
issues.fix: Show about a quarter of the flipped China landing on Argentina and Chile.

issues.problem: Visual: the 'shrinking arrows stall and reverse' (see the s054 major issue) would show an expanding Earth.
issues.fix: The arrows stall and fade. No outward arrows.

issues.problem: The on-screen '~2 MILES UP' rounds 1.76 mi (9,301 ft) up to 2 and does not match the spoken 'almost two miles'.
issues.fix: 'SOUTH POLE: NEARLY 2 MILES UP'.

issues.problem: 'Bacon said the likeness of Africa and South America wasn't an accident. He was half right.' Under the video's own answer, Africa's and South America's tapers are scars, so for the specific thing Bacon said he would be fully right; 'half' works only for the whole drip pattern. It also leaves out the other half of Bacon's claim, the matching necks of land (isthmuses).
issues.fix: Optionally ground the 'half' by naming the isthmus in s013: '...Africa and South America's matching necks of land and matching capes were...'. Or keep s105 and accept it as loose rhetoric about the drip as a whole.

issues.problem: 'It's far too weak' borrows science-13, which is about Wegener's spin force failing to move continents. The cleaner reason spin can't cause the drip is that its centrifugal pull is mirror-symmetric about the equator: it pushes toward the equator in both hemispheres, so it cannot favour south. As written the line is defensible but incomplete.
issues.fix: Optional: 'But spin tugs on both halves of the planet the same way, and it's far too weak to move a continent.'

issues.problem: 'Every week' is a factual promise about upload cadence that cannot be verified (the head-writer flagged it too).
issues.fix: Use 'Every video' unless a weekly schedule is confirmed.

issues.problem: Title 1, 'Why the Continents All Point South', overclaims, and the video itself refutes 'All' in s087. Thumbnail 3, 'ALL POINT HERE', includes Australia, but science-21 says Australia 'points' north (Cape York).
issues.fix: Prefer titles 2–5, or 'Why Most Continents Point South (It's Not Just Luck)'. Drop the Australia slab from thumbnail 3, or keep it unarrowed.

rewrites.new_text: And it's not just the poles. Almost everywhere you look, land has {m:avoid}ocean on its far side, not more land. Which brings us to a classic American playground myth.
rewrites.why: Fixes the inverted 'land and ocean avoid each other' and drops the 'all over the planet' overstatement (numbers-10, numbers-12, numbers-13).

rewrites.new_text: He even pointed out that most of North America sits opposite the {m:io}Indian Ocean. The same ocean you just dug into.
rewrites.why: Arctic Canada and Greenland are opposite Antarctica (numbers-21). Only 'most' is true. On screen: 'MOST OF NORTH AMERICA <-> INDIAN OCEAN'.

rewrites.new_text: Because the whole idea needed a cooling, shrinking Earth. But {m:rad}radioactivity, discovered just before the turn of the century, heats the planet from the inside. Over the next few decades, the shrinking engine stalled.
rewrites.why: Radioactivity was discovered in 1896, before the 1899 and 1918 beats; contraction theory faded over decades (science-5). Visual: the arrows stall and fade, never reverse.

rewrites.new_text: When the rest of the world read it, the reaction was brutal. One society president called it {m:rot}'utter, damned rot.' In Germany, he never landed a full professorship. It took a university in Austria to give him one.
rewrites.why: Wegener was made außerordentlicher Professor at Hamburg in 1921, but never held a full chair in Germany. Graz gave him one in 1924 (science-12 caveat).

rewrites.new_text: Then the {m:zip}South Atlantic unzips from the bottom up, splitting Africa from South America. The south tears open first. The last seam, near the equator, hangs on for millions of years more.
rewrites.why: The south-to-north zipper applies only to the South Atlantic (science-18). The central Atlantic opened earlier and the North Atlantic later (science-23). On screen: 'THE SOUTH ATLANTIC UNZIPS NORTHWARD'.

rewrites.new_text: Here's the best explanation geologists have. The pieces drifted apart, but roughly kept their orientation. Their points still {m:aim}aim back toward Antarctica, where they tore away.
rewrites.why: The core answer is medium confidence (science-21: one expert, no peer-reviewed study). The owner rule asks for a story-style hedge. 'Roughly' reflects the real rotations during drift, and 'Antarctica' replaces 'the South Pole'.

rewrites.new_text: So, the verdict. The big drips are most likely history: scars from a supercontinent that tore apart around {m:v_ant}Antarctica. The small drips have no single answer. And some of it may just be us, connecting dots.
rewrites.why: Hedges the medium-confidence answer. The ledger has no evidence for 'probably pattern-seeking', so 'may' is the honest level.

rewrites.new_text: A theory from {m:t1875}eighteen seventy-five that seemed to predict all of it, and was dead wrong. And the last one: the continent your country is going to {m:crash}crash into. Eventually.
rewrites.why: Green explained features already known (science-1); 'seemed to predict' keeps the hook without overclaiming.

rewrites.new_text: It sounds ridiculous. But watch what it {m:pred}explained. Most land in the north: {m:c1}check. Three continents ending in points aimed south: {m:c2}check.
rewrites.why: Explained, not predicted (science-1).

rewrites.new_text: So, hang on. If it explained all that, {m:how}how do we know it's wrong?
rewrites.why: Consistent with s048. The theory was retrofitted to known features.

rewrites.new_text: He wasn't snapping Africa and South America together like puzzle pieces. He was saying they're shaped {m:same}alike, side by side.
rewrites.why: Bacon said 'similar', not identical (pattern-3, pattern-6). On screen: 'NOT PUZZLE PIECES. LOOKALIKES.'

rewrites.new_text: So Bacon saw the drip, but never tried to explain it. For a very long time, nobody else could. And boy, did they try.
rewrites.why: Bacon gave no cause (pattern-1 caveat); 'couldn't' implies he tried.

rewrites.new_text: Captain Cook's naturalist, Johann Reinhold Forster, claimed that every great southern tip looks alike: high, rocky, the end of a {m:mtn}mountain chain.
rewrites.why: It is Forster's generalisation, not a fact the narrator should endorse. Cape Agulhas, for example, is low. In the visual, show Forster's own capes (Cape of Good Hope) for this beat.

rewrites.new_text: Three years later, a geologist published his own version of the joke. Hold on to him. He matters more than you'd think.
rewrites.why: Holden's 1976 paper does not cite de Kay. Morrison (1991) treats them as separate 'competing models', and Wikipedia says 'his own version'.

rewrites.new_text: Which brings us back to that joke. The geologist behind the second continental drip joke was named John {m:holden}Holden.
rewrites.why: Same reason as s023. No evidence that Holden built on de Kay.

rewrites.new_text: Now flip the globe {m:flip}over. The other half is {m:p89}eighty-nine percent water, centered in the empty Pacific near New Zealand.
rewrites.why: The numbers-9 caveat says to use 'near' or 'southeast of'. The centre is hundreds of miles from the main islands.

rewrites.new_text: Ocean on top, land at the bottom. Land that avoids land. It's a planet that looks strangely {m:lop}lopsided, and the drip might be just the part you can see.
rewrites.why: The ledger gives no shared cause for the drip and the antipodal pattern (numbers-13: unusual, not causal).

rewrites.new_text: Now let the clock run forward. Cracks open, and new ocean starts seeping in between {m:afant}Africa and Antarctica.
rewrites.why: Avoids claiming this was the first ocean in all of Gondwana. The West Somali Basin may be as old or older (science-17 only covers Africa–Antarctica).

rewrites.new_text: Some smaller drips have stories all their own. Several million years ago, the Pacific Plate grabbed {m:baja}Baja and started dragging it away from mainland Mexico. It's still going.
rewrites.why: Baja is in Mexico (science-24 says 'mainland Mexico'). On screen: 'BAJA: TORN FROM MAINLAND MEXICO'.

rewrites.new_text: {m:fla}Florida isn't a drip at all. It's the top of a gigantic limestone platform, miles thick, built up by sea life in warm, shallow water. And under all that limestone sits bedrock that started out next to {m:wafr}West Africa.
rewrites.why: It is a carbonate platform, not a reef (science-25), and 2–6 km thick, so 'miles thick' holds. The Gondwana basement wording matches science-26. On screen: 'FLORIDA: A GIANT LIMESTONE PLATFORM'.

rewrites.new_text: Even 'down' is our own invention. One of the most famous photos of Earth ever taken was shot with {m:bm}Antarctica on top. It got flipped to match the maps we're used to.
rewrites.why: Wikipedia says 'one of the most reproduced images'. No source in the ledger gives the reason it was flipped.

rewrites.new_text: And here's one more irony. 'Continental drip' started as a joke, but geologists have since found {m:realdrip}real drips. Under Nevada, a cold blob of rock appears to be sinking into the Earth like honey off a spoon. One of the scientists who found it admitted he'd been 'anti-drip' since his early days.
rewrites.why: It was a four-author paper, and the interpretation has been debated (science-29 caveat).

rewrites.new_text: One study ran the climate on one of these future supercontinents. Only about {m:tenth}one-tenth of the land would stay livable for mammals.
rewrites.why: It is a model projection, not an observed outcome (future-visuals-7).

rewrites.new_text: What happens if Africa splits in two? That's Part Two, right {m:here}here. And if you want to watch the map keep changing, subscribe.
rewrites.why: Rifts can fail. The ledger only says Africa 'starts to split' (science-22).

rewrites.new_text: You'd think Earth's {m:spin}spin did this. But spin tugs on both halves of the planet the same way, and it's far too weak to move a continent. A video with tens of millions of views called it {m:coin}just a coincidence.
rewrites.why: Optional. Adds the mirror-symmetry reason that spin can't single out south. 'Far too weak' keeps the s061 callback (science-13).

result.verdict:
Comedy and animation lens: 7/10. The draft does well on the basics. All 10 Explorer gags use real clip names, and most of them illustrate the point instead of interrupting it (the flood, the dig, the pyramid slide, being left on Antarctica, picking a neighbor). The Holden material is funny on its own merits, and there are no jokes during Wegener's death in s063-s068, which is the right call. The draft still has problems in four areas.
(1) Four gags have mechanical problems. s003 does not land on its line and spills into the s004 data beat. Interact on a loop will not read as digging in s031. Run_Back is the wrong clip for a hamster-wheel run in s090. Nobody can "glare" in s069.
(2) The s054 kick does not support the point. Radioactivity killed the pyramid idea, not a kick, and the gag plays over the densest explanation in Chapter 3. I replace it with a payoff to gag 5.
(3) There is a gap of about 90 s with no laugh, from the DRIP typewriter (~2:40) to the dig (~4:10). This is the opening of Chapter 2, which is the most important stretch for keeping viewers. I fill it with a North Pole beat that also replaces the Explorer's idle shot used only for scale.
(4) Several lines only smile where they could get a laugh (s012, s017, s019, s041, s077, s083, s103), and the cartoon sound effects are overused for this dry register.
With the rewrites below, the laughs land at about 0:08, 0:45, 1:13, 1:54, 2:11, 2:40, 3:10, 4:10-4:40, 5:40, 6:28, 7:11, 7:28, 8:22, 9:30, 10:33, 10:40, 11:20, 11:56, 12:25, 12:35, 13:35, 14:40 and 14:50. Leaving the death sequence aside, that is one about every 45-75 s. The count stays at 10 Explorer beats:
1. s003, catching the drip
2. s019, soaked by the flood
3. s025, NEW: North Pole vertigo
4. s031-032, the dig
5. s041, riding Australia
6. s047+s054, the pyramid ride and bounce (replaces the kick)
7. s060, recoiling from "rot"
8. s077, keeping the house
9. s090, the flip run with the Holden callback
10. s102-103, picking a neighbor and the mammal faint
Every rewrite keeps spoken numbers as words, 1-4 sentences per segment, on-screen text within limits, and no sources. Where a new joke states a fact, the fact is already in the ledger. The Santa, dashboard, refund, time-zone and reckless-driving lines are framed as jokes, not claims.

That puts comedy on top of a data reveal in the cold open (Lang overload). The 'out in the sun' simile is also generic.

The Explorer stands on Cape Agulhas on the Little-Prince Earth. A fat orange droplet swells under the tip. He leans out to catch it (Interact). It slips past his fingers with a plink and he wobbles at the edge (HitRecieve_2). Drop Run_Back. Raise pause_after from 0.4 to 0.8 so the gag finishes before s004. result.verdict: The draft has strong hook parts. Line 1 ("Spin a globe, and Earth looks like it's melting") is a scroll-stopper, frame 1 is the thumbnail in motion, the seven tip-pops are real visual proof, there's a joke and an Explorer gag by 0:10, the promise matches the title's wording, the China teaser hits the viewer's identity ("anywhere in America"), and the cut to black on "Eventually." is a great button. Four things fail my lens. (1) Length. Counting the 7-pop list at about 0.8 s per pop, the promise question doesn't start until about 0:32 and finishes about 0:38, content (Bacon) starts about 1:04, and Bacon's "not ... mere accident" (the title/thumbnail claim) lands about 1:31. Targets are: promise by 0:30, content by about 0:48, claim proven by 1:00. (2) The myth→refutation step is weak and logically leaky. s005 stacks two unproven refutations, spin ("far too weak") and the coincidence myth. "It isn't" comes right after the northern-land stat, so it reads as saying the northern pile-up isn't a coincidence, which s094 later contradicts ("a snapshot"). That is exactly the attentive-viewer letdown that hurts valued watch time. (3) Packaging honesty: "All" in title 1 is contradicted by s087's own list of exceptions. "Melting" in title 6 reads as climate change. "It's NOT the Spin" is never proven early. (4) The subscribe ask promises "every week", and the comment prompt sits between the wonder line and the cliffhanger. My rewrite of s001–s013 (78 words in the cold open) changes the hook to: thumbnail image → visual proof → stakes → the myth the viewer actually holds, limited to the points → refutation with a 1-s visual flash → a sharper promise tied to the thumbnail's ring. Estimated at 2.7 words/s: promise question about 0:27, promise done about 0:33, Bacon about 0:53, "not ... mere accident" about 1:08, first JUICE CHECK about 1:25. Fixed versions of the titles, thumbnails, subscribe ask and comment prompt are below. Timing notes are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/script/hook-packaging/ (timing.py, rewrite_open.json).
